entry.title: An Appetite for Experience
entry.content:
An Appetite for Experience

A personal essay on what I love, how I keep it, and what I want next

Personal essay · one appetite, traced through what I take in, what I make, and what I wish for

Andraž Đurič

Version 1 · June 2026

I consume a lot, and widely. Films, series, animation, anime, manga, comics, and books that run from science fiction to philosophy. There are few genres and few forms I have no appetite for, and if you asked me to the opera I would come. The two I love most are video games and anime. For a long time I described myself as an entertainment enthusiast and left it there, but that is only the surface. Under the breadth there is a single appetite, and naming it is the point of this essay. I want the widest and deepest range of experience I can get, both taking it in and making it. Almost everything below is one face of that.

A note on what this is, so it is not mistaken for something else. This is a personal essay. I am describing what I love and what I want, not arguing that anyone else should want the same, and not claiming any of it is correct. Whether chasing more and more vivid experience is the right thing to aim at is a real question, and it is out of scope here. I am drawing a map of an appetite, not defending it.

What I take in

The breadth is not indecision. It is the appetite showing its range. I would rather have the whole spread than a narrow shelf, and I resent almost nothing in it. Sport is the one place the appetite goes quiet, watching or playing, and I have made my peace with that. Within the spread, games and anime are where it runs deepest, and the reason is immersion. I do not play or watch at arm's length. I let myself be fully inside it, because the more completely I am in an experience the more it gives back. Intensity is not a side effect for me. It is the point.

Why I protect play

Play is not a break from my life. I treat it as one of the load-bearing parts. Other animals play, and I think play belongs in the same category of need as rest and food and water, not a notch below them. So I protect it, and I protect it without guilt.

The way I protect it is deliberate. The work in my life, the job inside this system and the obligations outside it that I would not choose, are real strains, and some of them simply leave my mind empty. So I watch myself. I keep an eye on my own patterns and my tiredness, I try to be as honest with myself as I can about how close to burnout I am, and when the signs start to show I inject more play. I will admit the method is rough. It runs on something close to vibes and it is open to every bias I have, and that is the most I can claim for it. But it has worked. I have not burned out, and I have produced more, and better, than at any point in my life.

Here is the part I want to be exact about, because it is easy to get wrong. The balance does make my work better, and that is true, but it is not why I do it, and it is not what play is for. If play were only fuel for work it would not be guilt-free. It would be one more task in a costume. Play is a good in its own right that I happen to also be able to spend, and the self-monitoring is not a productivity trick. It is how I keep an engine I love from burning out, so that I get to keep loving it.

What I make

I do not only take experience in. I make it, and the making is the same appetite from the other side. I know a fair number of the tools. I can model in 3D, do graphic design and the interface and experience side of websites, and I can draw, paint, and sculpt. None of them holds me the way building worlds in Minecraft does.

I know how that can sound, so I will say it plainly: it is the best canvas we have right now. A drawing or a model is a picture of an experience. A Minecraft world is one you can walk inside and see from any angle. I can build the structures, the schematics, the stories, the texture packs, the mods, and then fold them into a single thing a person can step into and move through. The whole world is a sandbox, and what I value is exactly that you are not looking at the thing I made, you are standing in it.

What I want next

My wishes are the same appetite thrown forward, and there are two.

The first is that the world move faster toward post-scarcity, so that the hours people now spend staying alive could go to thinking and making instead. I see artificial intelligence as the most likely key to that, the thing that could meet everyone's basic needs and then raise the floor from there. For me it would mean, plainly, the freedom to give as much time as I wanted to the intellectual and creative work I care about.

The second is the one people will file under science fiction, and we will see about that. I want brain-computer interfaces and simulated reality fully matured, and I want to live through thousands of fully realized, high-fidelity stories, indistinguishable from the real thing, with the freedom to step inside them and shape where they go. I would want to enter worlds like Attack on Titan or Frieren and act within them, not only watch. And I would want the medium mature in the full sense, able to hold the whole range of adult life rather than a sanitized slice of it, with each story open to be remade in countless directions, since the intelligence behind it could author them. That is the ceiling on experience coming off entirely, which is the thing the whole appetite has been reaching toward the whole time.

So that is the shape of it. One appetite, for as much experience as I can take in and as much as I can make, running through what I consume, how I play, what I build, and what I hope is coming. The balance I keep now, work and immersion held in proportion, is a small working prototype of the life I would want if the ceiling came off. Until the technology catches up to the wider wish, I will keep the balance, keep building worlds block by block, and keep letting myself be all the way inside the ones I step into. That is enough to be going on with.

Author: Andraž Đurič, Slovenia. Written in collaboration with Claude (Anthropic). Personal essay, offered as description rather than argument. Licensed CC BY 4.0.
entry.blogger:metaDescription: An appetite for deep immersion: from treating play as a load-bearing need to lifting the technological ceiling on reality.

entry.title: Relata-Indexed Objectivity
entry.content:
Relata-Indexed Objectivity

Why objectivity is not contextlessness, how claims become answerable to reality, and where indexing stops

Position and research-program note · objectivity, relations, levels, agency, logic, semantics, and falsification

Andraž Đurič

Version 1 · July 2026

Abstract

This essay develops a claim that has been implicit across the Epistemic Forge corpus: objectivity is not the absence of a frame, but the accurate specification of the relations that make a claim determinate.

The motivating slogan is that everything is objective once it is indexed correctly. Stated without qualification, that is too broad. The defensible version separates facts from claims. Relational, level-specific, agent-involving, and perspective-dependent facts can be objective. A truth-apt claim about them becomes objectively assessable when its minimally sufficient index fixes the relevant bearer, relata, level, boundary, coupling, frame, horizon, resolution, and uncertainty.

This yields a diagnostic. Many philosophical and semantic confusions arise when a relational or level-bound term is stripped of the structure that gives it truth conditions and then treated as an intrinsic, contextless property. The repair is localization: restore the missing index, distinguish the level, and identify what would make the claim true or false. The result may be a resolved claim, a split into several claims, a genuine open problem, a term whose ordinary context was merely implicit, or, in the strongest cases, an ill-formed residue with no stable truth conditions.

The account is physicalist and non-eliminative about levels. One ontology does not require one vocabulary. Higher-level patterns can be physically realized and still be real at the scale where they support explanation, prediction, intervention, or compression.

The method is bounded. It does not yet dissolve the phenomenal remainder of consciousness, does not justify logic from outside all inference, and does not by itself establish that persistence exhausts value. It is therefore presented as a position and a falsifiable research program, not as a universal solvent or completed scientific result.

1. The claim

The claim began in its most compressed form:

Everything is objective once you index it right.

The sentence points in the right direction, but it collapses several different theses.

Not every utterance is truth-apt. A command, expression, promise, question, or work of fiction may perform a function other than describing a state of affairs. Not every vague sentence becomes meaningful merely by adding detail. Not every interpretation can be rescued by inventing a frame after the fact. And indexing does not make a false external-world claim true.

The more precise position has two parts.

The first is ontological:

A fact does not cease to be objective merely because it is relational, level-specific, frame-dependent, agent-involving, or accessible from an asymmetrical perspective.

The second is semantic and epistemic:

A determinate truth-apt claim becomes objectively assessable when its minimally sufficient index fixes what it is about and what would make it true or false.

These claims are related but not identical.

The first concerns what kinds of facts can obtain. The second concerns what a sentence must specify, explicitly or through recoverable context, before evidence and argument can bear on it.

Objectivity, on this account, is not a magical property added by removing every relation. It is answerability to reality once the relevant relations have been located.

2. The observer belongs inside some descriptions

A familiar picture of objectivity begins by removing the observer.

Often that is correct. The chemical composition of a sample does not ordinarily vary with the observer's preferences. Adding those preferences would obscure the target rather than clarify it.

But removal becomes distortion when the observer is one of the causal or constitutive relata of the phenomenon.

Pain is not adequately described by tissue damage alone while deleting the organism that undergoes it. Beauty is not exhausted by an arrangement of matter with no perceiver, perceptual system, history, or evaluative architecture. Meaning is not located in a mark alone, independently of the users, practices, and worldly structures it tracks. An ought is not found in the agent-blind substrate without the agent whose conditions distinguish success from failure.

The correct rule is conditional:

Remove the observer when the observer is irrelevant. Index the observer when the observer is part of the phenomenon.

Suppose someone reports a demon in the room.

At least three claims must be separated:

  1. an external entity of the reported kind was present;
  2. the agent underwent an experience representing such an entity as present;
  3. the process producing that representation reliably tracked the external environment.

The first may be false. The second may be true. The third may explain why the two diverged.

Indexing does not vindicate the demon. It locates the experience and prevents a fact about representation from being confused with a fact about the represented world.

Under physicalism, the subject and the experience remain processes within reality. Asymmetry of access is an epistemic difficulty, not automatic metaphysical exile.

Subjective states can be objective facts about subjects. Their being subject-involving does not make them arbitrary or unreal.

3. What the index contains

Correct indexing does not mean appending every available detail.

The aim is minimally sufficient localization: enough structure to fix the target, preserve the relevant level, and state the conditions under which the claim succeeds or fails.

The recurring components are these.

  • Bearer: what kind of thing could possess the attributed property?
  • Relata: what entities, states, systems, or practices are related?
  • Level: physical, chemical, biological, psychological, social, legal, semantic, mathematical, normative, phenomenological?
  • Boundary: what distinguishes the system from its environment or from neighbouring systems?
  • Coupling: how do the relata causally, informationally, functionally, representationally, or institutionally connect?
  • Frame or standard: which laws, rules, model, measurement procedure, criterion, or constitutive practice makes the claim assessable?
  • Horizon and resolution: over what time and at what grain is the claim made?
  • Uncertainty: what is known, estimated, inaccessible, underdetermined, or dependent on an unbuilt model?

Not every claim needs every item stated aloud. Ordinary language carries background context. “It is cold” can be perfectly usable when speaker, place, time, and practical standard are obvious. “The patient is improving” can be determinate within a clinical context even if the sentence does not restate the patient, condition, metrics, and observation interval.

Omission is not automatically absence. A missing explicit index may be recoverable from shared practice. The strongest diagnosis, that a term is ill-formed or a ghost, requires failed charitable reconstruction, not merely an abbreviated sentence.

The index is right when it does four things.

It fixes the referent.

It preserves the level at which the phenomenon exists.

It identifies the conditions relevant to truth or successful performance.

And it leaves the claim exposed to correction.

Too little indexing produces ambiguity. Too much produces a description so particular that it cannot generalize or be tested beyond one case.

The right index is the smallest specification that preserves the distinctions the task cannot afford to lose.

4. One reality, multiple levels

The ontological position underneath this account is physicalist monism: everything that exists is physically instantiated or reduces to physical structure.

This is not treated as logical certainty. It is the standing hypothesis judged to fit the explanatory record best, and it remains revisable if a genuine counterexample appears.

But one ontology does not require one vocabulary.

A Lego castle is made of acrylonitrile butadiene styrene. The chemical description is true. The architectural description is also true. Learning what the bricks are made of adds a level of explanation; it does not make the castle disappear.

The same structure appears in more serious cases.

Love is physically realized through bodies and nervous systems. A symphony is physically realized in instruments, air, media, and brains. Justice is physically realized through agents, institutions, rules, enforcement, expectations, and consequences.

Reduction in principle does not entail elimination in explanation.

A higher-level pattern can be fully physical and still be the correct object of explanation at the level where its organization becomes visible.

This is the point of The Exclusivity Error. The illegitimate move is not studying the substrate. It is adding the word “just” and treating lower-level realization as proof of upper-level unreality.

But the protection runs in both directions.

A term such as “justice,” “meaning,” “authority,” or “ought” cannot be saved from elimination by allowing it to float free of every bearer, implementation, relation, or practice. A higher-level term must identify something real.

The architecture therefore holds two commitments at once:

Do not collapse the upper floor into the basement.
Do not build an upper floor with nothing underneath it.

The first blocks eliminative flattening.

The second makes higher-level vocabulary pay rent.

5. Three ways indexing can go wrong

The wizard's error

The wizard searches for meaning, value, validity, purpose, or authority in the agent-blind substrate. Failing to find it there, the wizard relocates it outside physical reality.

Ought becomes a non-natural command.

Meaning becomes intrinsic aboutness.

Number becomes separate furniture.

Authority becomes a property of office that binds independently of what the office does.

The phenomenon is protected by delocalizing it.

But an entity defined as frame-independent and causally disconnected inherits familiar debts. How does a physical mind track it? What distinguishes one purported fact from its negation? What makes successful reference different from a coherent fiction? How could the representation be corrected?

The problem is not merely that the posit is difficult to verify. Its content and truth conditions may never have been supplied.

The flattener's error

The flattener moves in the opposite direction.

Because every phenomenon is physically realized, the flattener tries to read every higher-level distinction directly from the substrate.

Thermodynamics itself commands persistence. Chemistry proves an ethical verdict. Neural activity makes psychological language dispensable. A social institution is declared unreal because no single molecule contains it.

This fails because the substrate realizes every trajectory alike: persistence and dissolution, truth and hallucination, valid inference and error, care and destruction.

The relevant distinction appears only after a system, level, boundary, rule-space, or standard has been selected.

The rescue error

Indexing can also be abused in defence of a preferred conclusion.

A claim fails under one frame, so the frame is changed after the result. A counterexample appears, so the horizon is lengthened or shortened. The bearer is redrawn. The standard is replaced. The level is moved. Each adjustment is locally plausible, but together they ensure that no possible result can count against the claim.

This is not correct indexing. It is retrospective rescue.

An index must be declared or independently justified before it is used to protect a claim from failure. A frame that moves only when the conclusion is threatened is part of the error, not its repair.

A mature version of the method therefore requires stable indexing rules, adversarial cases, and explicit conditions under which the frame itself must change.

6. Name the Relata as a diagnostic

Name the Relata is the operational instrument inside the larger theory.

Take a disputed term or operator.

Ask what kind of thing could bear it.

Name the relata and the relation.

Specify the level, boundary, frame, coupling, horizon, and truth conditions relevant to the question.

Then classify what remains.

Resolved

The restored index produces a determinate claim that can be true, false, probabilistic, or currently unknown.

Bifurcated

The original sentence contained several claims at different levels or under different frames.

Implicitly indexed

The ordinary context already supplied the missing structure. The claim was abbreviated, not defective.

Ill-formed residue

After charitable reconstruction and consideration of plausible rival semantics, no stable bearer, relation, or truth condition can be supplied for a term that purported to state a fact.

Boundary

The diagnostic removes part of the confusion but leaves a genuine explanatory remainder.

Out of scope

The target is not a stripped relational term, or the utterance is performing a non-descriptive function for which truth and falsity are not the primary standards.

The last three outputs are essential.

Without “implicitly indexed,” the method mistakes ordinary linguistic economy for metaphysical failure.

Without “boundary,” it absorbs genuine open problems into its vocabulary.

Without “out of scope,” it becomes a universal solvent and therefore unfalsifiable.

The diagnostic succeeds when it discriminates. A method that calls every disagreement delocalization has stopped detecting a specific error.

7. The same structure across different domains

Subjective experience

“This hurts” is indexed to a subject, time, bodily and experiential state, and mode of access.

Its subject-dependence does not make the occurrence unreal. Another observer may lack direct access while still possessing indirect evidence through report, behaviour, physiology, and intervention.

The experience-fact and the external-cause fact must remain separate. A person can genuinely feel threatened while being wrong about the source of the threat.

Aesthetic judgment

“This is beautiful” may compress a relation among an object, a perceiver, perceptual capacities, affective state, history, culture, and evaluative standard.

Indexing does not force all aesthetic judgments into private whim. It allows objective questions about the relation: whether the experience occurred, whether it is stable across observers or conditions, which features produce it, how standards cluster, and whether a work succeeds under a declared artistic function.

The object may contribute strongly without carrying beauty as a contextless molecule-level property.

Meaning

A sign does not mean by shape alone.

Meaning involves some combination of producer, user, interpreter, inferential role, convention, causal history, context, function, and relation to what is tracked or represented.

Conceptual-role approaches correctly emphasize that content depends on how a term functions within an inferential web. Externalist and informational approaches correctly emphasize that an entirely self-contained web faces difficulty distinguishing world-directed content from internally coherent emptiness.

Relata-Indexed Objectivity predicts that an adequate account will require both internal role and some form of anchoring or use relation. That prediction is substantive and contested. It is not established merely by naming the relata.

Validity

Formal validity is indexed differently.

Given a formal system, axioms, and rules of inference, some conclusions follow and others do not. The physical token of the proof may be ink, sound, pixels, or neural activity; its validity is not identical to any one token.

Three questions must be separated:

  1. how the symbols and rule-following activity are physically instantiated;
  2. whether a conclusion follows inside the formal system;
  3. whether the system applies to a target structure in the world.

A theorem can be internally valid while a proposed application is inappropriate.

Metatheoretic claims introduce another level. A system's consistency, completeness, or soundness is investigated using some metatheory, which itself employs inferential norms. This does not make all formal systems equal. It means there is no completely inference-free tribunal from which inference as such can be certified.

Authority

Authority is not one intrinsic property.

It relates an authority, an agent subject to it, a domain, a decision, and a standard under which deference is warranted.

A doctor may have epistemic authority concerning a diagnosis while having no corresponding authority over the patient's politics. A court may possess legal authority under a jurisdiction while lacking moral or epistemic authority in a particular case. An institution can preserve distributed knowledge an individual does not possess, but it can also be corrupt, obsolete, or systematically misaligned.

The office is part of the social relation. It is not, by itself, the complete justification.

Modality

Possibility and necessity are usually indexed to a space of configurations, constraints, and laws.

What is physically possible may differ from what is logically possible, technologically possible, biologically viable, legally permitted, or reachable from a specified initial state.

Naming the modal space resolves many apparent contradictions.

It does not by itself answer the deeper question of why these laws or constraints obtain. The method is clean given a modal frame and open at the grounding of the frame itself.

8. The is/ought case

The is/ought problem is one of the central applications of the framework and one of its most exposed joints.

On the position developed in this corpus, there is no categorical ought that binds independently of every agent, system, constitution, environment, or horizon. The universe as such issues no commands.

An ought is instead indexed to an agent or agent-like system.

Once the agent, boundary, environment, capacities, persistence conditions, and horizon are fixed, there are physical facts about what sustains it, what damages it, what preserves its organization, and what drives it toward dissolution.

The proposed semantic reconstruction is:

Agent A ought to do X, under conditions C and over horizon H, insofar as X is required or favoured by the indexed standard governing A.

For the persistence account, that standard is ultimately tied to the continued organization of the agent.

This is not equivalent to prediction.

“The cell will climb the glucose gradient” predicts behaviour.

“The cell ought to climb the glucose gradient” states that climbing is what its viability conditions require in the functional sense at issue. The cell can fail and dissolve. The failed action falsifies the prediction while leaving the viability relation intact.

What this does not establish. Physicalism alone does not force this semantics of “ought.” One could instead adopt error theory, desire-based reasons, a different constitutivism, species-relative natural goodness, or another naturalized account. The persistence reading is the corpus's defended proposal, not a theorem obtained from monism alone.

Two further restrictions remain.

First, a local ought must not be promoted into a categorical one by silently deleting the agent. Removing the bearer does not universalize the claim. It removes part of its content.

Second, a structural reduction is not a specific verdict. Even if all value reduces in content to persistence, it does not follow that the relevant multi-scale model has already been built for this agent in this situation. Biology, psychology, social structure, institutions, coupling, uncertainty, and horizon may all matter.

The is/ought firewall therefore remains useful.

It is not a wall between two ontologies.

It records an indexing requirement and an unpaid modeling debt.

The stronger claim, that every value reduces in content to persistence, remains open. The present method locates that bet; it does not settle it.

9. Where indexing bottoms out

The method eventually reaches its own conditions.

If every claim requires a frame, what frames logic?

If every justification requires inference, what justifies inference?

An attempted answer cannot step outside every inferential norm at once, because arguing for or against a norm already uses some pattern of inference. Particular logics can be compared for consistency, expressive power, inferential consequences, domain fit, and practical success. But the comparison occurs within a metatheory that is not itself inference-free.

This is a form of epistemic circularity, but not every circularity is the same.

“P is true because P is true” is premise-circular. It pretends to supply support while repeating the conclusion.

“Any justification of inferential norms must use some inferential norms” identifies a constitutive limit. The activity of justification cannot certify all of its own conditions from a standpoint containing none of them.

Logic is not justified from outside all logic. Some inferential structure is part of what makes justification possible.

This does not prove that one specific logic is uniquely correct for every domain. It marks the level at which external validation gives way to comparison within shared inferential practice.

The same caution applies to existence and ultimate grounding.

We can ask why a particular state occurred, why these laws describe a domain, or what earlier structure generated an observable universe. Those are contentful questions within some causal or explanatory framework.

At the level of total reality, an external ground cannot be specified without ceasing to be external to the totality being described. That does not prove that all explanatory structure must be spatially outside, that reflexive explanation is impossible, or that reality has no internal generative order. It supports only the narrower conclusion: the ordinary demand for another external reason may bottom out or change meaning at the maximal frame.

“It is what it is” is not an explanation of contingent structure.

It is a limit marker.

The tautology says nothing about which world obtains. Its role is to show that, once every external term has been removed, repeating existence cannot provide another layer of explanation.

Relata-Indexed Objectivity therefore does not claim a view from outside all frames.

It applies the localization demand until localization reaches the constitutive conditions of inquiry, then marks the boundary rather than pretending to transcend it.

10. What the method does not yet solve

A bounded method must say where it stops.

Consciousness

Part of the consciousness problem may belong to the delocalization family.

A physically identical philosophical zombie is not a physically distinct alternative after every physical difference has been denied. Questions about report, access, integration, self-modeling, and the contrast between being a state and representing a state may also be clarified by separating levels and modes of access.

But a remainder persists:

Why is there felt experience at all?

It has not been established that this is merely another relation with a missing index. A theory of self-modeling may explain access and report without explaining phenomenal character.

The current classification is therefore “boundary,” not “resolved.”

Non-descriptive language

Not every meaningful utterance states a fact.

Commands direct. Promises commit. Questions request. Expressions display a state. Institutional declarations can alter social relations under accepted procedures.

These acts still have relata, conditions of success, and physical realization, but they should not all be forced into ordinary truth conditions. Their objectivity concerns whether the act occurred, what practice enabled it, what commitments followed, and whether its uptake succeeded.

Prototype and family-resemblance concepts

Some useful concepts may have graded or overlapping application rather than one necessary-and-sufficient essence.

Indexing can clarify which use is active without guaranteeing a perfectly sharp boundary. “Game,” “species,” “person,” “institution,” and “agent” may remain contested at the margins even when their central cases are clear.

A fuzzy boundary is not automatically a ghost.

The reach of the method

The method targets a family of errors: relational, frame-bound, level-specific, or bearer-dependent terms used as though they were contextless intrinsic properties.

It does not follow that every philosophical problem belongs to that family.

A method that explains everything by one error-shape has probably begun erasing differences the territory contains.

11. From philosophical thesis to research program

The framework should not be protected by elegance.

It should be run.

The empirical hypothesis is:

For claims in the diagnostic's intended class, restoring the relevant indices will improve identification of truth conditions, evidence, and the remaining point of disagreement beyond what is achieved by a generic clarification of equal length.

The null hypothesis is:

Relata-indexing adds a preferred vocabulary but produces no reliable improvement over ordinary careful rewriting, domain expertise, or generic requests for clarification.

A first study could construct a corpus of disputed claims from philosophy, ethics, law, politics, aesthetics, science, artificial intelligence, and ordinary argument.

Each claim would receive at least three versions:

  1. the original formulation;
  2. a length-matched generic clarification produced without the relata-indexing protocol;
  3. a version produced by the full protocol.

Where possible, a fourth version should be prepared by a domain expert who does not know which hypothesis is being tested.

Independent raters, blind to condition, would then answer questions such as:

  • What would make the claim true or false?
  • What evidence would bear on it?
  • Which entities or systems does it concern?
  • At which level is it asserted?
  • What exactly do opposing sides disagree about?
  • Is the claim meaningful, ambiguous, false, non-descriptive, or ill-formed?
  • How confident are you that another careful reader would interpret it the same way?

Possible measures include:

  • inter-rater agreement about truth conditions;
  • agreement about relevant evidence;
  • number of distinct interpretations elicited;
  • successful localization of the disagreement's crux;
  • false-positive “ghost” classifications;
  • transfer to new domains not represented in the training examples;
  • and whether the method improves later prediction, decision, or resolution rather than clarity ratings alone.

The test should include adversarial cases selected by critics of the framework, not only examples chosen because the method handles them well.

Classification rules and primary outcomes should be fixed before the results are inspected. Otherwise the rescue error returns at the level of the study.

Current status. No blinded human study has yet been run. The support is conceptual, comparative, and case-based. The research design is a proposal, not an empirical result.

12. Falsification and kill conditions

The framework can fail in several distinct ways.

Semantic counterexample

A term inside the claimed family performs stable explanatory work, supports determinate truth conditions, is trackable by physical agents, and still requires no relevant bearer, relation, frame, rule-space, law, practice, or coupling.

One clear case would force the diagnostic's scope to contract or its semantic premise to change.

No advantage over generic clarification

In blinded tests, the protocol performs no better than an equally careful ordinary rewrite on truth-condition identification, evidence selection, or crux localization.

In that case the theory may remain philosophically suggestive while failing as a distinct instrument.

Unreliable classification

Independent trained users cannot agree when the method applies, which indices are relevant, or whether an output is resolved, implicit, ill-formed, boundary, or out of scope.

A diagnostic whose outputs depend almost entirely on the operator's prior commitments has weak intersubjective standing.

Systematic overreach

The method repeatedly labels genuine unresolved phenomena as ghosts, especially when the phenomena resist the framework's preferred naturalization.

Consciousness is a standing pressure test here.

Index laundering

The framework's users can preserve any conclusion by redrawing boundaries, changing horizons, or replacing standards after counterexamples appear.

If no principled rule distinguishes legitimate re-indexing from retrospective rescue, the method becomes immunized against correction.

Normative collapse

The indexed ought turns out to add nothing beyond prediction, preference, or stipulated goal-following, while continuing to borrow the force of ordinary normative language.

Alternatively, categorical force is quietly reintroduced after being denied.

Either result would require revision of the is/ought application.

Level arbitrariness

The framework cannot distinguish a real higher-level pattern from an arbitrary redescription using explanatory, predictive, compressive, causal, functional, or intervention-relevant criteria.

Then “name the level” becomes permission to posit whatever level is convenient.

Failure of the foundation

The underlying physicalism would be broken by a real phenomenon shown not to be physical and not to reduce to physical structure.

This is a break-condition for the ontology, not for every local use of indexing. The two levels of failure should not be conflated.

13. What success would look like

The prediction is not that indexing will make people agree.

Two parties may share a precise formulation and still disagree about evidence, values, boundary choice, institutional aims, or acceptable risk.

The narrower success condition is:

Disagreement moves from semantic fog to explicit cruxes.

Instead of arguing whether justice is simply “real” or “fake,” disputants identify whether they disagree about agents, harms, entitlements, procedures, institutional functions, distribution rules, or standards.

Instead of arguing whether morality is “objective” in one undifferentiated sense, they distinguish categorical normativity, agent-relative requirements, social coordination rules, personal evaluations, and empirical consequences.

Instead of arguing whether logic is invented or discovered without qualification, they distinguish physical tokens, constitutive validity, rule selection, metatheory, and application to worldly structure.

Clarity is not yet truth.

But a claim whose bearer, level, evidence, and failure conditions are visible is in a better position to be corrected than one whose ambiguity protects it from contact.

The method succeeds scientifically only if this improvement can be demonstrated against controls.

It succeeds philosophically if it identifies a real and recurrent error-shape without pretending that every hard question has that shape.

14. The architecture, compressed

Reality is one, but it is not flat.

Its facts can be intrinsic or relational, local or distributed, level-specific, frame-dependent, agent-involving, and accessible through asymmetrical perspectives.

None of those properties alone makes a fact arbitrary or unreal.

A claim about such a fact becomes objectively assessable when enough of its structure is fixed for truth, falsity, uncertainty, or successful performance to have determinate conditions.

Many philosophical confusions arise when this structure is deleted.

The wizard mistakes absence at the substrate level for existence outside physics.

The flattener mistakes physical realization for the unreality of higher-level organization.

The rescuer moves the frame whenever a conclusion is threatened.

The repair is localization:

Name the bearer. Name the relata. Name the level. Draw the boundary. Specify the coupling, frame, horizon, resolution, and uncertainty. Then state what would make the claim succeed or fail.

Where this produces stable truth conditions, the claim becomes answerable.

Where it splits one sentence into several, the dispute becomes cleaner.

Where context was already implicit, ordinary language is left intact.

Where no stable content survives charitable reconstruction, the residue can be rejected as ill-formed.

Where a genuine remainder persists, the method stops.

At the deepest edge, logic cannot be justified from outside every inference, and total reality cannot be given an external ground without changing what “total” means. The architecture marks constitutive self-support and brute remainder rather than disguising them as completed explanation.

The whole position can be compressed into one sentence:

A claim earns objectivity by locating itself inside reality closely enough that reality can answer back.

That is Relata-Indexed Objectivity.

Not a view from nowhere.

A view that says exactly where it is.

Standing of this essay

This is a position and research-program note, not a completed scientific result.

The strongest part is the bounded claim that relational, level-specific, frame-dependent, and subject-involving facts can remain objective, and that many claims become more assessable when their relevant indices are made explicit.

The diagnostic claim is stronger and more exposed: that a recurring family of philosophical and semantic confusions is produced by stripping those indices and treating the residue as an intrinsic property or mystery. The method's value depends on whether that family can be identified reliably and whether the protocol outperforms generic clarification.

The physicalist and level-structured background is a standing, defeasible commitment. The account is reductive in ontology and non-eliminative in explanation: higher-level patterns do not become separate substances, but neither are they automatically replaced by lower-level descriptions.

The is/ought application remains conditional on the corpus's semantic proposal that practical oughts are agent-indexed requirements, ultimately grounded in persistence conditions. Physicalism does not force that proposal, and the stronger reduction of all value to persistence remains open.

Logic and ultimate grounding are treated as foundation-edge cases. The claim is not that every specific logical rule proves itself or that all why-questions are meaningless. It is that justification cannot validate all inference from an inference-free standpoint, and that an external ground of total reality cannot be named without changing the frame.

Consciousness remains the principal boundary case. The method may clarify access, representation, and zombie intuitions while leaving phenomenal character unexplained.

No blinded empirical study of the protocol has yet been conducted. The proposed research program, controls, measures, and kill conditions are included so that the framework can become vulnerable to evidence rather than protected by conceptual elegance.

The framework should be judged by whether it improves correction, not by how much territory it can absorb.

References

  1. Anderson, P. W. (1972). “More Is Different.” Science, 177(4047), 393–396. — higher-level organization and the limits of treating microphysical laws as complete replacements for special-science explanation. Standard
  2. Block, N. (1986). “Advertisement for a Semantics for Psychology.” Midwest Studies in Philosophy, 10, 615–678. — two-factor approaches to content, relevant to the distinction between internal role and external anchoring. Standard
  3. Dennett, D. C. (1991). “Real Patterns.” The Journal of Philosophy, 88(1), 27–51. — the reality of higher-level patterns where recognizing them earns explanatory and compressive return. Standard
  4. Fodor, J. A. (1974). “Special Sciences (or: The Disunity of Science as a Working Hypothesis).” Synthese, 28(2), 97–115. — autonomy and multiple realizability in higher-level sciences. Standard
  5. Foot, P. (1972). “Morality as a System of Hypothetical Imperatives.” The Philosophical Review, 81(3), 305–316. — the possibility that moral and practical oughts need not possess categorical force. Standard
  6. Giere, R. N. (2006). Scientific Perspectivism. University of Chicago Press. — scientific representation from located perspectives without collapse into arbitrariness. Standard
  7. Harman, G. (1982). “Conceptual Role Semantics.” Notre Dame Journal of Formal Logic, 23(2), 242–256. — conceptual-role semantics, the principal family of alternatives to a primarily referential account of content. Standard
  8. Hume, D. (1739–1740). A Treatise of Human Nature, Book III, Part I, Section I. — the classical is/ought passage and the inferential constraint the corpus accepts while rejecting a nonphysical normative realm. Standard
  9. Korsgaard, C. M. (1996). The Sources of Normativity. Cambridge University Press. — constitutivist attempts to ground normativity in the conditions of agency. Standard
  10. Mackie, J. L. (1977). Ethics: Inventing Right and Wrong. Penguin. — error theory and the challenge to objective categorical values. Standard
  11. Massimi, M. (2022). Perspectival Realism. Oxford University Press. — realism compatible with perspectival and model-mediated access. Standard
  12. Nagel, T. (1986). The View from Nowhere. Oxford University Press. — the tension and relation between subjective and objective standpoints. Standard
  13. Popper, K. R. (1963). Conjectures and Refutations. Routledge. — criticism, refutability, and the requirement that a research program expose itself to failure. Standard
  14. Tarski, A. (1933/1956). “The Concept of Truth in Formalized Languages.” In Logic, Semantics, Metamathematics. Oxford University Press. — object-language and metalanguage distinctions relevant to formal truth and metatheoretic ascent. Standard
  15. Wittgenstein, L. (1921). Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus, especially 4.461. — tautologies as showing logical form while saying nothing about contingent states of the world. Standard
  16. Wittgenstein, L. (1953). Philosophical Investigations. Blackwell. — meaning, use, language-games, and the role of practice in fixing the function of expressions. Standard
  17. Wittgenstein, L. (1969). On Certainty. Blackwell. — hinge commitments and the point at which ordinary justification depends on conditions not justified in the same ordinary way. Standard

Verification key: “Standard” means the work and attribution are treated as canonical and were not independently re-checked during this conversion pass. The references support the surrounding architecture; they do not jointly entail the synthesis developed here.

Internal lineage

This note isolates and develops a structure already distributed across the Epistemic Forge corpus.

  • Name the Relata supplies the bounded diagnostic and its principal semantic exposure.
  • The Wizard's Error Is Delocalization supplies the relocation of disputed phenomena from free-floating essence to framed relation.
  • The Exclusivity Error supplies the protection of higher-level patterns from eliminative flattening.
  • The Is/Ought Firewall supplies the agent index, the distinction between structural reduction and specific verdict, and the modeling debt.
  • Where the Is–Ought Question Bottoms Out supplies the foundation-edge questions of brute remainder, tautology, and self-support.
  • What Can Bear an Ought supplies the bearer condition and the extension from ought to desert and authority.
  • High-Fidelity Maps and Build Maps That Reality Can Correct supply the correction discipline under which a claim must expose its limits and failure conditions.
  • The Natural History of Fidelity, especially its section on frame-specified objectivity, contains the earlier compressed statement. The present note extracts that component, distinguishes its ontological and semantic claims, narrows its strongest formulations, and adds the explicit falsification program.
  • Value as Persistence supplies the live persistence reduction that this note locates but does not settle.

The contribution claimed here is synthetic and methodological: the positive theory that connects these pieces, the minimally sufficient index, the three error modes, the diagnostic output classes, and the empirical design by which the method could be distinguished from ordinary careful clarification.

Author: Andraž Đurič, Slovenia.

Developed through the Epistemic Forge corpus and dialogue with ChatGPT (OpenAI), following earlier work developed with Claude (Anthropic) and other systems. This version was produced through a hostile editorial pass intended to narrow overclaims, preserve explicit boundaries, distinguish ontological facts from the assessability of claims, prevent ordinary implicit context from being misclassified as semantic failure, and turn the diagnostic into a research program with controls and kill conditions. The author retains responsibility for the claims, framing, synthesis, and final text. Contributions are assessed by their content rather than their origin.
