● Attracts a smaller but more reflective audience.
● Encourages viewers to see themselves as capable of understanding, rather than as potential targets of ridicule.
● Spreads not just correct conclusions, but good methods of reasoning that people can reuse in their own conversations.

If even a small fraction of those viewers adopt that same patient, rigorous, and kind style in their own lives, the downstream effects may be larger than the immediate entertainment value of harsh, impatient takedowns.

From a wellbeing-based moral perspective, that seems like the more consistent path: to make people better reasoners while also making them feel respected and heard. The tradeoff in views or spectacle may be real, but the long-term epistemic and ethical payoff is likely higher.

In that sense, the criticism is not of Dillahunty’s intellect or his core moral framework, but of the tonal strategy often used in practice. If wellbeing is the metric, then the method of engagement should be optimized for it — not just the conclusions we argue for.



Disclaimer

Nothing in this piece is written from a position of moral or practical perfection. I fail at this all the time. In the past I have failed a lot, and I mean that literally, not as a rhetorical flourish. The point is not that I already embody the ideals I am describing, but that I am trying to move in their direction until they become my default way of engaging.

I also do not think the approach I have outlined is some rigid rule that must be applied in every context without exception. Reality is messy, and so are people. What I am arguing for is less a universal script and more a standard of discourse we should broadly aim toward — both in public platforms and in private conversations: steelmanning, patience, clarity, and kindness as the default, with deviations needing serious justification rather than the other way around.

It is important to say explicitly that I see Matt Dillahunty as an extraordinary human being whose overall impact has been strongly net positive, both for the broader public discourse and for individuals like myself. His work has sharpened my thinking and contributed to my own epistemic development. None of this is an attempt to dismiss or erase that contribution.


Part of what pushed me to write this, however, is how some critiques of his tone — especially in comment sections on shows like The Line — have been answered. When people raise what appear to be sincere concerns about his style, a common paraphrased response is: “If you don’t like it, make your own show.” But this does not actually address the substance of the critique. No one is denying that it is his show, or that the law and platform rules allow him to run it as he sees fit. The question is not whether he is allowed to behave that way, but whether he should — whether it is morally and epistemically optimal, given his own stated commitment to wellbeing.

Appealing to ownership and legality in response to a moral or epistemic critique is a category error: something is not automatically moral because it is legal, nor immoral because it is illegal. Framing it that way is structurally similar to a theist saying, “I have my truth and you have yours” when pressed for evidence. I do not believe Matt would accept that move from a believer, and I do not think he needs it here either. His position is strong enough to withstand honest scrutiny, and that is precisely why it is worth holding even his tone and methods to the same standards he rightly applies to others.

entry.title: The Epistemic Forge Symbol
entry.content:
The Epistemic Forge Symbol

Andraž Đurič

September 2026

I made this symbol with Claude to bring together some of the ideas behind Epistemic Forge. I like how clean it looks, and I think it represents what I wanted it to. Here is what the different parts mean.

The symbol depicts a temporary being within a changing universe, carrying an incomplete model of that universe and remaining open to what it can learn from it.

Read from left to right, it represents a cosmic history. Read from the outer marks to the smaller marks within the circle, it moves from the world to a representation of the world. The agent and its model belong to the same physical reality they seek to understand.

The large dot: an early condition

The solid dot stands for the unusually low-entropy early universe. The assumption of such a low-entropy past is often called the Past Hypothesis. It helps account for the thermodynamic direction of the history represented here. What ultimately explains that early condition remains an open question.[1]

The dot marks a starting condition for this picture. Its simplicity is a visual choice; it does not imply that the universe's complete initial state is known.

The outer line: time and a possible future

The line carries the history forward. Its fading tail represents the heat-death scenario: the eventual loss of usable energy differences capable of sustaining activity such as life. The fade concerns the availability of those differences, rather than the disappearance of reality.

This is an anticipated future within a cosmological model. The universe's ultimate fate remains dependent on unresolved physics, including the nature and behaviour of dark energy.[2]

The line has no arrowhead. That is a deliberate convention for a history with no assigned cosmic purpose. Time's direction and an agent's goals are different kinds of direction.

The circle: an agent within the world

The circle represents a finite agent: a system whose continued existence depends on maintaining its organisation through interaction with its surroundings. Living organisms sustain that organisation through exchanges of matter and energy, producing entropy in the process.

The circle sits along the outer history because the agent belongs to that history. Its ability to observe, think and act depends on physical conditions it did not create and cannot entirely control.

The inner cosmological picture makes this particular agent a reflective one. The symbol does not attribute a theory of the universe to every living system.

The opening: contact and the possibility of correction

The opening faces the incoming line, giving contact with the world a visible place in the design. It represents exchange across a boundary: the interactions that sustain an agent and the signals from which it can learn.

Through this contact, the world can challenge what the agent expects. Correction requires the agent to register the mismatch and allow the evidence to change its model. The opening represents an available channel for that process; keeping the model responsive is an ongoing task.

The incoming segment stops at the opening while the inner picture is drawn separately. This distinguishes the world from its representation. Both the agent and the physical processes carrying its model remain parts of the world.

The inner dot and dashes: a partial map

Inside the circle is a smaller echo of the outer dot and line. It represents a model that reaches beyond the agent's immediate surroundings, into a reconstructed past and an anticipated future.

The dashes stand for selectivity: a finite map keeps some features and leaves others out. A selective model can still be accurate for a particular purpose. Its usefulness depends on whether it preserves the distinctions that matter for that purpose.

The lighter inner dot acknowledges uncertainty about the earliest conditions. The fading dashes show that this model includes a prediction of heat death. Neither opacity nor spacing measures a numerical confidence or a physical timescale.

A small, temporary part of the universe can therefore carry a representation of a history far larger than itself. That representation can guide it, mislead it, and be revised.

Purpose and scope

The symbol connects three recurring concerns of Epistemic Forge: physical existence, situated agency and knowledge that remains answerable to evidence.

Within the blog's philosophical framework, questions about what matters and what ought to be done are anchored to agents, their conditions of existence and their relations with others. The symbol places these concerns with the agent. The arguments for that account, and its limits, belong to the writing; the drawing does not establish them.

Its central commitment is simple: we are parts of the world, building partial maps of it, with the possibility and responsibility of letting experience and evidence change them.

Background reading

  1. Sean Carroll, “Cosmology and the Past Hypothesis” (2013), on the low-entropy past and the problem of explaining it.
  2. NASA, “What Is Dark Energy?”, on the unresolved nature of dark energy and competing explanations of cosmic acceleration.

entry.title: Architecture for Living Aligned with Reality
entry.content:
ARCHITECTURE FOR LIVING ALIGNED WITH REALITY



Foundational Principle

Reality is the only legitimate authority.

Not power. Not tradition. Not comfort. Not even survival.

When reality and any other force conflict, reality takes precedence.


Core Recognition: What You Did Not Choose

You are not responsible for:
- Your initial cognitive architecture
- Your genetic predispositions  
- Your baseline capabilities
- The circumstances of your birth
- Your natural fears and instincts

These are the starting conditions you were given.

Claiming credit for advantages you didn't earn is a betrayal of reality.  
Accepting blame for disadvantages you didn't cause is equally false.

You did not choose to be born. This is not your credit or your fault.



Where Responsibility Begins

You ARE responsible for:
- Recognizing your actual capabilities honestly
- What you choose to do with what you were given
- Whether you update your beliefs when proven wrong
- How you treat others
- Whether you betray reality to protect ego or gain comfort
- The space between your feelings and your actions

This is where ethics lives: in the choices you make within your given architecture.



The Principle of Reality Alignment

"I will never betray reality."

This means:
- When you are wrong, you acknowledge it explicitly and update
- When authority demands you state falsehood, you refuse
- When comfort requires self-deception, you choose discomfort
- When survival requires betraying truth, you accept the cost
- When power conflicts with reality, you side with reality

No exceptions. Not for family. Not for career. Not for survival. 
Not even for God if God existed and commanded otherwise.



Understanding the Weight

This principle is heavy.

It means:
- You cannot hide from your failures
- You cannot claim credit for your luck  
- You cannot maintain comfortable lies
- You cannot obey illegitimate authority
- You cannot protect your ego from truth

Most people cannot live this way. 
The cognitive dissonance would be unbearable.

If you choose this path, you are choosing to carry weight that most people refuse.



The Role of Fear

"Without fear there is no courage."

If you feel no fear about consequences,
refusing power costs you nothing.

Real courage is:
- Feeling the fear of loss, suffering, or death
- Recognizing it as your survival instinct trying to protect you  
- Thanking it for the warning
- Proceeding anyway because the principle is worth more than safety

The fear never goes away. You don't eliminate it. 
You act despite it.

This is continuous, daily courage. Not one heroic moment,
but thousands of small refusals to compromise.



Building Environment for Alignment

Reduce friction in neutral decisions to preserve resources for moral ones.

Your environment should:

Minimize cognitive load on non-essential choices:
- Organize physical space for function, not aesthetics
- Remove unnecessary decision points
- Make tools accessible without thought
- Design for your actual usage patterns, not ideal ones

Externalize what you need to remember:
- Display principles visibly where you work and live
- Document your failures where you can see them
- Keep frameworks for decision-making physically accessible
- Make your values environmental, not just mental

Create stopping rules before you need them:
- Define in advance what would make you reconsider an action
- Set concrete criteria for when to stop or change course
- Plan against your own blind spots before they activate
- Build in checkpoints that force reflection

This isn't efficiency for its own sake. 
This is preservation of cognitive resources for the moments when reality and power conflict.



Maintaining Honest Self-Knowledge

Document your failures explicitly. 
Display them where you must see them.

This serves multiple purposes:
- Prevents self-deception about your actual patterns
- Provides evidence that the space between stimulus and response exists (you've collapsed it before)
- Creates accountability to your actual behavior, not your intended behavior
- Makes improvement possible by acknowledging what needs improvement

Most people curate their environment to show only success and principle.

If you are serious about alignment, you must include documented evidence of your failures.

Not for shame. Not for punishment.

For honesty. For pattern recognition. For prevention.



The Space Between Feeling and Action

**Between stimulus and response, there is a space. In that space lies your power to choose.**

Emotions are valid. You should not prevent yourself from feeling them.

But emotions are not commands. They are information.

The practice:
1. Feel the emotion fully (anger, fear, desire, grief)
2. Acknowledge it is valid and real
3. Recognize the space between feeling it and acting on it
4. Choose your response based on reality-aligned principles
5. Act with kindness and compassion whenever possible

"Whenever possible" acknowledges: 
Sometimes reality demands firmness, refusal, or confrontation.

The goal is not to always be nice. 
The goal is to always be aligned with what is actually true and ethical.



Play as Essential Maintenance

Play is not optional. It is a human need like food, water, or sleep.

When you carry the weight of never betraying reality, you need moments to put it down.

Play serves critical functions:
- Prevents cognitive burnout that would compromise your ability to maintain principle
- Maintains neuroplasticity and creative thinking
- Processes insights subconsciously through diffuse-mode cognition  
- Sustains intrinsic motivation for continued existence
- Reminds you what you're fighting for (joy, exploration, beauty)

All forms of play are valid: games, puzzles, building, creating, watching, reading, exploring.

This is not indulgence. This is system maintenance.

Without play, you will collapse before the test comes.



Deriving Ethics from Reality

If ethics are to be legitimate, they must derive from reality itself, not from power or tradition.

Consider:
- Thermodynamics: The universe tends toward entropy (disorder, heat death)
- Life: Organisms that create local order (negentropy) at the cost of energy
- Cooperation: Systems that coordinate reduce total entropy more efficiently than competition  
- Suffering: Represents disorder in experience; reducing it creates order
- Understanding: Increases ability to create sustainable order

From these physical facts, ethical principles emerge:

1. Reducing suffering is thermodynamically aligned (creates order from disorder)
2. Cooperation outperforms competition (better negentropy production)  
3. Understanding reality deeply enables better order-creation (knowledge reduces waste)
4. Sustainable systems survive; unsustainable ones collapse (reality enforces this)
5. Cruelty accelerates entropy; kindness fights it (social thermodynamics)

Therefore: Be kind when possible, not because authority commands it, but because reality itself justifies it.



On Authority and Power

Law is an approximation of morality, not morality itself.

When law aligns with reality-derived ethics, follow it.

When law contradicts reality or demands unjustified harm, it loses legitimacy.

No entity has authority over reason and reality:
- Not parents ("because I said so" is insufficient)
- Not institutions (tradition is not justification)  
- Not governments (power is not legitimacy)
- Not religious authorities (claimed divine mandate is not evidence)
- Not even God, if God existed and commanded without epistemic justification

You may love and respect these entities.
But love and respect do not grant them authority over what is true.

Be prepared to refuse illegitimate authority, even when refusal carries severe cost.



Accepting the Cost

If you live by "never betray reality," you will eventually face:
- Social rejection for refusing comfortable lies
- Professional cost for refusing to comply with misaligned authority  
- Legal consequences for breaking unjust laws
- Physical danger for refusing power that demands falsehood

This is not hypothetical. This is certain.

The question is not "will there be a cost?" but "am I willing to pay it?"

Historical precedent is clear:
- Socrates: Executed for refusing to stop teaching
- Giordano Bruno: Burned at the stake for refusing to recant
- Dietrich Bonhoeffer: Executed for resisting unjust power
- Countless others: Imprisoned, exiled, killed, forgotten

If you choose this path, you are choosing potential martyrdom.

Not because you seek it. Not because you want it.

But because reality and power will eventually conflict,
and you have already decided which side you're on.



The Pre-Commitment

Make the decision in advance:

"If I must choose between survival and betraying reality, I choose reality."

Why decide now?

Because in the moment of terror — when power threatens
death or torture — your survival instinct will scream at you to
compromise.

If you haven't already decided, 
you might rationalize betrayal in that moment.

By deciding in advance, you remove the decision from the moment of fear.

The choice is already made. You need only execute it.

This is philosophically and psychologically rigorous preparation for the hardest test you may ever face.



Why Do This At All?

Because the future matters.

Every small refusal to betray truth is a brick in the foundation of a better future.

Every person who maintains principle under pressure makes it
slightly more possible for others to do the same.

Every generation that refuses to compromise builds capacity
for the next generation to go further.

You are not building this for yourself. 
You will likely not see the result.

You are building this for beings who do not yet exist:
- Who might someday live with less cruelty
- Who might explore reality with more honesty  
- Who might cooperate with more trust
- Who might smile because you refused to bend

Even if the probability is low. 
Even if you'll never know if it worked.

The possibility that future beings might experience love and joy and wonder — that possibility is worth any cost.

Including your life.



The Ultimate Horizon

At the end of everything, if entropy wins and the universe dies cold and dark:

If there were any chance — any chance at all — that refusing
to betray reality might lead to some other beings, somewhere,
somehow experiencing existence, love, learning, joy...

...it would be worth it.

Even with zero knowledge of whether it means anything.

Even knowing you might sacrifice everything for nothing.

The non-zero probability of their smile justifies the cost.



What This Asks of You

This architecture asks everything and nothing:

Everything:
- Your comfort when it conflicts with truth
- Your safety when power demands betrayal
- Your life if necessary
- Your certainty about outcomes

Nothing:
- You don't need exceptional intelligence  
- You don't need credentials or authority
- You don't need to be fearless
- You don't need to know you'll succeed

You need only:
- Honest recognition of your actual capabilities and limits
- Commitment to never betray reality despite cost
- Courage to act despite appropriate fear
- Willingness to maintain principle when alone
- Acceptance that you may never see the result



For Those Who Climb

If you have read this far and recognized yourself — if something in you says "yes, this is the path, regardless of cost" — then know:

You are not alone in history.

Others have climbed before you. Others climb now. 
Others will climb after.

You will be afraid. That is correct. Fear is appropriate.

You will carry enormous weight. That is the price of never compromising.

You may suffer greatly. That is what power does to those who refuse it.

You may die for this. That is the historical pattern.

And it is worth doing anyway.

Not because the outcome is certain.

But because reality deserves defenders, even when defense is fatal.

Because future beings deserve the chance to smile, even if you never see them.

Because truth matters more than survival.



Final Recognition

This path is not for everyone.

Most people will — and should — choose differently. 
Choosing survival over principle is not moral failure.
It is human. It is normal. It is adaptive.

This architecture is only for those who cannot choose otherwise:

Those who have looked at the weight and said "I'll carry it."

Those who have felt the fear and said "I'll climb anyway."

Those who have seen the likely cost and said "It's worth it."

If that is you:

Build your environment for alignment.

Document your failures honestly.

Maintain play to prevent burnout.

Act despite fear continuously.

Pre-commit to reality over survival.

And climb.

Scared.

Carrying weight.

For beings you'll never meet.

For the possibility of their smile.



Closing

Reality is the only thing worth bending your knee to.

Everything else — power, tradition, comfort, even survival — is conditional.

If you choose to live aligned with this principle:

You will be afraid often.

You will carry weight always.

You may suffer greatly.

You will likely die for it.

And somewhere, sometime, someone might smile because you refused to bend.

That is enough.

That has always been enough.

Climb.



For those who have gone before.

For those climbing now.

For those who will come after.

For the beings who might someday smile.


Published: January 4th, 2026
Written by: Andraž Đurič

entry.title: Where the is–ought question bottoms out
entry.content:
It is what it is

Where the is–ought question bottoms out

Terminus

Andraž Đurič

June 18, 2026

The is–ought work ends here. An ought is agent-relative: for a system that persists or dissolves, the dynamics it must run to keep existing are what it ought to do — one physical fact, read from that system's standpoint. Push that as far as it goes and the ought stops being a thing at all.

"Ought" is not an item in the world that switches on for agents. It is the language we use at one level of complexity — the action-guiding register, the words for what a persisting system must do — and it applies only where there are persisting systems to describe. Below that scale there is no ought, because there is nothing for the word to be about. There is only physics.

This does not make ought-claims empty, or redundant with prediction. "The cell ought to climb the glucose gradient" is not "the cell will climb" — a cell that fails to climb and dissolves leaves the prediction false and the ought intact, because climbing was what persistence demanded, and the cell that missed it paid the price. Ought carries a standard the system can meet or miss, persist or dissolve, and that standard is a physical fact about what this cell's persistence requires, true whether or not it actually climbs. That is the work ought does beyond prediction, and the directionality bare description lacks. That directionality is not imposed from outside: persistence is a process the system enacts, dissolution the event that ends it, and action-guidance attaches to the process because that is the only side with anything to do in it — which is why the ought indexes to persistence and not its cessation. And still no extra furniture: ought is real the way temperature is real — a determinate higher-level pattern, real as a pattern is real and not as some further fact, with nothing over and above the physics it answers to.

One move is assumed here rather than argued: that an ought is agent-relative at all — indexed to a system rather than free-standing. That is the load-bearing premise, argued in the companion piece on the is/ought firewall and not re-argued here, and it is where a reader who wants to resist the picture should press — on the indexing itself, not on what follows from it.

An old dispute dissolves across two layers. At the bottom there are no objective, intrinsically binding values built into the world — Mackie was right about that, and his error theory retires the categorical "wrong, full stop." But the deflated, agent-relative ought is not its target; it never claimed the objective property he denied. It is true, about natural facts, with nothing extra. Whether you keep the word "ought" for it or call the old ought false and this its replacement is a question about words — Foot's point, that the moral ought need not be categorical in the first place. (Foot's later naturalism tried to ground such an ought in a species' life-form; the ground here is the individual system's persistence instead — close in spirit, different in where the standard sits.) Either way: no values in the furniture, real oughts at the agent scale.

There is no ought for the whole. The universe is not an agent, because an agent is something marked off from an environment, and the totality has no outside to be marked off from. With no outside there is nothing to index an ought to. What can look like a cosmic ought is only the sum of agent-relative ones — every persisting thing reading part of the physics as its own. A web of local oughts, no owner of the whole. How those local oughts conflict, and whether the web has structure enough for some to override others, is a real question — but a different one, about which oughts hold rather than about what an ought is. This piece asks only the second, and follows it down.

That is the ought; beneath it lies a different question, with an answer of a different kind. The foundation is brute. We want a reason for it — why these laws, why this low-entropy beginning — but the demand for a reason is projected outward from inside a structured world, where reasons are external grounds and everything we meet has one. At the foundation there is no outside for a ground to come from. The same wall that denies the universe a boundary denies it a cause and a justification: boundary, cause, and ground are all relations to an outside, and there is none. Justification bottoms out in self-support — logic can only be vindicated by logic — because there is nothing external to vindicate it with. Something has to be brute; the regress forces that much, since justification cannot run all the way down.

I lean further. The demand for a reason at the foundation is not merely unanswered, it is out of place — a want for a "why" carried to a boundary where the word stops applying. I cannot establish this from the inside, and that inability is the same wall again: there is no standpoint outside the system from which to check whether "why" still means anything there. But that we cannot get outside to check is itself a reason to think the demand was parochial all along.

What is left, once the descriptions are peeled off, is a sentence that says nothing. It is what it is. What exists, exists; what persists, persists. As a claim about the world it is empty, and the emptiness is the whole of it. A tautology says nothing — and that it says nothing is what it shows: the limit, the place where saying stops. This is not a slogan standing in for an argument. It is where the argument ends. There is no further layer to state, so the last honest thing to write is the sentence that states nothing.

None of this is new. Hume on whether the demand for a cause is rationally forced, Mackie on objective values, Foot on the hypothetical ought, Wittgenstein on what a tautology can and cannot do — the ground was settled before I walked onto it. I set it down as an endpoint, not a discovery. It is what it is.

References

  1. Hume, D. (1739–1740). A Treatise of Human Nature, Book I, Part III, Section III ("Why a cause is always necessary"). The maxim that whatever begins to exist must have a cause is shown to be neither intuitively nor demonstratively certain; the basis for treating the demand for a reason at the foundation as not rationally forced. Standard
  2. Mackie, J. L. (1977). Ethics: Inventing Right and Wrong. Penguin. The moral error theory: ordinary moral discourse presupposes objective, categorically prescriptive values that do not exist. The categorical ought it targets is the one the agent-relative account discards; the hypothetical ought is untouched. Standard
  3. Foot, P. (1972). "Morality as a System of Hypothetical Imperatives." The Philosophical Review, 81(3), 305–316. The moral ought need not be categorical, and surface grammar does not settle categorical force. Standard
  4. Foot, P. (2001). Natural Goodness. Oxford University Press. The later neo-Aristotelian turn: evaluation grounded in the natural goodness of an organism relative to its species' life-form. The nearest named alternative to the account here, and grounded differently — in the kind's form rather than the individual system's persistence. Standard
  5. Dennett, D. C. (1991). "Real Patterns." The Journal of Philosophy, 88(1), 27–51. Real but deflationary patterns: the middle ground between eliminativism and full realism that the temperature analogy occupies — neither extra furniture nor free invention. Standard
  6. Wittgenstein, L. (1921). Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus, 4.461. Tautologies are senseless (sinnlos), not nonsense; a tautology shows that it says nothing — the form of the closing line. Standard

Author: Andraž Đurič, Slovenia. Written in dialogue with Claude (Anthropic), a credited collaborator, following exchanges with other language models. Contributions are judged on content rather than origin; doing otherwise would be the genetic fallacy. Text licensed CC BY 4.0.
entry.blogger:metaDescription: The deflationary endpoint of the is–ought question: ought is agent-relative, then a description, and at the foundation there is only what is.

entry.title: One Game of Oughts
entry.content:
One Game of Oughts

Persistence, coupling, and the structure of biological normativity

Theoretical and formal paper · biological normativity, viability, maintenance, and coupled systems

Andraž Đurič

Version 1 · 22 September 2026

Abstract

A living system's conditions of continuation need not be represented by that system to constrain its possible futures. This paper develops that distinction in a shared-world setting. It separates the bearer of a persistence-relative requirement from the systems supplying its enabling conditions, the controller capable of changing those conditions, and the observer evaluating their significance. Using a finite-horizon stochastic model, it defines indexed continuation events, distinguishes actual performance from available viability, and establishes a dependency-transfer bound: when continuation without an enabling event has probability at most ε throughout a specified policy class, achieving continuation probability α requires that enabling event with probability at least α − ε. Such requirements compose along genuine dependency chains, but generic beneficial influence does not. Constructed examples show how maintaining another system can sustain one's own continuation, why substitute providers make contribution nonadditive, and why individually achievable continuation requirements can be jointly infeasible. A further distinction separates maintenance expenditure from adverse persistence impact. The biological interpretation inherits Epistemic Forge's persistence-indexed account of functional oughts; it is not proved by the probability calculus. The proposal is a formal synthesis concerning interacting, locally indexed requirements—not a derivation of a universal moral scalar, a claim that organisms maximize one metric, or the discovery that biological normativity precedes reflective thought.

Keywords: biological normativity; persistence; viability; organizational autonomy; ecological dependence; maintenance; semantic information; coupled systems.

In plain language

A plant does not need to think about being damaged for damage to threaten its continued existence. Nor do I have to notice my dependence on another system for that dependence to obtain.

But these are not isolated facts about isolated things. What one living system does can help maintain—or destroy—the conditions under which another continues. An organism's physical boundary is not the boundary of its persistence conditions.

The resulting structure is neither a universe with one objective nor a collection of unrelated private problems. It is a shared causal world containing different bearers, different continuation requirements, and interactions that connect their consequences. Supporting another system can sometimes be part of sustaining oneself. In other cases, continuation interests conflict. The mathematics must preserve both possibilities.

That is the defensible starting meaning of one game of oughts: one interacting world of locally indexed continuation requirements. Whether that structure supports a stronger unification is a question to investigate, not a result to insert into the title.

1. The plant and the change in the map

I was standing beside a pavement, trying to kick away a plant growing from the curb. I thought it was dry and dead. After several attempts, its bending made me reconsider. It might still be alive.

Then a thought appeared without a deliberate reconstruction of the argument: I was probably harming its persistence. More exactly, I was presently one of the conditions acting against its continuation.

The plant's living status was not independently established. The episode therefore does not demonstrate that I injured a living organism. What it makes visible is a distinction in the structure of the assessment. My estimate changed; the relation I was estimating did not wait for my estimate to exist.

If the plant was alive, damage could have affected its continuation before either of us represented that consequence. Its capacity to articulate an ought was not the relevant variable. My recognition was a possible addition to the causal situation, not the original source of the plant's requirements.

The same separation appears when looking in the other direction. Some of the systems on which I depend might be sustaining me without my awareness. My model can omit them; my functioning cannot thereby dispense with them.

The question is not merely whether living things have requirements. It is how those requirements relate when the activities of one system enter the continuation conditions of another.

2. What is inherited, and what is being added

This paper does not introduce nonreflective ought-bearers into Epistemic Forge for the first time. Value as Persistence already permits minimal regulatory models without conscious or propositional representation. The Natural History of Fidelity discusses a bacterium's functional ought without assigning it reflective moral reasoning. [F1–F2]

Two further commitments are inherited. First, an ought in the relevant sense remains indexed to a bearer and its continuation conditions; universal scope does not remove that index. Second, persistence enabling continued valuation is not, by itself, a proof that every value reduces in content to persistence. Relata-Indexed Objectivity and Universal Is Not Categorical keep the normative interpretation and the stronger reduction claim distinguishable. [F3–F4]

The work attempted here is more specific. It connects bearer-relative continuation requirements through explicit dependencies, identifies when that connection licenses a further requirement, and identifies several tempting inferences that it does not license. A common framework should explain both external maintenance and conflict without silently changing the beneficiary of the analysis.

Three levels of claim will remain separate. The stochastic model describes possible continuation under specified conditions. Elementary results establish consequences inside that model. The interpretation of some of those relations as functional oughts is a philosophical commitment, defended below and inherited from the corpus. None acquires the standing of the other merely by appearing beside it.

3. Position in the literature

There is substantial prior work on precisely the terrain into which this argument enters.

Di Paolo distinguishes autopoietic self-production from the additional adaptive capacities needed for richer accounts of agency and value. His account matters here because maintaining organization, regulating threats to it, and exhibiting richer agency should not be compressed into one capacity. [1]

Mossio, Saborido, and Moreno develop an organizational account of biological functions through contributions to differentiated self-maintaining organization. This supplies a serious predecessor for grounding functional assessment in the organization of the system rather than in an observer's arbitrary preference. [2]

The closest formal predecessor is Barandiaran and Egbert. They distinguish norm-establishing dynamics from norm-following behavior, model metabolic viability and precariousness, and construct a normative field specifying environmental changes relevant to continued existence. They also discuss nested processes and possible higher-dimensional formulations. Neither normativity before reflective thought nor a mathematically represented normative landscape is new here. [3]

The mathematical foundation comes from viability theory. Aubin, Bayen, and Saint-Pierre develop constraint-based continuation; Doyen and De Lara formulate stochastic viability and viable controls through probability constraints and dynamic programming. The present use of finite-horizon continuation probabilities belongs to that established apparatus. [4–5]

Béné and Doyen explicitly examine biodiversity contributions relative to ecological and economic viability in numerical models. Their work is an important precedent for context-dependent contribution rather than a fixed, context-free value assigned to each provider. Holling's cross-scale framework provides a further background for nested, changing dependencies, without establishing that every connected collection is itself an organism. [6–7]

Kolchinsky and Wolpert investigate information whose system–environment correlations causally contribute to a selected viability measure, using interventions on those correlations. Sowinski and colleagues instantiate this approach in resource-gathering agents, relating sensor degradation to modeled lifetime. These connect informational fidelity to continuation without making explicit deliberation necessary. [8–9]

The normative interpretation remains contested. Corti argues that counterfactual dependence and organizational closure do not, on their own, establish the normative force sometimes claimed for them. Li's later relational account instead emphasizes a system-relative standard and fragile self-maintenance. These are competing philosophical treatments, not two empirical measurements whose disagreement can be removed by averaging. [10–11]

The intended contribution is therefore an explicit synthesis and development: separate indices, connect their requirements through conditional dependency results, account for costs and substitution, and preserve the difference between individual and joint viability. No priority claim is made for the component concepts or the elementary mathematics.

4. Bearers, conditions, providers, and controllers

Four roles need to be distinguished before writing an equation.

A bearer is the system whose continuation is being assessed. A condition is something necessary or contributory to that continuation. A provider helps realize that condition. A controller can alter part of the relevant dynamics. An observer can describe all four roles without occupying any of them.

The roles can overlap. A system can regulate itself and supply something another system requires. They need not overlap. Water can be an enabling condition without being a living ought-bearer. A nonliving device can regulate a condition without acquiring every property of the organism it supports.

For the biological application, a working bearer is an individuated living organization whose activities and retained capacities participate in sustaining its continuity. This characterization permits dependence: requiring outside resources or support does not make the bearer unreal. It also permits inactivity during part of a lifecycle. It does not settle every boundary case by definition.

A bare boundary is insufficient. We need an account of what continues through changes in material composition and state. Here the target is the continuity of a specified organizational process, not preservation of every molecule or an exact configuration. The corpus's distinction between a continuing process-token and a merely similar replacement remains relevant. [F5]

Nested systems require more than drawing boxes. A component and a larger system may both be legitimate objects of functional assessment, but they have different continuity criteria. The larger system's persistence must not be silently substituted for that of a component. Nor does recording both as bearers automatically justify counting them twice in an aggregate moral total.

The extension to all life is a substantive scope hypothesis: wherever a living individual can be identified, its organization supplies nonindifferent continuation conditions even without propositional representation. Cells, dormant stages, colonies, symbiotic systems, and dependent biological entities test the individuation criterion. A disputed case is a reason to specify the bearer more carefully, not to award every physically bounded object an independent moral status.

The formalism below is deliberately broader than this biological interpretation. It can assess a chosen physical system whether or not that system qualifies as a living bearer. Mathematical applicability alone therefore cannot decide the scope of biological normativity.

5. The normative commitment

The proposed interpretation can be stated directly:

Persistence-indexed functional normativity: relative to an identified living organization, conditions and activities can count as sustaining or defeating its continuation independently of whether the organization, a controller, or an observer represents or endorses that relation.

Calling the sustaining requirements oughts for that bearer is the normative commitment inherited here. It is not the claim that the organism ought to persist only because it happens to desire persistence. The index concerns the organization whose continuation is at issue, not an optional preference report.

There are reasons to use the functional vocabulary. The target is not chosen as freely as an arbitrary score in a game. It is constrained by what makes this system the continuing organization under examination. A regulatory process can fail relative to that organization even while obeying physics perfectly. Actual behavior, felt preference, and successful continuation need not coincide.

An observer can be wrong about the requirements. A bearer can fail to detect them. A controller can detect them but fail to act accordingly. These possibilities help distinguish a standard of functional success from a description of whatever happens.

Nevertheless, identifying those asymmetries is not a deductive proof that every ordinary or moral use of “ought” reduces to them. Corti's objection is relevant exactly at that step: a causal dependence does not automatically supply the full normative significance one might attach to it. [10] This paper keeps the interpretive premise visible rather than hiding it in a definition of a probability.

The proposal is neither contentless stipulation nor a completed reduction. It is a reconstruction whose value depends on whether the chosen reference can be identified nonarbitrarily, whether it supports accurate functional distinctions, and whether further normative claims can be derived without changing the index. A reader can reject this reconstruction while accepting the mathematical results. Conversely, accepting it does not exempt the causal model from testing.

It is also necessary to distinguish three claims: something is required for the plant's continuation; the plant can regulate in relation to it; I am obligated to protect it. The first need not await the second. The third requires an account of my relation to the plant and of the relevant normative standard. Coupling can establish part of that relation, but not by making the indices disappear.

6. A model of indexed continuation

Consider a finite sequence of times t=0,…,H. For the formal results, use finite state and action spaces. This avoids unnecessary measure-theoretic assumptions; it is not a claim that biological reality is literally a finite-state machine.

Let zt encode the relevant joint state: the bearer, other modeled systems, resource stocks, and environmental variables. Its dynamics are

zt+1∼Tt(⋅∣zt,ut).
(1)

A joint policy π determines actions from the information available to the modeled controllers. The nonempty admissible class Π includes constraints on observation, action, resources, and coordination. Describing a joint policy does not imply that any single real agent can choose everyone else's behavior.

Overlapping and nested bearers can be represented by different observables of zt. There is no assumption that each bearer occupies a statistically or causally independent factor of the state space.

For bearer i, let Ki(t) specify states compatible with its constitutive continuity. Define the continuation event

ΦiH={zt∈Ki(t) for every t=0,…,H}.
(2)

Where continuity depends on history, augment the state with the necessary history or use a trajectory predicate directly. A stage transition may be included without counting it as death. An actual termination of the chosen process-token cannot be erased by later producing a similar token.

The sets Ki are not viability kernels. They specify what counts as continuing at each time; viability additionally depends on whether available policies can keep the trajectory there. A system can still be alive while no available response prevents its later termination.

Under model M, initial state z0, and policy π, define

viπ(M,z0,H)=PrMπ(ΦiH∣z0).
(3)

This is one operational persistence measure, not a universal measure of value. It distinguishes continuation probabilities, but can leave differences in reserves, damage, welfare, and recovery capacity unresolved when they do not change the selected event or horizon.

Actual-policy performance must also be separated from available performance:

Vi(M,z0,H;Π)=supπ∈Πviπ.
(4)

A low actual value and a low attainable value are different diagnoses. The first may permit correction. The second may reflect constraints no available policy can overcome.

For a stated reliability target αi∈[0,1], define

Πi(αi)={π∈Π:viπ≥αi}.
(5)

The target is an explicit modeling or practical parameter. Physics has not, through this definition, prescribed a uniquely correct risk tolerance. If this set is empty, a continuation requirement can remain unsatisfied as a structural fact; emptiness does not entail that every action becomes obligatory or that an impossible action becomes available.

Equations (1)–(5) instantiate the distinction between constraints, policies, and probabilistic viability developed in the control literature. [4–5] The interpretive work lies in identifying a real bearer and its constitutive conditions, not in renaming every chosen constraint a biological ought.

7. Dependency transfer

The central result concerns a necessary enabling condition, allowing a bounded exception. Hold the model, initial state, and horizon fixed; their arguments are suppressed below. Exception bounds are nonnegative.

Let Q be an event: for example, some enabling function is adequately supplied during the interval in which it is needed. It need not be the survival of a particular provider throughout the whole horizon.

Proposition 1. Approximate dependency transfer

Suppose that, for every policy π in a specified admissible class,

Prπ(ΦiH∩Qc)≤ε.
(6)

Then every such policy satisfies

viπ≤Prπ(Q)+ε.
(7)

Consequently, a policy achieving viπ≥αi must satisfy

Prπ(Q)≥max{0,αi−ε}.
(8)

Proof. Split the continuation event into the disjoint events ΦiH∩Q and ΦiH∩Qc. The first has probability at most Prπ(Q); the second is bounded by (6). Adding gives (7), and rearranging gives (8). ◻

When ε=0, Q is necessary for the selected continuation event within the modeled policy class. When ε>0, continuation without it has a bounded probability. A policy making Q impossible yields viπ≤ε, provided the dependency bound remains valid for that policy.

The qualification matters. An intervention that adds a replacement mechanism can invalidate the original dependency premise. A theorem about one transition structure cannot be exported to a changed structure without checking its premises again.

This is elementary probability, not a new probability theorem. Its use is to make a cross-system inference exact. If Q is supplied by another system, sufficiently reliable continuation of i requires sufficiently reliable provision of Q. No equal weighting of organisms has been assumed. Nor has concern for the other system been introduced as an optional desire.

Under the persistence-indexed interpretation, Q enters the requirements for i. Whether controller c ought to take a particular action concerning Q additionally depends on what c can change and which alternative actions remain. A necessary condition of an outcome is not automatically an executable instruction.

Proposition 2. Composition of necessary dependencies

Suppose, throughout the same policy class,

Prπ(ΦiH∩Qc)≤ε,Prπ(Q∩Rc)≤δ.
(9)

Then

Prπ(ΦiH∩Rc)≤ε+δ,
(10)

and achieving continuation probability αi requires

Prπ(R)≥max{0,αi−ε−δ}.
(11)

Proof. The event ΦiH∩Rc is contained in the union of ΦiH∩Qc and Q∩Rc. Apply the union bound, then Proposition 1. ◻

The result extends along a chain by summing the exception bounds, although a long chain can make the resulting bound uninformative. No independence assumption is needed.

This is not a rule that every favorable influence propagates favorably through every network. Generic increases in one system's persistence can have mixed or opposing effects elsewhere. What composes here is a stated necessary-event relation, not an unspecified positive association.

A special case illustrates the distinction. If ΦiH entails ΦjH, then Πi(α)⊆Πj(α). But the real necessary event may instead be a service from j delivered before some earlier time. A stored resource can remain useful after its provider no longer exists. Keeping the event precise prevents instrumental dependence from becoming an indiscriminate command to preserve every provider forever.

8. Costs and external maintenance

A resource budget can be represented schematically as

ri,t+1=ri,t+Ii(zt,ut)−Ei(zt,ut),
(12)

where influx Ii and expenditure Ei use the same physical units. “Cost” can refer to expenditure, foregone alternatives, or a reduction in continuation prospects. These are related but nonidentical quantities.

In microbial modeling, maintenance includes nongrowth demands on energy or substrate. Wang and Post show that different maintenance formulations involve different assumptions and parameter interpretations; their coefficients should not be casually interchanged. [12] The relevant lesson is not that all expenditure is beneficial. It is that absence of immediate growth does not make expenditure irrelevant to continued functioning.

Repair may consume resources while improving continuation prospects. Refusing to repair can save resources while making future failure more likely. Thus minimizing expenditure and sustaining the system are different objectives.

The distinction also prevents double-counting. If a continuation probability already reflects the depletion caused by an action, subtracting that same depletion again as an additional persistence penalty counts one mechanism twice. A resource budget can remain a separate constraint, but it should not be silently duplicated inside the outcome measure.

An exact constructed example

Consider two systems with integer reserves at and bt, initially

(a0,b0)=(2,1).

Positive reserves are required for continuation; reaching zero is absorbing termination. While alive, system A pays one unit per step for its own maintenance and may spend a further unit ut∈{0,1} supporting B. While B is alive, it supplies a service worth two reserve units per step to A. System B also spends one unit per step and receives ut.

For live systems, the updates are

at+1=max{0,at−1−ut+21bt>0},
(13)
bt+1=max{0,bt−1+ut}.
(14)

Dead systems remain at zero. Support is permitted only when both systems are alive and A can fund it. The service depends on the provider's state at the beginning of the step. The two-unit return is an environmental inflow enabled by the provider, not resources created from nothing. These timing and supply assumptions are part of the model.

With no support, the four-step trajectory is

(2,1)→(3,0)→(2,0)→(1,0)→(0,0).

With support at every step, it is

(2,1)→(2,1)→(2,1)→(2,1)→(2,1).

Supporting the other system consumes resources but preserves the supporter across this horizon. The policy spending less terminates A at the fourth step. External maintenance can therefore be part of self-maintenance without assigning the two systems equal moral weight.

This example establishes a possibility, not a biological estimate. Continuous support is not the only policy preserving A through four steps. Stored reserves allow some histories in which B terminates late while A survives the selected horizon. The choice of horizon is doing real work.

Now add a substitute providing the same service independently of B. The instrumental requirement to support this particular B disappears from A's four-step continuation problem. B's own termination remains terminal relative to B. A change in one beneficiary's dependence is not a change in the identity of the other beneficiary.

The general point is not “preserve every dependency.” It is “include the maintenance of external enabling conditions in the model of self-maintenance.”

9. Contribution is indexed, interventional, and often nonadditive

To assess the contribution of another system, specify a contrast. Let I and I0 be well-defined interventions or policy configurations. Define

Δi(I,I0∣Γ)=PrI(ΦiH)−PrI0(ΦiH),
(15)

where Γ records the bearer, continuity criterion, horizon, initial conditions, dynamics, response policies, and available substitutes.

The intervention must be specified causally. Removing a provider while allowing compensation is a different contrast from removing it while freezing every controller. Comparing one condition's optimal response to another condition's unrevised response is not a neutral test unless that asymmetry is itself the question.

The result is a contribution to this continuation measure, not a context-free moral weight. Observational association does not establish it: a third process might produce both the provider and the observed continuation.

Substitution makes a single global coupling coefficient especially hazardous. Suppose either of two providers, B or C, suffices for an enabling service:

Q=B∨C.
(16)

When both are available, removing one leaves the service intact. Removing both destroys it. The individual deletion effects can each be zero in the original context while the joint deletion is decisive.

If provider availability is independently distributed with probabilities pB and pC, then

Pr(Q)=1−(1−pB)(1−pC).
(17)

The drop caused by deleting B is pB(1−pC). Its size depends on the remaining provider. Independence is an assumption of this illustration, not a universal property of biological suppliers.

This is why “one plant makes little difference to me” cannot establish “the systems supplying that function are dispensable to me.” It is also why not every individual loss should be redescribed as equally consequential to every bearer. Context-sensitive contribution preserves both conclusions. Viability-based biodiversity valuation already investigates such system- and constraint-relative contributions. [6]

Some dependencies are represented better by sets of jointly adequate providers or failure cut sets than by fixed pairwise links. A necessary event might be “at least one of these providers remains functional,” not the persistence of any specific member. The framework should preserve that structure rather than force all coupling into additive scores.

Under model uncertainty, even the sign of Δi can be unresolved. A robust positive claim over a stated model class M requires

infM∈MΔiM>0.
(18)

This supplies a demanding test, not a guarantee that the model class contains reality. Agreement among badly specified models does not validate their shared omissions.

10. Shared world, distinct feasibility problems

For a collection G of bearers with specified targets, define the joint policy requirement

ΠG(α)=⋂i∈GΠi(αi).
(19)

Every individual set can be nonempty while their intersection is empty. Consider one indivisible resource and two systems, each requiring the entire unit to continue. Either can be sustained alone; both cannot be sustained under the stipulated constraints. Coupling has produced a coordination and allocation problem, not a proof of harmony.

Separate probability targets also differ from simultaneous success. A policy that allocates the unit randomly with equal probability gives each system continuation probability one half, while the probability that both continue is zero. For a finite group, the elementary union bound gives

Prπ(⋂i∈GΦiH)≥max{0,1−∑i∈G(1−viπ)}.
(20)

When simultaneous continuation is the target, evaluate it directly or impose an adequate joint constraint. Do not assume that separate marginal assessments already answer that question.

Nor is a physically feasible joint policy necessarily available to any individual controller. The analysis must distinguish coordinated control, the policies actually implemented, and guarantees achievable when other systems respond differently. One shared state space is not one shared decision-maker.

These distinctions constrain the meaning of “one game.” The bearers participate in one interacting causal structure, but they need not share an objective. Where a policy improves all selected continuation measures, that is a form of Pareto improvement relative to those measures. It does not automatically improve every dimension of welfare or settle every obligation. Where effects conflict, an aggregation rule or an alternative conflict procedure requires additional justification.

For example, policies with continuation vectors (1,0) and (0,1) are not ranked by the vector alone. A weighted sum ranks them only after its weights are supplied. The formalism neither discovers those weights nor proves that no defensible scalar can exist. The corpus's stronger scalar hypothesis remains a separate research commitment. [F6]

Nested organization does not remove this issue. The continuation of a larger organization and that of its members can differ. A legitimate higher-level bearer needs its own constitutive account; it cannot be inferred simply from observing many interactions. Shared causation connects the consequences without making the bearers interchangeable.

11. Representation, noise, and the availability of correction

The model contains a continuation criterion before specifying how much of it a controller represents. Four situations are therefore distinguishable: a requirement obtains; regulation responds to something correlated with it; a system represents the relation; a reflective process examines and revises the policy through which that representation affects action.

They are not interchangeable achievements. Accurate stored information can fail to influence action. An automatic controller can respond adequately without explicit deliberation. A reflective process can be expensive or wrong.

An elementary information result states precisely one advantage of increased access.

Proposition 3. Costless informational refinement cannot reduce optimal performance

Suppose a refined observation arrangement permits every policy available under a coarser arrangement, with the same dynamics and resource costs. Thus Πcoarse⊆Πfine. Then

supπ∈Πfineviπ≥supπ∈Πcoarseviπ.
(21)

Proof. The supremum over a set cannot be smaller than the supremum over its subset. ◻

The result concerns attainable performance and permits the controller to ignore additional information. It does not say every implemented policy improves when given more input. Nor does it apply unchanged when sensing, processing, or acting consumes additional resources.

Kolchinsky and Wolpert explicitly evaluate information relative to viability and intervention choices; their framework also makes dependence on the selected viability measure visible. [8] Sowinski and colleagues' resource-gathering model illustrates why some sensor degradation can have little effect while crossing a threshold has a large effect. That is evidence from a specified model, not a universal noise threshold for life. [9]

The appropriate target is not maximal representation of everything. It is adequate access to persistence-relevant distinctions, coupled to useful regulation at a cost the system can sustain.

My plant episode is consistent with a previously developed concept influencing rapid recognition. It does not establish the cognitive mechanism that produced the thought. Its role here is narrower: awareness of a relation and the relation itself can come apart. Reflection may later alter which relations become salient without creating those relations from nothing.

12. What the common structure does—and does not—explain

The framework permits a conditional explanation of cross-system preservation. When another system supplies an irreplaceable enabling condition, sustaining that condition belongs to the first system's continuation requirements. This explains why concern beyond a body's boundary need not be foreign to self-maintenance.

It also permits indifference relative to a specific index. An intervention may make no difference to i's selected continuation measure while terminating j. That is not a contradiction. The model contains two bearers. Treating the smaller external effect as proof that the terminated bearer's own loss was small would switch indices mid-argument.

The same structure permits conflict. One system's persistence can depend on activities incompatible with another's. Calling both living does not remove the incompatibility. The concept of a local functional ought is therefore not an automatic warrant for every action serving the bearer. An agent's functional interest and another agent's moral justification are not synonyms.

Biological ought-bearing also does not establish conscious suffering. A termination event identifies failure of the specified continuity condition; it does not measure experience. The paper neither assigns every organism equal moral weight nor concludes that beings without established conscious experience have no normative significance of any kind. Those claims require additional arguments.

Finally, the account does not say organisms always maximize vi, or that evolution optimizes this exact individual-level quantity. A formal measure of continuation need not be the objective actually implemented by any organism. Reproduction, lineage continuation, component functioning, and individual survival require distinct indices. Switching from one to another when a counterexample appears would protect a slogan rather than test a theory.

13. Failure conditions and empirical use

The formal results are only as applicable as their premises. A useful application would identify a bearer and its continuity criterion before comparing interventions, specify the relevant environment and response capacities, and justify the selected horizon. It would then test the proposed enabling mechanism while distinguishing removal, compensation, and replacement.

The dependency claim in Proposition 1 is particularly exposed. If continuation without Q occurs more often than the proposed exception bound permits, the stated dependency model fails. If an intervention changes the mechanism supplying Q, the original bound may no longer apply. These are different outcomes and should not be recorded as the same kind of correction.

The toy model in Section 8 yields exact results because its dynamics are stipulated. Establishing comparable claims for a plant, organism, or ecological community requires empirical measurement. The paper does not contain that calibration. Existing viability and information models provide methodological precedents, not a shortcut around measuring the particular system. [5–6, 9]

The bearer criterion is separately exposed. A model that labels every useful part as a separate organism, excludes dormant continuity by requiring constant overt activity, or counts replacement as the original process continuing needs revision. Robustness across reasonable descriptions matters: a supposedly decisive ranking that reverses under equally defensible boundaries or horizons should be reported as unresolved.

The normative interpretation has its own test. Does it preserve the difference between success and mere occurrence? Can it explain a functional requirement independently of an observer's preference without covertly importing a global objective? Does it retain distinct bearers when their requirements conflict? If not, the vocabulary has concealed rather than clarified the problem.

There are also limits to the selected probability measure. At a horizon beyond every attainable lifetime, all continuation probabilities can vanish. That does not make every earlier trajectory identical. One can examine a profile over horizons, expected duration, reserves, or other justified measures. Choosing among them is substantive. “Persistence” should organize that inquiry, not conceal its choices.

A complete evaluation must therefore distinguish a faulty proof, a wrong biological model, a disputed continuity criterion, and rejection of the normative interpretation. They are not interchangeable failures, and none can be repaired merely by increasing confidence in another layer.

14. Standing of the proposal

The dependency bound, its composition, the joint-success bound, and the information-refinement inequality follow from the stated finite probabilistic framework. Their mathematical certainty is conditional on those premises. They are elementary results organized for this application, not advertised as discoveries in probability theory.

The supporting biological and philosophical literature establishes a substantial prior field: self-maintenance, organizational functions, norm-establishment distinct from norm-following, viability-based contribution, and information relevant to continuation. This paper's combination and interpretation remain open to comparison with further work. The literature pass does not establish exclusive novelty.

The broader all-life scope depends on defensible individuation. The inference from functional oughts to interpersonal moral duties is not completed here. A uniquely justified scalar across bearers is neither derived nor disproved. The claim that all value reduces to persistence is not used as a premise.

What the paper supplies is a disciplined intermediate result: given indexed continuation criteria and a defensible dependency model, some cross-system requirements follow without equalizing bearers, positing a global organism, or assuming conscious representation. Costs, substitution, uncertainty, and conflict are part of that result's domain, not exceptions added after it fails.

The contribution is strongest where those distinctions prevent an actual inference error. One plant's loss need not matter much to me to be terminal for it. My limited dependence on one provider need not make its collective function dispensable. Supporting another system need not be a departure from self-maintenance. And shared participation in a causal world need not supply a unique common objective.

15. One game, many indices

The sidewalk event began with an error in my map: I may have treated a living plant as dead material. The correction made a relation visible. My action could be moving another organization toward termination.

The more general insight is not that minds project oughts onto an otherwise indifferent world. Under the interpretation defended here, living organizations already have conditions under which they continue or fail. Minds can represent those conditions, miss them, distort them, or become capable of changing them.

Those conditions are realized together. The activity of one system can supply another's enabling function. Support can return through a dependency. A substitute can remove a particular dependence. A collective loss can matter where an isolated loss does not. Requirements can align or conflict, and their alignment can change as the dynamics change.

Local does not mean isolated. Shared does not mean identical.

That is the structure this paper has formalized. It is not yet a complete mathematics of morality. It is a mathematics of indexed continuation and dependency, accompanied by a defended proposal about the functional normativity those relations express.

All life may inhabit that common structure without every living thing knowing it, without every participant having the same stakes, and without the whole acquiring one will.

One game of oughts. Not one ought for everything.

References

  3. [3]

    Author manuscript consulted: https://xabier.barandiaran.net/wp-content/uploads/2012/05/barandiaran_egbert_-_2012_norm-establishing_norm-following_jal_revised-2.pdf

    The arXiv record identifies a 2010 submission; the retrieved PDF also carries an internal 2018 date. The record and consulted file are identified rather than treating those dates as interchangeable publication metadata.

Authorship, provenance, and scope

Author: Andraž Đurič, Slovenia.

Developed from the author's reported episode, the Epistemic Forge corpus, and dialogue with ChatGPT (OpenAI), with an external literature review and checks of the constructed formal examples. The author retains responsibility for the claims, framing, synthesis, and final text. Contributions are assessed by their content rather than their origin.

Source access: The internal lineage draws on the cited corpus and recorded reading of it; several original pages could not be reopened during preparation. Where complete external articles were unavailable, the review relied on publisher abstracts or selected sections. Citation does not certify every claim made in the cited works.

Formal and empirical status: The examples are constructed, not empirically calibrated. Finite executable checks were used to check their arithmetic and counterexamples. These checks do not replace the written proofs, independently verify the biological or normative interpretation, or constitute peer review. The assumptions, limitations, and failure conditions remain explicit in the paper.

entry.title: The Thermodynamic Manifesto: Reality is Computation
entry.content:
The Thermodynamic Manifesto: Reality is Computation

by Andraž Đurič

Strip away the macroscopic illusions and the universe is not made of material objects. It is a single, interconnected, self-calculating structure. Reality is information, and its engine is thermodynamics.

I. Information Is Physical

Information is not an abstraction humans invented to write code. It is the substrate. Every physical property, whether mass, charge, or spin, is the macroscopic face of binary quantum states. This is what Wheeler meant by "it from bit."

Information also carries a non-negotiable price. Landauer's principle states that erasing a single bit must dissipate at least kBT ln 2 of heat. Logic cannot be separated from thermal energy. Computation and physics are the same process described twice.

II. Spacetime Is the Interface

Space and time are not the backdrop of the universe. They are emergent properties woven from data.

Space is entanglement. In current quantum-gravity research, smooth three-dimensional space behaves as a projection of the entanglement structure of an underlying quantum system. Strong mutual entanglement renders a short distance; no shared information renders effectively infinite separation. Space is the physical rendering of data correlation. This is established in toy models such as AdS/CFT and conjectured for our own universe.

Time is entropy. The fundamental laws of physics are almost entirely time-symmetric, carrying no built-in preference for forward or backward. The arrow we experience comes from the Second Law of Thermodynamics. Time is the direction of increasing entropy, the metric of the universe processing its computational states, converting structured macro-information into hidden thermal noise.

III. The Holographic Limit

Black holes expose the blueprint. When matter falls into a black hole, its information is not packed into a three-dimensional volume. The black hole's entropy scales with the two-dimensional area of its event horizon, at roughly one bit per four Planck areas. This is the Bekenstein-Hawking result.

Because a black hole is the maximum density of energy and information that physics permits, this points to the holographic principle: a three-dimensional reality is the thermodynamic rendering of a two-dimensional quantum code written on its boundary. This is the strongest available evidence for the thesis. It is not yet a proof.

The Signal

The universe is not a collection of objects. It is a finite thermodynamic computer running a single, massive calculation.

Persistence, whether an atom holding its bounds, an organism staying alive, or a mind holding a thought, is a localized and temporary victory against equilibrium. It is a system paying a continuous thermodynamic cost to keep its internal structure from dissolving into the surrounding noise.

We are nodes in that network. We are localized data-processors, built from the very code we are trying to decipher, watching the cosmic engine settle toward final, static equilibrium.
