entry.title: Formal Dissolution of the Is-Ought Problem via Thermodynamic Realism
entry.content:
Formal Dissolution of the Is-Ought Problem via Thermodynamic Realism

Formalization of Andraž Đurič's Framework
January 20, 2026
Abstract: We present a formal dissolution of Hume's is-ought problem by demonstrating that the apparent gap between descriptive and normative statements is a linguistic artifact arising from the miscategorization of normative phenomena as non-physical. By grounding "ought" in the thermodynamic constraints of self-maintaining systems, we show that normative statements are reducible to descriptive statements about physical necessity in goal-directed agents.

I. The Traditional Is-Ought Problem

1.1 Classical Formulation

Hume's is-ought problem, as standardly understood, can be formalized as follows:

Axioms:

  1. Descriptive Domain: ∀x: P(x) → [P(x) ∈ D]
    All physical facts belong to the descriptive domain
  2. Normative Domain: ∀y: O(y) → [O(y) ∈ N]
    All ought-statements belong to the normative domain
  3. Categorical Separation: D ∩ N = ∅
    Descriptive and normative domains are disjoint

Invalid Derivation:

Premise:    P(x)        (some physical/descriptive fact)
            ⋮           (intermediate steps)
Conclusion: O(y)        (some ought-statement)

Problem: The conclusion invokes category N (normative), but all premises are in category D (descriptive). By Axiom 3, this is a categorical violation—no valid inference can cross the boundary.

1.2 The Standard Responses

Historical attempts to resolve this have included:

  • Non-naturalism: Accept the gap; treat normativity as irreducible
  • Moral naturalism: Identify specific natural properties with moral properties
  • Error theory: Deny that normative statements have truth values
  • Prescriptivism: Treat oughts as commands, not truth-apt statements

Shared failure: All accept Axiom 3—that descriptive and normative are fundamentally distinct categories.

II. Thermodynamic Realism: Core Definitions

2.1 Physical Foundations

Definition 2.1 (Self-Maintaining System):

A physical system S is self-maintaining if and only if:

∃B, t: S maintains boundary conditions B over time interval [t₀, t₀ + t]

where B defines the existence criteria for S (e.g., cellular integrity, homeostatic ranges).

Definition 2.2 (Entropic Constraint):

For a self-maintaining system S with boundary B:

∃S(t + Δt) ↔ ΔS_internal(S, [t, t+Δt]) < 0_local

S persists to the next time step if and only if it locally reduces entropy relative to its boundary

Note: This is consistent with the Second Law of Thermodynamics globally; local entropy reduction is achieved through energy input and waste export.

Definition 2.3 (Constraint Function):

Let F be a set of functions/behaviors. F is a constraint function for S if:

¬F(S) → ¬∃S(t + Δt)

Failure to execute F results in system termination

2.2 The Normative Reduction

Definition 2.4 (Ought-Statement):

For a self-maintaining system S and constraint function F:

"S ought to execute F" :≡ "F is necessary for ∃S(t + Δt)"

Formally:

Ought(S, F) ≡ [¬F(S) → ¬∃S(t + Δt)]

Critical Point: This is a definition, not a derivation. We are identifying what "ought" is in physical terms, not deriving normativity from non-normative facts.

III. The Dissolution

3.1 Revised Formalization

Under Thermodynamic Realism:

Revised Axiom Set:

  1. Physical Monism: ∀x: x exists → x ∈ Physical
    All existing phenomena are physical
  2. Self-Maintenance Constraint: ∀S self-maintaining: ∃F[Ought(S,F)]
    All self-maintaining systems have constraint functions
  3. Ought-Identity: Ought(S,F) ≡ [¬F → ¬∃S(t+Δt)]
    Ought-statements are identical to necessity statements for persistence

Valid Derivation:

Premise 1:  S is a self-maintaining system               (physical fact)
Premise 2:  S exists at t                                (physical fact)
Premise 3:  ∃S(t+Δt) requires ΔS_internal < 0           (thermodynamic law)
Premise 4:  ΔS_internal < 0 requires execution of F     (physical fact)
Premise 5:  Ought(S,F) ≡ [¬F → ¬∃S(t+Δt)]              (Definition 2.4)
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Conclusion: S ought to execute F                         (by substitution)

Analysis: Every step remains within the domain of physical description. The conclusion is normative in language but descriptive in content.

3.2 Category Error Diagnosis

The traditional is-ought problem committed:

Error := {Axiom: "ought" ∉ Physical} ∧ {Observation: "ought" affects behavior}

This is logically incoherent because:

  1. Physical systems are causally closed (all physical effects have physical causes)
  2. Organisms demonstrably alter behavior in response to normative judgments
  3. Therefore, normative judgments must be physical processes

The resolution: "Ought" was never outside physics. The gap was created by definition, then treated as a discovery.

IV. Formal Proof of Dissolution

Theorem 4.1: The is-ought gap is a linguistic artifact, not an ontological divide.

Proof:

  1. Assume "ought" refers to non-physical normative domain N where N ∉ Physical
  2. Observation: ∀organism O: O modifies behavior in response to ought-judgments
  3. Causal Closure: ∀physical effect e: ∃physical cause c
  4. From (2,3): Ought-judgments must have physical causes (else violates causal closure)
  5. Disjunction: Either (a) ought-judgments are physical, or (b) ought-judgments are non-physical but causally inert
  6. From (2): Ought-judgments are not causally inert
  7. From (5,6): Ought-judgments are physical
  8. Contradiction with (1)
  9. Therefore: Assumption (1) is false
  10. Conclusion: "Ought" does not refer to a non-physical domain ∎

Corollary 4.1: If "ought" is physical, then ought-statements are descriptive statements about physical constraint structures in self-modeling systems.

Corollary 4.2: The is-ought "gap" dissolves when normative terms are properly grounded in their physical referents.

V. Implications and Extensions

5.1 Ethics as Applied Thermodynamics

If normativity reduces to entropy management in self-maintaining systems, then:

Ethics = Study of optimal constraint-satisfaction in multi-agent environments

Virtue = Low-entropy behavioral strategies (stable, efficient, predictive)

Vice = High-entropy behavioral strategies (unstable, costly, friction-inducing)

5.2 Testable Predictions

This framework generates empirical predictions:

  1. Cooperation should correlate with energy efficiency in social groups
  2. Deceptive strategies should show higher metabolic costs (cognitive load of model management)
  3. Moral development should track predictive modeling capacity (theory of mind = moral reasoning substrate)

5.3 Philosophical Consequences

Resolved:

  • Is-ought problem (dissolved via proper categorization)
  • Moral realism vs. anti-realism debate (realism wins, but naturalized)
  • Fact-value distinction (distinction is linguistic, not ontological)

Open questions:

  • Optimal multi-agent equilibria in specific contexts
  • Reconciliation of individual vs. collective entropy minimization
  • Role of suffering in thermodynamic ethics

VI. Conclusion

The is-ought problem was never solved because it was never properly formulated. By treating "ought" as a non-physical category, philosophy created a pseudo-problem—a gap that existed only in its own definitions.

Thermodynamic Realism corrects this by identifying the physical basis of normativity: ought-statements describe constraint structures in self-maintaining systems. This is not a bridge across the gap, but a recognition that there was never a gap to bridge.

Final Formalization:

∀S self-maintaining, ∀F constraint-function:
  [Ought(S,F)] ≡ [¬F → ¬∃S(t+Δt)]

Normative language is simply high-level compression of thermodynamic necessity in goal-directed agents. The ought was always an is—we were just using the wrong grammar.

References

Foundational:

  • Hume, D. (1739). A Treatise of Human Nature
  • Schrödinger, E. (1944). What is Life?

Thermodynamics & Information Theory:

  • Shannon, C. (1948). "A Mathematical Theory of Communication"
  • Jaynes, E.T. (1957). "Information Theory and Statistical Mechanics"
  • Friston, K. (2010). "The Free-Energy Principle: A Unified Brain Theory?"

Moral Naturalism:

  • Railton, P. (1986). "Moral Realism"
  • Boyd, R. (1988). "How to Be a Moral Realist"

Evolution & Cooperation:

  • Axelrod, R. (1984). The Evolution of Cooperation
  • Nowak, M. (2006). "Five Rules for the Evolution of Cooperation"

Acknowledgment: This formalization is based on the theoretical framework presented in "The Singularity of Thermodynamic Realism" by Andraž Đurič (2026)

entry.title: Metacognition and Memory Anchoring
entry.content:
In this post I want to outline a tool, something I place in the cognitive workshop where a meta-agent selects how to engage with reality, and a method I consider foundational for any agent striving for greater self-control, clarity, and directed action: metacognition, and a method I call memory anchoring. Metacognition is widely known; memory anchoring is something I developed for my own use, built on top of metacognitive practice. I am certain that established terms and existing frameworks overlap with what I describe here; I do not claim originality, only that these approaches arose independently through my own process.

My first encounter with metacognition happened long before I had a name for it. I was about seven, riding in a car on long family trips. At some point, out of boredom, my attention turned inward. What followed is difficult to describe, but it felt like an abrupt shift: a moment of intense awareness of being alive, present, and observing myself. Time felt a tiny bit slower, the world more solid, and I felt in control rather than on autopilot.

The moment passed quickly, but later I recalled it, and the same state returned like flipping a switch. I realized that the original lapse wasn’t due to inability but distraction. So I tried to hold the state intentionally. I didn’t know it then, but I was experimenting with sustained self-awareness.

Many years later, close to age 24, I tried to describe that childhood experience to an AI. It identified the pattern as metacognition, which pulled me into deeper research and exploration. The more I learned, the clearer it became that metacognition is not just a philosophical concept; it is a practical tool that can be deliberately trained and applied.

With practice, I managed to stay metacognitively aware for extended periods (sometimes hours per day) though it came with a metabolic cost. Maintaining continuous monitoring of one’s own cognition is taxing, and pushing it too far is counterproductive. It was precisely because it felt metabolically expensive that I started thinking about how to activate metacognition more efficiently, only when needed, without trying to sustain it continuously. That line of thought eventually led me to the idea of memory anchoring.

The real challenge was applying metacognition under stress. It’s easy to stay self-aware in peaceful conditions; it’s much harder when someone is yelling at you, when you’re afraid, or when the conversation involves someone you deeply care about. Those are precisely the moments when autopilot, emotion, and cognitive shortcuts dominate, and when awareness is needed most.

For me, metacognition is guided by a central question: How can I respond in a way that produces the best outcome under a utilitarian ethic—maximizing wellbeing and minimizing unnecessary suffering? Staying aligned with that question requires awareness, emotional regulation, and logic working together.

To make metacognition reliably available in real-world situations, I developed what I call memory anchoring. It’s a personal method for linking specific memories, emotions, or contextual cues to a deliberate switch from autopilot to metacognitive mode. Again, I am fully aware that there are likely established psychological concepts, therapeutic techniques, or cognitive-science terms that overlap with this, this is simply the name I gave to the version I arrived at through my own experimentation.

The idea is simple: take an emotional state or situational pattern, and associate it with both a metacognitive trigger and a conceptual framing that supports rational, stable action.

For example, I anchor the emotion of fear to a metacognitive cue paired with the phrase: “To be courageous, you must be afraid.” The emotion becomes a signal to activate awareness rather than a force that pushes me into reactive behavior. Without that anchor, fear tends to produce scattered, irrational responses. With the anchor, it becomes a prompt for clarity.

This approach extends to other emotions and contexts; anger, stress, confusion, conflict, high-stakes decisions. Each can be tied to a self-constructed “switch” that reliably invokes awareness, logic, and intentional action.

Closing Perspective

Metacognition and memory anchoring are not abstract philosophies for me; they are functional tools. The first provides the capacity to observe and steer one’s own cognition. The second creates doorways into that state at the exact moments when it’s needed. Together, they help shift behavior from reactive to deliberate, from emotional turbulence to controlled response, and from autopilot to agency.

Disclaimer

Everything described here comes from my own subjective experimentation with my own mind. While I aim to be precise, all of this should be held with appropriate epistemic uncertainty. In simple terms: treat these observations as personal experience, and take them with a few grains of salt.

entry.title: Thermodynamic Realism: A Unified Framework for Existence, Knowledge, and Value
entry.content:
Thermodynamic Realism: A Unified Framework for Existence, Knowledge, and Value Abstract This thesis develops a unified philosophical framework grounded in the second law of thermodynamics and the information‐theoretic limits of computation. The central claim is that ontology, epistemology, ethics, aesthetics and meaning emerge from the physical constraints faced by self‐maintaining systems. Living agents exist only by exporting entropy; they must therefore perform thermodynamic work to sustain the patterns that constitute them. From this fact follow three further imperatives: accurate world‑modelling (epistemic clarity), cooperative behaviour (kindness), and efficient pattern compression (beauty). The framework connects classic results such as Landauer’s bound on erasure and the variational free energy principle to moral philosophy, showing that deception and misalignment impose measurable energetic costs. It proposes falsifiable predictions across biological, cognitive and artificial systems and outlines a methodology inspired by Nobel‐laureate polymathy and cross‑disciplinary synthesis. Throughout, the exposition maintains logical rigor, explicit assumptions, and epistemic humility.

1. Ontological Foundation: The Thermodynamic Universe

1.1. Matter–Energy Configuration

Physics describes the universe as a collection of matter–energy configurations obeying conservation laws. The second law of thermodynamics states that in any spontaneous process the total entropy of an isolated system either increases or remains constant 1 . Entropy measures the dispersal of energy; disorder increases because there are overwhelmingly more disordered microstates than ordered ones. Structures such as stars, cells or brains temporarily resist entropy increase by exporting disorder to their surroundings.

1.2. Origin and Innocence

No conscious agent chooses its initial conditions—genetic makeup, neural architecture or socio‑historical context. These parameters result from prior causal chains and, under the second law, from low‑entropy fluctuations. Because agents do not control their origin, they bear no moral blame for their starting points. This establishes baseline innocence and shifts ethical responsibility to actions performed after self‑maintenance begins.

1.3. Existence as Gradient Climbing

To exist is to create local order against a global trend toward disorder. Agents extract usable energy from gradients (food, light, electrical potential) and transduce it into work to repair and reproduce. The creation of order must be balanced with rest and playful exploration; otherwise, resource depletion and accumulated damage cause collapse. The continuous management of energy budgets underpins the rest of this framework.

1

2. The Epistemic Engine: Dissolving the Is–Ought Gap

2.1. Information Constraints and Landauer’s Bound

Computation is physical. Logical irreversibility—erasing or merging information—dissipates energy. Landauer’s principle states that the minimum energy required to erase one bit of information is k<sub>B</ sub>T ln 2, where k<sub>B</sub> is Boltzmann’s constant and T the absolute temperature 2 . At room temperature this corresponds to roughly 2.9×10⁻²¹ J per bit. Real devices dissipate far more energy per operation. This limit implies that deceptive behaviour, which requires overwriting internal states to maintain contradictions, must incur additional energy costs.

2.2. Variational Free Energy and Active Inference

Modern neuroscience proposes that adaptive systems minimize variational free energy—an upper bound on surprise. In the free‑energy principle, the brain constructs generative models of its environment and acts to minimize prediction error. As Gershman summarises, the free energy principle (FEP) states, in a nutshell, that the brain seeks to minimize surprise 3 . Under FEP, perception, learning and action are unified: agents update their beliefs to match sensory input and act to make the world conform to their predictions. Minimizing surprise conserves metabolic resources and improves survival.

2.3. From “Is” to “Ought”

Hume’s is–ought problem holds that prescriptive statements cannot be derived from descriptive facts. The present framework dissolves the gap by recognising that agents are physical processes with persistence constraints. If an agent exists and wants to continue existing, and if existence requires resisting entropy (second law), then it ought to act in ways that minimise free energy and maximise negentropy. This is not metaphysical magic; it is a restatement of the engineering requirement for self‑maintenance. Ethical imperatives are therefore descriptive of optimal strategies for goal‑directed systems under physical law.

3. Ethical Architecture: Reality Alignment

3.1. Reality as Sole Authority

Reality—the set of physical facts and regularities—exists independent of any agent’s preferences. Consequently, it is the only non‑arbitrary authority. Traditions, institutions and dogmas derive legitimacy only insofar as they correspond to reality. Misrepresenting or ignoring reality creates prediction error, which increases free energy and accelerates entropy production.

3.2. The Principle of Non‑Betrayal

The core normative commitment of this thesis is: Never betray reality. When reality and any other force—comfort, power or survival—conflict, reality takes precedence. Betraying reality (lying, self‑deception) forces a system to maintain inconsistent states. According to Landauer’s bound, each bit of overwritten information dissipates energy 2 ; therefore, systematic misalignment incurs a measurable energetic “consistency tax.”

2

3.3. Responsibility and the Stimulus–Response Gap

Agents are responsible not for their starting conditions but for what they do with them. Responsibility lives in the gap between stimulus and response: how we update our beliefs, which actions we choose given our capacities, how we treat others, and whether we adjust when proven wrong. Pre‑commitment to reality alignment must be made outside moments of acute threat because survival instincts can override judgment. Fear is data—an indicator of risk—not a valid argument against reality‑aligned action.

3.4. Dual Ethical Imperative

From the thermodynamic analysis emerge two complementary moral imperatives:

  1. See clearly: minimize prediction error by seeking accurate information, updating beliefs when confronted with evidence, and cultivating epistemic humility. FEP frames this as minimising free energy 3 .
  2. Act kindly: minimize friction and collective free energy. Cooperative coupling reduces the metabolic cost of persistence. When two systems integrate their generative models, the total free energy of the combined system can be lower than the sum of the parts. Social virtues such as compassion, honesty and fairness are strategies that optimize energy efficiency across scales.

These imperatives converge: clarity without kindness leads to brittle isolation; kindness without clarity devolves into sentimentality. Long‑horizon persistence requires both.

4. Aesthetic Integration: Art as Compression

4.1. Beauty as Pattern Recognition

Artistic beauty is traditionally treated as subjective. Here it is reinterpreted as the subjective reward for recognising high‑fidelity compression of real patterns. Information theory shows that ordered structures are compressible, whereas randomness is not. When an artwork captures genuine structure—whether physical (light behaviour), mathematical (symmetry), psychological (emotional salience) or temporal (impermanence)—the brain rewards the observer with a feeling of beauty. Patterns that exist in reality can be compressed efficiently; noise cannot.

4.2. Lessons from Empirical Testing

Experience with generative models and human audiences provides three constraints on art as compression:

  1. Direct observation: Compression requires first‑hand perception. Borrowed patterns (e.g. recreating Van Gogh’s sky) can produce aesthetic impact but lack emotional truth. Compressing one’s own observation (e.g. a childhood memory of crushing a ladybug) produces a deeper response.
  2. Specificity over universality: Abstract representations of “entropy,” “growth and decay” or “cosmic dissolution” fail because they attempt to compress generalities. Effective works compress specific instances—this nail, this ladybug, this moment. The universal emerges from the particular.
  3. Restraint: Efficient compression demands saying one thing clearly rather than many things simultaneously. Overloading an image with multiple metaphors results in noise. A single compressed theme allows the underlying pattern to be perceived.

3

The aesthetic module thus complements the ethical one: beauty rewards the detection of reality and punishes arbitrary noise. Training in art becomes training in pattern recognition; disagreement among observers reflects differences in pattern attunement rather than relativism.

5. Consciousness, Emotions and Meaning

5.1. Thermodynamic Telemetry

Emotions are not arbitrary feelings but signals about the system’s thermodynamic state. Mapping emotional valence to energy gradients yields a taxonomy: fear detects high‑entropy trajectories, anger mobilizes energy against external misalignment, love reflects low‑free‑energy coupling, joy signals alignment with optimal trajectories, grief marks abrupt entropy increase, and guilt indicates self‑caused entropy growth. These signals guide agents toward energy‑efficient strategies.

entry.title: Slovenia Is Complicit in a Genocide
entry.content:
Slovenia Is Complicit in a Genocide

How a small state funded it at arm's length, exempted the one thing that mattered from its own embargo, declined the court, and then sponsored it openly

Investigative position note · the embargo's exemption, the dependency, the veto, graded responsibility, and the index on which the verdicts rest

Andraž Đurič

Version 1 · published 17 September 2026 · events current to 10 September 2026

In plain language

For years Slovenia bought Israeli missiles through a German company — which is how a country buys Israeli weapons without ever writing a cheque to Israel. Then in July 2025 it became the only country in the European Union to ban the arms trade with Israel, and was praised for it. The ban had an exception written into it from the first day: Israeli computer and security systems could still come and go, because the country needs them. That is the one thing Slovenia actually buys from Israel. The state's own computer network runs on it. So does the network at the nuclear plant. So do the police. The ban forbade what Slovenia was not buying and allowed what it was. Seven months later the government sat down behind closed doors and decided not to join the genocide case South Africa had brought against Israel at the world court, and the reason it gave was that Slovenia depends on Israeli systems. The one dependency the ban had been careful to leave alone had become the reason for staying home — and nobody has ever checked whether that dependency was real, because the meeting was secret. That was the government people remember as the good one. The next one simply stopped pretending: it scrapped the measures, blocked a European statement against illegal settlements, opened the embassy, and signed a deal covering defence and artificial intelligence. So this is not one man's doing, though one man is doing the loudest part of it. Two governments built it, and between them they were put in office by more than half of everyone in this country who can vote. None of this is the crime of helping to commit a genocide. That needs a court, and nobody here is accused of it. It does mean it was done in our name and with our money, and that there is no way to do the arithmetic that leaves any of us standing outside it. Myself included.

A simplified statement of what this document concludes, for a reader who will not read the thirty thousand words below it. It carries no sources and no standings; every claim in it is established, qualified and sourced in the sections that follow, and where the two differ the sections govern. It is revised whenever the Conclusion is.

Abstract

On 9 September 2026 Israel opened an embassy in Ljubljana. The Israeli foreign minister signed a cooperation programme running to 2030 that covers defence and artificial intelligence, a state secretary offered Israeli firms Slovenia as their entry point to the European single market, and the prime minister attended. A criminal complaint alleging war crimes, genocide and torture had been filed against the visiting minister with Slovenian prosecutors two days earlier. Outside, protesters demanded the embassy be closed.

This document establishes a narrower and more durable claim than the one the day invites. Slovenia's complicity did not begin in June 2026 and does not belong to one party. Slovenian purchases of Israeli weaponry were reported at €57.5 million across 2019–2023 with €31.5 million more programmed through 2026, including Spike missiles funded by the same government that imposed the European Union's only arms embargo on Israel, though the source audit below establishes that this money reached the Israeli state manufacturer Rafael through equity and licence in a German-majority joint venture rather than by direct payment. The same audit establishes something sharper: the arms embargo of 31 July 2025, the measure that made Slovenia a European first, contained from adoption a written exception for equipment needed for security and resilience, which the government identified as information and cyber-defence systems. That is the precise category of Israeli supply that seven months later was cited as the reason Slovenia could not go to court. The embargo prohibited what Slovenia did not need. Bilateral trade reached a record €244 million in 2025, during that embargo. Slovenia's state administration network, its nuclear power plant and its police run on Israeli security and forensic products. On 12 March 2026, in a classified session, the Golob cabinet declined to join South Africa's genocide case at the International Court of Justice; the reasons reported were that Israeli firms manage the cybersecurity of Slovenia's critical infrastructure, and that Israel facilitates Slovenian humanitarian and evacuation operations. A state said, in substance, that it could not go to court against another state because it runs on that state's equipment. Whether that constraint was real has never been tested: the session was classified and the reasoning has not been published, and the empirical literature on supplier leverage gives some reason to doubt it. Slovenia may not have lost the capacity to act. It may only have believed it had.

The election of 22 March 2026 was won by Robert Golob's Freedom Movement, not by Janez Janša. Janša is prime minister because Golob failed to assemble a coalition and he did not. His government then converted quiet material complicity into declared policy: revoking every restrictive measure in June, announcing that Slovenia will freeze its recognition of Palestine and move its embassy to Jerusalem, blocking the EU27 statement on the E1 settlement plan in August, and signing the cooperation programme in September.

Complicity is used here in one sense, fixed in section 1 before it is applied to anyone: a state under a triggered duty to prevent has, in its material conduct, moved consistently in the other direction, and since June 2026 has done so as declared policy. It is not the criminal offence under Article III(e) of the Genocide Convention, which is not asserted. Responsibility is graded across six tiers, and the grading is indexed rather than free-floating: the normative weight is carried by a treaty Slovenia signed and by an account of Slovenia's own persistence conditions, not by a direct duty to the Palestinians, which runs through an open problem this corpus has not solved and which is therefore not relied upon. The Slovenian citizenry bears political guilt in Jaspers' sense for the conduct of its state, graduated by participation; the unqualified claim that the electorate is guilty is rejected, because it asserts the one species of guilt no voter bears.

The prime minister's public defence is that no competent institution has established genocide under international law. One third of that is true and the rest is not, and even the true third licenses at most agnosticism about a word. It does not license the acts.

Epistemic key

Claims below do not inherit one another's standing because they appear in one document.

MarkMeaning in this document
DocumentedMultiple independent sources, or a primary record. The fact is not in dispute between parties who disagree about its meaning.
ReportedOne credible source, or several tracing to one. Attributed in the text rather than asserted.
ContestedAsserted by one party and denied by another. This mark awards no parity. A denial is a fact about what a party said, not evidence about what happened, and an interested party's bare denial does not offset a record. Every contested entry states which side is weaker and why. Where the sides are genuinely matched, the entry says so, because that is also a finding.
Legal statusWhat a court, commission or convention has and has not formally concluded. Bodies with different mandates and proof thresholds are not collapsed.
ArguedA conclusion reached by derivation rather than observation, holding relative to a named index. This does not mark a claim as non-factual. An ought, once its agent and frame are named, is a determinate fact about what that agent's persistence requires. The mark records that the claim is agent-relative, that its index is stated in section 9, and that the reduction from the stated ought to the physical floor is owed rather than paid. Reject an entry here by rejecting the index or the derivation. An ought with its index stripped off is not a bolder claim; it is an ill-formed one.

Status at the time of writing. Events in this document are current to 10 September 2026, and several things in it are live rather than settled. The relocation of the embassy to Jerusalem and the freezing of Palestine's recognition are announced and not executed. The constitutional charge against the prime minister has been filed and needs 46 votes. The interpellation of the foreign minister has been announced. The petition to rename Dimičeva ulica falls to be decided in October. The merits case at the International Court of Justice will not be heard for years. The Conclusion near the end is a live section, revised whenever the audit changes what the evidence supports; its stamp names the audit version it was drafted against. The section before it states how to correct this document and what happens when someone does.

Trigger check, 17 September 2026, re-run at publication. None of the events listed below has occurred. The constitutional charge against the prime minister has been filed but not voted; the interpellation of the foreign minister has been announced but not heard; the cabinet session of 12 March remains classified; the defence ministry's procurement record remains unpublished; the embassy has not moved and the recognition of Palestine has not been formally touched. The foreign minister answered the charges publicly on 10 September and his answer is in section 8. The document stands as written.

A Version 2 is owed if any of the following occurs: the embassy moves or the recognition is formally withdrawn; the constitutional charge or the interpellation is voted on; the defence ministry publishes the procurement record; the cabinet session of 12 March 2026 is declassified; or the Commission of Inquiry revises its findings.

Confidence is claim-specific. Very high for the procurement figures, the trade figures, the election result, and the sequence of acts from June to September 2026. High for the genocide finding on the current total evidence, and for the account of why Slovenia declined the ICJ intervention. Lower where a single outlet carries a fact, or where a government denial and a documentary record conflict and neither has been tested under oath.

1. The claim, and the word in the title

Slovenia has, over seven years and under four governments of both political orientations, transferred public money to Israeli arms manufacturers, built operational dependencies on Israeli security products, and expanded bilateral trade throughout the destruction of Gaza. That is the material record, and it belongs to nearly everyone.

Since June 2026 a second thing has been true, and it is not the same thing. The government formed by Janez Janša has converted a quiet material relationship into declared political sponsorship. These are separate charges with separate evidence and separate defendants. Collapsing them produces tribal accounting in which each reader's own side is clean. Keeping them apart produces something harder to dismiss and harder to live with.

Complicity is doing precise work and is fixed now, before it touches anyone:

Complicity, as used here. A state under a triggered duty to prevent has, in its material conduct, moved consistently in the other direction, and since June 2026 has done so as declared policy.

Everything in the title is that claim and nothing more. It does not mean Slovenia committed genocide. It does not assert the criminal offence of complicity in genocide under Article III(e) of the Convention, which requires knowledge of the principal's specific intent together with the provision of aid or assistance to it; whether Slovenian conduct meets that threshold is not established here and I do not claim it. It does not mean Slovenian equipment killed anyone in Gaza, because the transfer runs the other way, as sections 4 and 5 set out.

The claim is smaller than the placards on Dimičeva and larger than the government will concede. It also cannot be answered by observing that Slovenia is small, which is the answer it will get, and which section 11 addresses directly.

2. Distinctions and concessions

This subject is structurally vulnerable to the errors it condemns, and a document that names voters is vulnerable to one in particular. Four of the six below hold apart categories that this argument routinely collapses; two concede facts that cut against it. Both kinds are part of the argument, not throat-clearing before it.

  1. No collective criminal guilt, in any direction. Jews are not the Israeli state; Israelis are not their cabinet; Palestinians are not Hamas; and no Slovene acquires criminal liability by voting. Section 10 does hold that Slovenian citizens bear political guilt for their state's conduct, graduated by participation, and it argues for that against Arendt's objection rather than assuming it. The two claims are compatible because the species differ, and the document names the species every time.
  2. Criticism of a state is not hatred of a people. Antisemitism is false and morally corrupt, and it is not made true or excusable by anything in this document. Naming a Slovenian government's conduct toward Israel is a claim about Ljubljana, not about Jews.
  3. Hamas committed atrocities on 7 October 2023 — deliberate killing of civilians, hostage-taking, war crimes and crimes against humanity. Verified crimes do not authorise genocide, and the reverse is equally true: a genocide finding does not retroactively excuse 7 October.
  4. The previous government's real acts are not erased by its inconsistency. Recognising Palestine, imposing the Union's only arms embargo and declaring three Israeli ministers persona non grata were genuine and costly. Section 6's charge against that government is inconsistency at the point of expense, which is a lesser charge than the one in section 10's first tier, and it is stated as a lesser charge.
  5. Public figures are named for public acts. Every quotation attributed to a named person here was verified in the body of a published article, never from a headline alone; one widely circulated remark was cut at the drafting stage because it could not be verified that way. Where a publication's headline is the only thing I could retrieve, section 5 says so and treats it as a headline. No private individual is named.
  6. Slovenia's causal contribution to events in Gaza is negligible and nothing here suggests otherwise. The argument is about the character of Slovenia's own acts under its own obligations. Section 11 explains why negligible causal contribution does not dissolve the question, and section 15 records the assumption on which that rests.

3. What is being financed

In a report dated 18 June 2026 and announced on 23 June, the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory (A/HRC/62/CRP.2, covering 7 October 2023 to 31 March 2026) found that Israeli authorities and security forces “have deliberately targeted Palestinian children resulting in genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes in the Gaza Strip and war crimes in the West Bank.” It recorded the deliberate killing and injuring of children, the targeting of neonatal and maternity care, the destruction of orphanages and schools, sexual violence against children, the imprisonment and torture of children, and starvation imposed through blockade and siege. It found these continuing after the October 2025 ceasefire, and recorded at least 20,179 children killed and 44,143 injured on its own verification standard. This was its second such determination; the first came in September 2025 (A/HRC/60/CRP.3). Documented.

The ceasefire that began on 10 October 2025 reduced the scale of hostilities without ending them. By 17 June 2026 Medical Aid for Palestinians recorded at least 1,005 Palestinians killed and 3,157 injured since it took effect, no fully functioning hospitals, 62 per cent of primary healthcare medications out of stock, and Israeli control of roughly 60 per cent of Gaza's territory beyond the agreed lines. Documented.

I published the casualty arithmetic in April 2026 and will not restate it beyond the anchor: roughly 72,300 named direct deaths, approximately 21,300 of them children, 88 per cent of the population displaced, and a peer-reviewed indirect-mortality projection above 186,000. That analysis stopped deliberately at the border of attribution, noting that intent was a legal determination then before the International Court of Justice. This document crosses that border, because the question has since been answered by the body competent to examine it and because a government has made the answer load-bearing for policy.

The prime minister's objection, at its strongest

On 28 August 2026, responding to President Nataša Pirc Musar, Janša wrote:

“Prisegati na mednarodno pravo in hkrati govoriti o genocidu v Gazi ali v Judeji in Samariji (znanih tudi kot Zahodni breg), ki ga po mednarodnem pravu nobena pristojna institucija ni ugotovila – je politična izbira posebne vrste.”

“To swear by international law and at the same time speak of a genocide in Gaza or in Judea and Samaria (also known as the West Bank) which no competent institution has established under international law — is a political choice of a particular kind.”

Take it seriously, because one third is correct.

True. No court has issued a merits judgment. On 21 May 2026 the ICJ fixed South Africa's Reply for 22 November 2027 and Israel's Rejoinder for 22 May 2029. A ruling is years away and may arrive after everyone named here has left office. Anyone claiming a court has convicted Israel of genocide is wrong, and should be corrected every time. Legal status.

False. “No competent institution” is not a description of the record. The Commission of Inquiry is a competent institution, established under the Human Rights Council, and it made the finding twice. What Janša means is no court. What he wrote is broader and untrue, and the difference does the work in the sentence.

Insufficient. The obligation does not wait for the merits. Under Article I of the Genocide Convention, as the ICJ construed it in Bosnia and Herzegovina v. Serbia and Montenegro (2007), the duty to prevent arises “at the instant that the State learns of, or should normally have learned of, the existence of a serious risk that genocide will be committed.” The Court has issued three sets of provisional measures and found that Palestinians in Gaza face a real and imminent risk of irreparable prejudice. Slovenia is a party to the Convention. The trigger has been pulled irrespective of the merits timetable. Documented.

So the strongest version of the government's position licenses agnosticism about a word. It does not license the acts. Nothing in “the court has not yet ruled” permits lifting an arms embargo, blocking a statement on illegal settlements, or signing a defence and artificial-intelligence cooperation programme. A government genuinely waiting for the court would have left the measures in place until it ruled.

A category error, already named in this corpus

The deeper problem with the objection is one I have set out elsewhere in general form. In Matt Dillahunty, Tone, and the Ethics of Debate I wrote that appealing to legality in answer to a moral or epistemic critique is a category error: something is not automatically moral because it is legal, nor immoral because it is illegal. In Relata-Indexed Objectivity the same point appears in its institutional form: a court may possess legal authority under a jurisdiction while lacking moral or epistemic authority in a particular case.

Those were written about other subjects and they govern here without amendment. “No competent institution has established it” is an argument about the status of a legal finding offered as an answer to a question about conduct. Even if the legal claim were fully true, it would settle what a court has said and not what Slovenia should do. This is not a technicality retrieved for convenience; it is a standing commitment of this corpus, and it would apply just as forcefully if a court's ruling were the one I preferred.

The point has a long legal pedigree on both sides of the positivist divide. Gustav Radbruch's post-war formula holds that statutory law reaching an intolerable degree of injustice ceases to be law; H. L. A. Hart replied that the honest course is to concede the law's validity and disobey it, precisely so that the moral question is not concealed inside a definitional one. The disagreement is about where to locate the objection, not about whether legality settles morality. Neither position gives Janša his conclusion.

4. The money, and where it actually went

The headline figures first, then the correction that the source audit below forced on them, because the correction is more interesting than the figures.

Reporting in November 2024, drawing on defence ministry plans and material obtained by Levica, put Slovenian purchases of Israeli weapons and ammunition at €57.5 million across 2019–2023, with a further €31.5 million programmed for 2024–2026, including €15.3 million for Spike missiles — €12.3 million in 2025 and €3 million in 2026. Reported. The 2024–2026 figure describes planned expenditure, not executed payments.

What the ministry actually said, and why it matters

I originally recorded the defence ministry's denial as evasive. That was wrong, and the audit below records the correction. The denial is specific and, on its own terms, true:

“Slovenija od začetka vojne v Gazi v Izraelu ni kupila nobenega orožja, streliva ali druge vojaške opreme. Prav tako ni izdala nobenega dovoljenja za izvoz tovrstnega blaga iz Slovenije v Izrael.”

“Since the beginning of the war in Gaza, Slovenia has not purchased any weapons, ammunition or other military equipment in Israel. Nor has it issued any permit for the export of such goods from Slovenia to Israel.”

On the Spike systems specifically, the ministry stated that the 2022–2023 acquisitions were made through NATO's procurement agency and through EuroSpike, the European manufacturer majority-owned by the German firms Rheinmetall and Diehl, and that “ministrstvo pri tem nakupu ni izvajalo plačil izraelskim proizvajalcem orožja”, the ministry made no payments to Israeli weapons manufacturers, all system components having been produced by European manufacturers. Documented.

Levica's answer is that EuroSpike is co-owned by Rafael Advanced Defense Systems, the Israeli state-owned firm that developed Spike, holds the intellectual property and receives licence revenue on every unit sold. Documented.

Both are true, and that is the finding

This is not a case where one party is lying. Slovenian money for Spike systems went to a German-registered joint venture, for components manufactured in Europe, under a NATO framework. Israeli revenue nonetheless flowed from those purchases, by equity and licence rather than by invoice. The ministry's statement is literally true and materially incomplete; Levica's charge is materially true and literally imprecise. Each side's formulation is chosen to make the other's inaudible.

Three consequences follow, and the third is larger than Slovenia.

  • The piece cannot claim Slovenia paid Israeli manufacturers directly, and no longer does. The composition of the 2019–2023 figure — how much was direct acquisition and how much routed through European intermediaries — is not established by any source I have traced. It is recorded in the audit as an open gap.
  • The relationship is real regardless. Revenue reaching Rafael through a joint venture is revenue reaching Rafael. A licensing structure changes the route, not the destination, and no honest accounting treats a state-owned arms manufacturer's equity and licence income as unconnected to it.
  • The route is not a Slovenian peculiarity. It is the standard European one.

The EuroSpike route, and who else uses it

EuroSpike GmbH is owned 40 per cent by Rheinmetall, 40 per cent by Diehl Defence and 20 per cent by Rafael. Eighty per cent German, twenty per cent Israeli state-owned, and it is the vehicle through which European states buy the Spike family. Two cases show what the structure does. Documented.

Spain. In June 2025 Pedro Sánchez's government suspended a €285 million contract with Rafael for Spike LR2 — 168 launchers, 1,680 missiles — signed in October 2023, as part of Spain's arms embargo on Israel. In February 2026 Spain acquired the same weapon: MELLS, the European designation of the Spike LR2, through EuroSpike. The stated justification was that MELLS components are manufactured in Europe. Spain also bought €7 million of Israeli defence products in 2024 and €10.2 million in 2025, embargo notwithstanding.

Germany. In August 2025 the Merz government suspended arms exports to Israel that could be used in Gaza. In October 2025 Germany signed a Spike procurement of roughly €2 billion through EuroSpike, executed under a NATO framework — its largest ever. Industry sources quoted at the time said the joint venture's European ownership structure was what made the deal possible despite the diplomatic position Berlin had taken.

The Spanish justification and the Slovenian defence ministry's are the same sentence in two languages: the components are European. It is true in both cases. It is also the formula by which a European state that has announced an arms embargo on Israel continues to buy an Israeli-designed weapon from a company an Israeli state firm part-owns, and this is understood well enough inside European defence ministries to be described to the trade press as the thing that made a two-billion-euro deal possible.

One precision, because it cuts the other way. Germany's measure restricted exports to Israel and never covered procurement, so nothing there was circumvented; the inconsistency is political rather than legal. Spain's and Slovenia's measures did cover imports, which makes the routing question sharper for them than for Berlin.

5. What the embargo did not touch

Slovenia's arms embargo of 31 July 2025 is the act everything else is judged against. It is cited whenever the previous government's record is defended, it is what made Slovenia a European first, and it is the thing the current government revoked. It is therefore worth establishing what it actually covered, which is not what its reception assumed.

What the Slovenian decree actually said

Here the Slovenian case stops being an instance of a European pattern and becomes something more specific. The decree of 31 July 2025 prohibited the export, import and transit of military weapons and equipment to and from Israel. It also contained an exception, and the exception was not discovered later by anyone. It was announced the next day, 1 August 2025, by State Secretary Boštjan Pavlin of the defence ministry, in the same breath as the measure itself. The government permitted

“uvoz, izvoz in tranzit tistih sredstev iz Izraela, ki so za Republiko Slovenijo pomembna z vidika odpornosti in varnosti naše države”

“the import, export and transit of those means from Israel which are important for the Republic of Slovenia from the standpoint of the resilience and security of our country”

and named the category it had in mind: “različna informacijska oziroma sredstva za kibernetsko obrambo” — various information or cyber-defence means. Documented, by a named official, on the record, at the time.

The corroboration matters because of what it rules out. Two Slovenian outlets carried it on 1 August 2025, and so did the foreign press: a Ukrainian outlet reported the same day that the restrictions did not apply to technologies of strategic importance to Slovenian national security, listing cybersecurity, information systems and other resources ensuring the state's defence capability. Three independent reports, two languages, one day. The exemption was not a domestic framing that international coverage missed. It was how the measure was described to the world at the moment Slovenia was being credited with the European Union's first arms embargo on Israel.

The European Union's only arms embargo on Israel exempted, in its own text, the exact category of Israeli supply that Slovenia actually depended on, and seven months later that same dependency was the stated reason Slovenia did not go to the International Court of Justice.

On the arms component, the measure prohibited what Slovenia did not need and permitted what it did.

The qualification matters and is not a retreat. The July 2025 package was not only an arms ban: it also prohibited settlement products and declared three Israeli ministers persona non grata, and those were real measures that touched real things. The compression above applies to the arms prohibition specifically, which is the component that made Slovenia a European first and the component the exemption hollowed. A reader entitled to hold this document to its own standards is entitled to that distinction.

Two readings are available and the honest position does not choose between them, because the record does not. A security and resilience carve-out is defensible on its face: no government is obliged to break its own critical infrastructure to make a gesture, and a state that had wired its administration, its nuclear plant and its police to Israeli products could not have unwired them by decree in a month. On the other reading, a government that knew where its dependency lay wrote the exception that spared it, announced the remainder as a European first, and was credited accordingly.

What the measure did establish

The section so far says what the embargo was not. It owes the other half, because a document that only ever subtracts is not describing a thing; it is prosecuting one. Stripped of its reception, the decree says something coherent: Slovenia will not trade in weapons with this state, and will keep running the systems its own administration is wired to. That is a position, not a vacancy. No other member state held it at the time; Spain’s total embargo followed in September 2025. Slovenia went first, ahead of the Union rather than behind it, with no European decision requiring it and against the standing practice of the two states that between them supply ninety-nine per cent of Israel’s major arms imports. Documented. Being first is also the only evidence of self-direction this document can offer, and it carries the narrow form of that claim and not a wider one: a state cannot be following when nobody is ahead of it. Whether domestic pressure moved the government is not established either way. Argued.

The measure was also not cost-free in the way the compression above implies, only cheap in the one dimension the audit can measure. It cost Slovenia nothing in foregone arms purchases because there were none to forego. What it cost in standing with Washington and Berlin, and inside the Union, is not quantified anywhere in this document and is not claimed to be zero.

Both halves hold at once, and the second is what this document is about. A measure can be genuinely creditable, which this one was and which twenty-five other member states cannot say, and taken without being asked, and still have left standing the exact dependency that was given, seven months later, as the reason not to go to court. Neither fact cancels the other. A reader who leaves with only the first has taken the comfortable half; a reader who leaves with only the second has taken the easy one.

What is not available is the version in which the embargo was what it was said to be. Whether the carve-out was prudence or design, its effect is not in dispute, and nobody in the government that wrote it has been asked to say which it was.

Read the dates against the political calendar. That span covers the government of Marjan Šarec, Janša's third government, and the government of Robert Golob. It covers the period in which Slovenia recognised Palestine by parliamentary vote on 4 June 2024, the period in which the Golob government described Israel's conduct as genocide, and the period beginning 31 July 2025 in which Slovenia became the first EU member state to prohibit all trade in military equipment with Israel. The Spike allocation for 2026 was budgeted by the government that imposed that prohibition.

The Ministry of Defence denied purchasing Israeli weapons and ammunition. Delo reported the denial under a headline stating that the ministry conceals a great deal, and Levica responded publicly afterwards. The full text of neither report could be retrieved, so the exchange is recorded here only at the level those published headlines support. Contested, asymmetrically. The denial is a ministry's characterisation of its own conduct, offered without publishing the underlying procurement records; the figures come from budget lines and answers to parliamentary questions. A denial that does not engage the documents it contradicts is weaker than the documents. The figures stand until the ministry publishes the record, and its not having done so is itself a finding.

Trade tells the same story more plainly. Bilateral trade reached a record €244.03 million in 2025 — €130.96 million in Slovenian exports and €113.07 million in imports, with exports at their highest recorded level in the year the embargo was in force. The first seven months of 2026 ran ahead of that pace. Documented.

What Slovenia sent, and what it did not watch

One inference needs separating from the fact it was drawn from.

Slovenia issued no arms export permits to Israel after October 2023. That is accurate, and the conclusion that Slovenia therefore sent nothing does not follow from it. On 7 July 2025, three weeks before the embargo, Defence Minister Borut Sajovic stated that since October 2023 Slovenia had exported defence products worth €98,905 to Israel under previously issued licences: nineteen rough-worked mortar forgings at €94,905, two hundred and three rough-worked aluminium castings at €4,000, and thirteen free samples. No new permits; continuing exports. Documented.

The sum is trivial against a €244 million trade relationship and the items are unfinished components rather than weapons. It is still not nothing, and the difference between “issued no permits” and “sent nothing” is the kind of difference this document exists to keep. Slovenia shipped mortar forgings to Israel during the war in Gaza. Whoever wants to argue that rough-worked forgings are not arms should make that argument rather than have it made for them by a sentence about permits.

The second half of Sajovic's statement is larger than the first. Asked about the transit of European weapons to Israel across Slovenian territory, he said the defence ministry “ne izdaja tranzitnih dovoljenj, niti ne vodi evidenc o vrsti in količini” — does not issue transit permits, nor keep records of the type and quantity — and that it “praviloma ni seznanjeno s količino in vrsto obrambnih proizvodov v tranzitu”, is as a rule not informed of what is passing through. Three transit approvals were granted in the period, all of them equipment going back to Israel after servicing or demonstration. Documented.

Three weeks after the ministry said it does not track what transits Slovenia, the government prohibited the transit of military equipment to Israel and announced it as the first such measure in the European Union.

A prohibition on movements nobody records is not a prohibition; it is a statement of intent about movements nobody records. This does not prove that arms crossed Slovenia after the ban, and no source I have traced says they did. It establishes something narrower and sufficient: the state that announced the ban had told the public, on the record, that it lacked the instrument to know whether the ban was being observed. Nobody has since said that changed.

Two precisions the argument still needs, both cutting against its loudest version. The export flow to Israel was tiny, pre-licensed, and composed of components. And, per the section above, Slovenia is not straightforwardly paying Israel either: it is buying Israeli-designed systems from European intermediaries in which an Israeli state firm holds equity and licence rights.

Neither precision is exculpatory. Revenue is fungible; the Israeli defence sector is a strategic state asset whose export performance is declared national policy; and a customer participates in an industry's viability whether it pays the manufacturer or the manufacturer's joint venture. But the honest version of the charge is that Slovenia funded, indirectly and through European structures — not that Slovenia armed, and not that Slovenia wrote cheques to Tel Aviv. Anyone making this case should say so before an opponent says it for them, because an opponent will, and the ministry's statement is sitting there ready to be quoted.

6. The dependency that decided a court case

On 12 March 2026, in a session classified so that voting positions remain undisclosed, the Slovenian cabinet declined to join South Africa's genocide case at the International Court of Justice. The proposal came from Foreign Minister Tanja Fajon's ministry and failed to secure majority support. Ministers from the Social Democrats and Levica supported it. Documented.

The reasons reported were three. Israeli companies manage cybersecurity systems protecting Slovenia's critical infrastructure and defence systems. Israel plays a role in Slovenian humanitarian operations in Gaza. Israel assists in evacuating Slovenian nationals from the region. Reporting also indicated that the minister for digital transformation, Ksenija Klampfer, opposed joining on grounds of dependence on Israeli software. Reported.

Fajon afterwards:

“Eno je načelo, drugo so vprašanja nacionalne varnosti.”
“One thing is principle, another is questions of national security.”

“Če bi se Slovenija pridružila tej intervenciji, bi to pomenilo podporo delu sodišča in ne izbiranje strani.”
“If Slovenia had joined this intervention it would have meant support for the court's work, not taking sides.”

President Pirc Musar: “Take nedoslednosti ni mogoče z ničimer upravičiti” — such inconsistency cannot be justified by anything. Amnesty International: the prevention and punishment of genocide tolerates neither excuses nor calculated compromises. The Pirates put it most economically: if national security depends on Israel, we have a serious problem. Documented.

What the dependency actually consists of

Mladina's investigation of Israeli technology in Slovenian institutions gives the dependency concrete shape, and it is larger than the phrase “cyber cooperation” suggests. Reported.

  • Check Point products secure HKOM, the central state administration network connecting some 1,100 locations, 2,000 local networks and 30,000 users. An October 2022 upgrade contract was worth €961,211; a December 2024 renewal runs to 2028 at €2.5 million. The same products are used at the Krško nuclear power plant (€455,261, July 2023) and under a €3.4 million framework agreement at Ljubljana Pharmacy (June 2023).
  • Cellebrite mobile-forensic systems are used by the Slovenian police to bypass device security and extract data. Contracts include €488,583 in November 2023, €678,099 in September 2024 and €705,405 in October 2024.
  • The framework was laid on 23 August 2021, when a cybersecurity memorandum was signed during the visit of then foreign minister Anže Logar — by Uroš Svete for Slovenia's information security administration and Yigal Unna for the Israeli National Cyber Directorate. Officials say no business followed from it directly.

Two things about that last item should be stated separately, because they have different standings. That the memorandum was signed during Logar's tenure and visit is documented. That it caused the dependency which later blocked the ICJ intervention is an inference made by critics, not an established causal chain: the Check Point deployment predates it by more than a decade, and the officials involved deny commercial consequences. What is not in dispute is the shape of the result. Anže Logar's party is now a coalition partner in the government that revoked the measures, and the dependency cited in March as a reason not to go to court is being deepened in September by treaty.

One further fact belongs in the record without being leaned on. Since December 2024 the chief executive of Check Point Software Technologies has been Nadav Zafrir, founder of the Israel Defense Forces' Cyber Command and a former commander of Unit 8200. This is a matter of public corporate record. It establishes nothing about the security of Slovenian systems, and it is included because the phrase “a commercial supplier” carries an implication of distance from the state, and in this sector that distance is not obviously earned. Documented.

This is the single most important fact in the ledger, and it was produced by the government that called it genocide. A state said, in substance: we cannot go to court against this state, because we run on its equipment. That is what accumulated procurement buys the seller. It is not a bribe and requires nobody to be corrupt. It converted seven years of purchasing decisions, none of which was ever an election issue, into a constraint on Slovenia's own legal conduct at the moment that conduct would have counted.

Prior art, and a complication that makes it worse

The general mechanism has a name. Henry Farrell and Abraham Newman's weaponized interdependence describes how a state occupying a hub in an economic or informational network acquires coercive power over states that route through it — the panopticon effect, which is informational, and the chokepoint effect, which is denial of access. Any account of technological dependency shaping a small state's foreign policy is working in that frame and should say so.

The Slovenian case is a variant their framework does not quite cover, and the difference is the point. Weaponized interdependence describes leverage exercised. Nothing in this record shows Israel exercising anything. No threat is alleged, no demand is reported, no call is described. Slovenian officials identified the dependency themselves and constrained their own cabinet with it. Call it anticipatory self-deterrence: it leaves no fingerprints, produces no incident to protest, and gives the dependent state nobody to blame.

Then the complication, which cuts against the strong reading of this section and has to be stated. The empirical literature on arms-transfer leverage does not find that suppliers reliably get the influence they expect. Jennifer Spindel's study concludes that transfers fail to deliver leverage over recipients, that what leverage exists “is based on rhetorical and symbolic moves, rather than material preponderance,” and that junior partners routinely extract more from senior ones than the reverse. If that generalises, the dependency Slovenian officials cited may not have carried the power they attributed to it.

That possibility does not rescue the decision. It makes it worse, and this is the sharpest thing in the document:

The capacity may never have been lost. It may only have been believed lost. A state that yields to pressure has at least been pressed. A state that forfeits its standing before an international court on an unexamined estimate of its own dependence has done something with less excuse, and Slovenia left no record of having examined it, because the session was classified and the positions were never published. The one document that would settle whether the constraint was real does not exist in public.

This is argued, not documented. Spindel's finding is general and the Slovenian case is one instance; it is entirely possible that Israeli-origin systems in a state administration network are a harder dependency than the arms transfers she studies. What cannot be maintained is that the constraint was self-evidently real. It was asserted inside a closed room and has never been tested.

Note precisely what this shows and what it does not. It does not show that the Golob government was pro-Israel; its declaratory record was the most critical in the Union. It shows that the declaratory record was the part that was free, and that when a decision carried a cost, the dependency won. On this account Slovenia had already lost the capacity to act before the question of will arose.

7. How the government changed hands

The election of 22 March 2026 produced no mandate for what followed, and any account that says it did is wrong on the arithmetic. Documented.
