Turnout was 70.25 per cent: 1,190,932 of 1,695,249 registered voters, yielding 1,179,769 valid ballots. Janša's party lost, by 9,179 votes and one seat. He is prime minister because Golob failed to assemble a coalition by 20 April and he then did, with NSi, SLS and FOKUS, the Demokrati, and external support from Resni.ca. He was confirmed on 22 May 2026 by 51 votes to 36 in a secret ballot. Those four blocs together took 49.32 per cent of votes cast, 581,862 voters, 34.3 per cent of the registered electorate.

Israel was not the platform of any party that won seats. Janša's programme address covered economic management, anti-corruption, deregulation, decentralisation, lower taxes and private provision in education and healthcare. No party put the relocation of an embassy to Jerusalem to voters as a proposition; the announcement came five weeks after he took office.

It is not true, though, that the question was absent from the ballot. Mi, socialisti! — founded on 16 November 2025 by Miha Kordiš, the MP who had put the Israeli arms purchases to a parliamentary question a year earlier and was expelled from Levica in spring 2025 — contested the election on a platform demanding “umik Slovenije iz vojskovanja v Ukrajini, sankcije zoper Izrael in izstop iz pakta Nato” and “konec orožarskih nabav”: withdrawal from the war in Ukraine, sanctions against Israel, exit from NATO, an end to arms purchases. The list took 5,657 votes, 0.48 per cent, eleventh place, no seats. Documented.

That matters for what can be said about the electorate, and it cuts both ways. A voter in March 2026 could not have known an embassy would be promised to Jerusalem in June. A voter could have known that one list had built its foreign policy around ending exactly the relationship this document describes. Roughly one in two hundred voted for it. Whether that measures indifference or the ordinary fate of a three-month-old party with no money and no coverage, the number does not say, and neither does this document.

Asked in June whether the Demokrati supported the relocation, their parliamentary group leader Elena Zavadlav Ušaj said the party would support whatever the member states collectively agreed, and described the freezing of Palestine's recognition as a matter of the coalition agreement. That is not endorsement. It is also not refusal. Reported.

The campaign nobody has explained

On 16 March 2026, six days before the vote, Inštitut 8. marec alleged that Janša had engaged Black Cube, the Israeli private intelligence firm. It cited flight records showing an Israeli VIP aircraft landing in Slovenia three times between November 2025 and February 2026, and named Black Cube co-founder Dan Zorella and retired major general Giora Eiland among four operatives it said met Janša at SDS headquarters on 22 December 2025. Its director Nika Kovač asked Janša why he brought the agency to Slovenia, who was paying, and what he owed. Secretly recorded videos damaging to figures associated with the governing side circulated in the same period. Reported.

SOVA subsequently confirmed to the parliamentary oversight commission KNOVS that Black Cube representatives arrived in Slovenia on 22 December, supplied their names and reported further visits, while stating that it had not monitored the meeting and had no data confirming that a meeting with Janša took place. The foreign ministry summoned the Israeli ambassador. SDS said it was hearing of Black Cube for the first time, and added that if the firm had exposed corruption on the left, a monument to it should be erected in central Ljubljana. Fajon called the affair a direct attack on state sovereignty. Contested, asymmetrically.

The two positions are not evenly matched, and writing “contested” without saying so would hide a finding inside a label. On one side: flight records, an intelligence service's confirmation to a parliamentary oversight body, named individuals. On the other: an interested party saying it had not heard of the firm, offering no account of why four operatives of an Israeli private intelligence agency flew to Ljubljana three times during its campaign. A bare denial from a party with everything to lose does not offset a record. So the allegation is better supported than the denial and still short of established — SOVA confirmed an arrival and explicitly did not confirm a meeting, and that gap is real rather than rhetorical. It is why this passage carries no weight anywhere else in the document. The unresolved question is large enough alone: nobody has explained it, and the government formed weeks later has not been asked to under oath.

8. The conversion: June to September 2026

What follows took roughly a hundred days. Documented throughout.

  • 11 June 2026. The government revokes every restrictive measure: the arms-trade ban, the entry bans on Netanyahu, Ben-Gvir and Smotrich, and the ban on settlement products. Its stated purpose is to restore conditions for normal political dialogue. Gideon Sa'ar praises Janša's “swift and just decision” and calls him “a bold leader and a true friend of Israel.” The Palestinian flag comes down from the government building on Gregorčičeva.
  • 26 June 2026. Janša tells the Israeli daily Israel Hayom that Slovenia will move its embassy from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem and freeze its recognition of Palestine, which he calls an unlawful decision of his predecessors, describing the previous government's approach as having brought relations to their historic low. No EU member state has an embassy in Jerusalem.
  • The freezing, legally. Two Slovenian authorities put on the record that the announced act does not exist as described. Ernest Petrič, former ambassador and former constitutional court judge: “Poimenovanje zamrznitev, ki ga v mednarodni praksi glede priznanja države ni” — there is no such thing in international practice as freezing the recognition of a state; and “Prenehanje diplomatskih odnosov ne pomeni, da smo prekinili priznanje. Ko smo enkrat dali priznanje, še vedno priznavamo to drugo državo” — ending diplomatic relations is not withdrawing recognition; once given, recognition stands. Milan Brglez, former speaker of parliament and professor of international relations, adds that recognition was granted by a parliamentary vote in 2024 and that reversing it by executive action alone would lack the procedure its granting had, and that moving the embassy would amount to “de facto priznanje izraelske suverenosti nad Jeruzalemom”. Documented.
  • 26 August 2026. Slovenia withholds consent from the EU27 statement condemning Israel's plan to build 1,200 settler homes in E1. Consensus fails, and High Representative Kaja Kallas must issue the statement in her own name at lower diplomatic standing. The foreign ministry says it would add no value at this time. Germany, Austria, the United Kingdom, Canada and Australia issue a separate condemnation.
  • 4 September 2026. A joint session of parliamentary committees runs six hours without establishing who authorised the decision — the prime minister, the foreign minister's office, or the cabinet. Four proposed resolutions are never put to a vote. Foreign Minister Tone Kajzer states there was no veto and no blockade.
  • 9 September 2026. Israel opens its first residential embassy in Slovenia, Sa'ar's being the first visit by an Israeli foreign minister in sixteen years. Sa'ar and Kajzer sign a cooperation programme running to 2030 covering education, science, culture, youth and sport, technology and cybersecurity, defence and artificial intelligence, agriculture, medicine and water management. Svoboda and Levica file a constitutional charge against Janša, citing the Constitution, the Foreign Affairs Act, the UN Charter and UN resolutions; it needs 46 votes to proceed. SD declines to co-sign and files an interpellation against Kajzer instead.

Also on 9 September, at a business forum closed to the press at Israeli request and with the participant list withheld by the Chamber of Commerce, State Secretary Štefan Kušar told twelve Israeli and more than thirty-five Slovenian companies that Slovenia, as an EU and eurozone member, gives firms access to a single European market of more than 450 million consumers. Israel's Eden Bar Tal described Slovenia as an important entry point to European markets. The sectors named were advanced technologies, artificial intelligence, healthcare, agribusiness, water technologies, transport and tourism.

Kajzer's framing of the day was economic and unguarded: “Mislim, da smo gospodarske odnose z Izraelom v zadnjih letih zanemarili” — I think we have neglected economic relations with Israel in recent years. And: “Želel bi biti optimist in napovedati, da se bo naslednje leto, ko se spet dobimo, menjava med državama bistveno povečala” — I would like to be an optimist and predict that next year, when we meet again, trade between the two countries will have substantially increased. Both were said about a relationship that had just set a trade record.

Two days earlier the Belgian-based Hind Rajab Foundation had filed a criminal complaint with Slovenian police and prosecutors against Sa'ar, alleging responsibility for war crimes, genocide and torture on the basis of his participation in security cabinet decisions on Gaza. The government received him. He called the opening a historic day and described Israel as the only democracy in the Middle East and a partner for Europe. Outside, on Dimičeva, the Movement for Palestinian Rights and the student society Iskra protested under the banner “Ne genocidnemu veleposlaništvu”, joined by former president Milan Kučan, who said the arrangement is cooperation between two regimes rather than between two states. The movement has petitioned the Ljubljana municipal commission to rename Dimičeva ulica as Palestinska ulica; the commission decides in October.

What the veto was

A European joint statement requires unanimity, so any single state can stop one. Slovenia stopped one. EUobserver's reporting, followed by the Slovenian press, attributes the failure of consensus to Slovenian opposition; I have not been able to establish whether any other member state also withheld consent, and one Slovenian outlet implies it may not have been alone without naming a second state. This does not change Slovenia's position: under unanimity a state that withholds consent has blocked the statement whether or not another did too. But the claim that Slovenia stood alone is weaker than the claim that Slovenia blocked it, and only the second is made here. Robert Golob has characterised it as the first Slovenian veto ever cast in Israel's interest; that is his characterisation, not a verified first. Reported.

The subject matter matters more than the count. E1 is the plan that would sever East Jerusalem from the West Bank and divide the West Bank in two. The illegality of settlements in occupied territory is not a contested question of international law; it is the settled position of the ICJ, the Security Council and the European Union. Slovenia did not decline to endorse a contested claim. It declined to let the Union restate a settled one.

Janša's defence was that the Union applies double standards, is silent on the persecution of Christians in Nigeria and on antisemitism in Europe, and that its statements change nothing: “Pravzaprav smo samo umaknili Slovenijo iz začaranega kroga izgubljanja kredibilnosti” — in fact we have only removed Slovenia from a vicious circle of losing credibility.

The argument is self-defeating in a way worth naming. If EU statements change nothing, blocking one costs nothing and gains nothing, and no explanation exists for why the government spent its first veto on it. If blocking one was worth doing, the statements are not nothing. The government cannot hold both, and it has offered both within a fortnight — the foreign minister's version being that peace will not be achieved through statements, which is an argument for not issuing them, not for preventing others from issuing them.

Kajzer's later claim that there was no veto and no blockade is contested, asymmetrically, and the asymmetry is total. It is contradicted by his own ministry's account that Slovenia did not support the statement after consultations, by his prime minister's defence of the act as having removed Slovenia from a cycle of lost credibility, and by the statement's failure. It has no standing.

Two Slovenian presidents have said the rest. Pirc Musar: “Mednarodno pravo ni stvar politične izbire” — international law is not a matter of political choice. Danilo Türk: “Ves svet nas vidi kot instrument izraelske zunanje politike” — the whole world sees us as an instrument of Israeli foreign policy.

On the same day the Israeli embassy opened in Ljubljana, twelve states — France, the United Kingdom, Canada, Denmark, Spain, Finland, Ireland, Iceland, Norway, Poland, Portugal and Sweden — announced trade restrictions on goods from Israeli settlements and sanctions on entities servicing settlement expansion. Slovenia was not among them. Thirteen months earlier it had been the only EU state with an arms embargo.

9. Naming the relata

What follows grades responsibility, which means it makes ought-claims. On the diagnostic this corpus runs on, an ought asserted with no agent and no frame attached is not a bolder claim than an indexed one. It is an ill-formed one: a term with the grammar of a claim and nothing left to refer to. So the frame is named before anyone is graded.

Three routes can carry the weight. Two close and one does not, and this document rests on the two that close. Naming which is which is the point of doing it this way.

Route one: the treaty. No metaethics required.

Slovenia is a party to the Genocide Convention. The duty to prevent triggers on serious risk rather than on judgment. Slovenia has acted in the other direction. Nothing in that chain is an ought I am deriving; it is an is-fact about an obligation the Slovenian state contracted into, has not renounced, and is not honouring. A reader who rejects every metaethical commitment in this corpus still owes an answer to it, which is why it is placed first. Documented.

Route two: Slovenia's own persistence conditions. Closes in one form, not two.

Name the agent: the Slovenian state. Name what sustains it. Slovenia is a small system in an environment of much larger ones, and what keeps it bounded is not force, which it does not have, but a general norm — that a people's right to self-determination does not depend on whether larger powers find it convenient. Name the horizon, because without one the index is incomplete: the relevant span is the lifetime of the present European security order, decades rather than centuries, and the claim is not made beyond it.

This route was drafted in a stronger form than it can carry, and the attack on it is set out here rather than left to a reader, because the version that fails is the one that sounds best.

The erosion form fails. It said: a norm applied where it is cheap and suspended where it is expensive stops being a general norm, so a Slovenian government that suspends it degrades the structure its own persistence runs on. The trouble is that this makes a causal claim about the norm's general strength, and Slovenia's contribution to that is nil. Norms of this kind are eroded by states with the power to make exceptions stick. If Slovenia's veto does not change European policy — and section 11 concedes that it does not — then Slovenia's inconsistency does not measurably change the norm either. The erosion version therefore dies on exactly the smallness objection that route two was supposed to sidestep, and it should be abandoned rather than defended.

The standing form survives. The cost is not the norm's global health, which Slovenia cannot move. It is Slovenia's own standing to invoke it. A state that has published the conditions under which it sets the norm aside has supplied the answer to its own future appeal, and that answer is in its own voice and cannot be attributed to anyone else's malice. This mechanism is not causally negligible, because it does not run through third parties at all: no other state's conduct has to change for Slovenia to have forfeited a claim it previously held. It is closer to estoppel than to pollution.

On that reading the ought follows as a hypothetical with an is-antecedent, and the antecedent is no chosen goal but a redescription of what a self-maintaining structure is: if this system is to persist, it ought not spend the standing on which its persistence depends. Agent named, frame named, horizon named, verdict determinate. Argued.

One attack remains undefeated and is recorded as such. It may be that the general norm is not Slovenia's persistence condition at all but a proxy for it — that what actually keeps Slovenia bounded is alliance membership and the absence of a neighbour with both capacity and motive, interest-based structures that would hold even if the norm's standing collapsed. The reply available is that those alliances are institutional expressions of the norm and that a small member's position inside them depends on its generality; I believe that, and I cannot presently demonstrate it. If the proxy objection is right, route two indexes to the wrong thing and section 10 loses its index. That is the live vulnerability of this document and section 16 records it as the kill condition worth attempting.

Route three: what Slovenia owes the Palestinians. Open.

At the Palestinian end the ought is clean and I take it as settled: for every agent A, A ought not undergo A's own residue-free dissolution. Genocide is the attempted residue-free dissolution of a lineage, which is the case that description names most exactly.

What is not clean is the step from their ought to Slovenia's duty. That is a transitive ought, and transitive oughts in this corpus run through κ, coupling density, which remains the open crux of the positive ethics and is not resolved. I could close it here by assertion and the conclusion would be more moving. I am not going to, in the one document where doing so would be most convenient, because a framework that suspends its own open problems when the stakes feel high was never doing any work. κ open. Not relied upon.

So the route carrying the most force in ordinary moral speech, the direct obligation to the people being destroyed, is the one this corpus cannot presently close. The two that do close are a treaty Slovenia signed and Slovenia's own persistence properly described. Anyone who wants to reject section 10 should attack the index, not the sentiment.

On the firewall

The reduction from the oughts named above down to the physical floor is not built, here or anywhere in this corpus. The label records a debt, not a wall: these verdicts are asserted at the agent-relative level while the descent to thermodynamics remains owed. That is the standing condition of every normative claim in this corpus and no special weakness of this one. What would be a special weakness is stripping the index off to make the sentence sound stronger, which is the move this section exists to refuse.

10. The grading of responsibility

Responsibility is not a single quantity a country has or lacks. Two literatures give it structure — one about the kinds of guilt a citizenry can bear, one about how blame grades across secondary agents, and neither was invented for this case.

Karl Jaspers, writing in 1946 about the country he lived in, distinguished four kinds of guilt: criminal (violation of law, judged by a court), political (borne by citizens for the deeds of the state whose power governs them, and, his own qualification, graduated according to their degree of participation in the regime), moral (individual, judged by conscience, and never discharged by the fact that orders were orders), and metaphysical (arising from solidarity among human beings, where failure to prevent what happens in one's presence is itself a failure). The distinction exists to stop the two errors that dominate this argument in Slovenia: assigning criminal guilt to a whole electorate, and using the absence of criminal guilt to establish innocence.

Hannah Arendt refused the second category, and the disagreement is not cosmetic. She held that “there can be no such thing as vicarious guilt,” that guilt “unlike responsibility, always singles out; it is strictly personal,” and that the postwar cry we are all guilty “has actually only served to exculpate to a considerable degree those who actually were guilty.” Where all are guilty, nobody is. Her replacement is collective responsibility: vicarious, political, borne for what one did not personally do.

This document takes Jaspers' side, and the reason is not that the harsher word is more satisfying. Arendt's objection is consequentialist about vocabulary rather than about the underlying relation: she does not deny that citizens bear something in virtue of their state's conduct, she denies that calling it guilt does anything but launder the perpetrators. That worry is real and it is answered structurally rather than lexically. Guilt here is always named by species and graduated. Nothing said about the fifth or sixth tier reduces what is said about the first, because the species differ and the document says which is which every time. Under those conditions the word is doing work Arendt's substitute cannot: responsibility is forward-looking and discharged by acting, and it leaves no name for what a citizenry carries backward, having already let something be done in its name.

The cost of taking Jaspers' side is one Arendt would have pressed and it is stated here rather than absorbed: “the electorate is guilty”, unqualified, is a false sentence, and it is false in the direction that helps the government. It reads as criminal guilt, which no voter bears; it flattens a graduated liability into a uniform one; and it invites the reply that a charge covering two million people convicts nobody. The true sentence is longer and survives: the Slovenian citizenry bears political guilt for the conduct of the Slovenian state, graduated by participation, and separately from whatever moral guilt attaches to particular people for what they knew and did not do.

Chiara Lepora and Robert Goodin supply the analytic grading. Blameworthiness for a secondary agent varies with the badness of the principal wrong, the agent's voluntariness and knowledge, the centrality, proximity, reversibility and timing of the contribution, whether the agent was plan-maker or plan-taker, and the degree of shared purpose. Applied to the record, this produces six tiers rather than a verdict. Argued throughout, on the index in section 9, chiefly route two.

First: those who decided

Janša and the cabinet that revoked the measures, blocked the E1 statement, and signed a defence and artificial-intelligence cooperation programme with a state a United Nations commission had twice found to be committing genocide. Maximum on every axis: they acted, the findings were public and in front of them, and each decision had an available alternative costing Slovenia nothing but a call not made.

Janša's specific aggravation is not that he supports Israel. It is that he adopted the settlement movement's own terminology, Judeja in Samarija, in the voice of a Slovenian prime minister, inside a sentence arguing that international law forbids the conclusion he dislikes. A country that exists because a right to self-determination was recognised does not get to use the vocabulary of annexation as neutral geography. He knows what the word does. That is why he used it.

Kajzer belongs here for a separate reason: he told parliament there was no veto and no blockade while his own ministry's account said Slovenia had withheld support after consultations. Both cannot be true, and a foreign minister's statement to a parliamentary committee is not a place where that distinction is optional.

Second: those who sustain it

The parliamentary groups of NSi, SLS, FOKUS, the Demokrati and Resni.ca. They did not order the veto. They keep in office the government that cast it, and a constitutional charge and an interpellation now put that choice on the record with a date attached. “This is a matter of the coalition agreement” describes a bargain; it does not defend one. Whatever they were promised in exchange, this is part of the price and they are paying it in public.

Their responsibility is real and lighter than the first tier's, because a coalition partner's alternatives are genuinely more costly than a foreign ministry's. Lighter is not zero. In Lepora and Goodin's terms they are plan-takers whose contribution is reversible, and reversibility is the axis on which they will be judged, because it is the one still open to them.

Third: those who bought the equipment and called it opposition

The Golob government and those before it. This tier gets the charge the current argument in Slovenia will not make, because both camps have an interest in not making it.

Recognising Palestine and declaring three Israeli ministers persona non grata were real acts and I do not discount them. But the embargo, which is the measure always cited and the one that made Slovenia a European first, exempted in its own text the category of Israeli supply Slovenia actually relied on. On the arms component it prohibited what Slovenia did not need. Seven months later the government declined to join the ICJ case, and the stated reason was the dependency the embargo had left untouched. It programmed €3 million of Spike expenditure for 2026 while that embargo was in force, lawfully, through a German joint venture the ban did not reach.

One charge that appeared in earlier drafts is withdrawn here, because it does not survive the standard this document applies elsewhere. That bilateral trade reached a record in 2025 was cited as evidence against the Golob government. Trade is conducted by firms, not by cabinets, and a government does not set bilateral volumes. Attributing a private trading record to state policy is exactly the inference this document would refuse from an opponent, and it is refused here. The trade figure is evidence about something, but the something is the subject of the next tier, not this one.

The precise charge: it purchased moral standing with declarations and paid for it with nothing, while the material relationship grew underneath. The acts themselves were real and, as section 11 records, almost unmatched in the Union; what was worse than useless was the settlement they produced, a country that believed it had already acted. It is also the tier that made the fifth tier possible, since an electorate told the question was settled had no reason to make it an election issue.

Section 6 adds a second charge that is separable from the first and may be graver. The government did not only decline; it declined on an estimate of its own dependence that it never published and, so far as the record shows, never tested. If Spindel is right that supplier leverage is generally weaker than recipients believe, the Golob cabinet may have surrendered Slovenia's standing at the ICJ to a constraint that would not have held. Nobody can say, because the session was classified. A government that keeps the reasoning secret cannot later be credited with having had good reasons.

Fourth: the firms that conduct the relationship

This tier was absent from earlier drafts, and its absence was an asymmetry of the same kind as the one corrected in the tier below: a category applied to citizens who did nothing and withheld from companies that signed contracts. A voter who stayed home was being assigned political guilt while a firm booking €244 million of trade was assigned no tier at all. That cannot be right on any grading the rest of this section uses.

The trade is not conducted by ministries. It is conducted by companies, and the figures cited against two governments are in fact the aggregate of private commercial decisions. Thirty-five Slovenian firms attended the business forum on 9 September, in sectors named as advanced technologies, artificial intelligence, healthcare, agribusiness, water technologies, transport and tourism. The forum was closed to the press at Israeli request and the Chamber of Commerce declined to publish the participant list. Documented.

On Lepora and Goodin's factors these actors sit low and not at zero. Centrality: low, since no single firm's withdrawal changes anything. Proximity: distant. Shared purpose: absent, and it would be a serious error to impute one — a company selling pharmaceutical intermediates or logistics services is not endorsing a policy. Voluntariness and knowledge: present, and increasingly so, since the findings are public and have been since September 2025. Reversibility: high, which is the axis that matters, because a commercial relationship can be ended at a cost the party bearing it can calculate.

What follows is narrow. No firm named or unnamed is accused here of anything unlawful, and lawful trade with a state under a genocide finding is not a crime in Slovenia or anywhere else. The claim is that a commercial actor who continues a relationship after notice is making a decision, not merely occupying a market, and that a document willing to say so about a voter cannot decline to say it about a company. The gradient runs inside this tier too: a firm attending a state-organised forum three days after a criminal complaint was filed against the visiting minister has done something a firm shipping components under a pre-existing contract has not.

One asymmetry is left standing deliberately. The Chamber of Commerce's refusal to publish who attended means this tier cannot be populated. Companies that would be named are protected by an opacity they did not have to request and the state did not have to grant. That is a fact about the tier, not a reason to omit it, and section 13 asks for the list.

Fifth: the voters who conferred the mandates

An earlier version of this section counted only the 581,862 voters of the four blocs that put Janša in office, and swept everyone else into the sixth tier. That was incoherent on this document's own principle, and the incoherence ran in a direction convenient to one side of Slovenian politics, which is how such errors usually run. If political guilt is graduated by participation in the regime, then conferring a governing mandate on the government that did the things is participation. It cannot be lighter than conferring one on the government now living off them.

So the tier is larger, and the arithmetic is not comfortable for anyone.

And the bloc that was larger than any party

Every figure above is a share of votes cast, which understates the population the question reaches. 504,317 registered voters did not vote in March 2026 — 29.75 per cent of the electorate, half again as many people as voted for the largest party, and fifty-five times the margin that separated first place from second. The biggest single bloc in the election was nobody.

Two things follow, and they are not the same thing.

The arithmetic first, since it answers the obvious question. Had everyone voted and the distribution held, the parties that have held or now hold power over this would carry 1,321,927 people — 78 per cent of the country rather than 54 per cent of it. That is a hypothetical and nothing rests on it. It is worth stating only because the 54 per cent figure is an artefact of turnout, and anyone tempted to read the other 46 per cent as a dissenting remainder should see what it is actually made of.

The moral question is harder and the answer is narrower than it first looks. Abstention does not add political guilt, because political guilt was never conditional on voting: it attaches to citizens as such, so the 504,317 already carry it on the same terms as everyone else, and nothing about staying home either incurs or avoids it. Nor is abstention directional. Non-voters are not a bloc with a suppressed preference; they cannot be assigned an outcome they expressed nothing about, and some part of that number is structural rather than chosen — abroad, ill, or without a real option. What abstention can incur is moral guilt, individually, in the same structure as the voter who now knows and does nothing: for a particular person who understood what was at stake, had the means to act, and did not. That is unassessable from a turnout figure and this document does not attempt it. The claim is only that not voting is a choice about an outcome, made in an election decided by 9,179 votes, and that it is not the same as having no part in it.

The claim made about all of these groups is not the one being shouted in Slovenia this week, and it is not milder than it either. It is differently shaped, and the shape is what lets it survive.

They did not vote for this. It was not offered. Most voted on wages, housing, health waiting lists and exhaustion with the incumbent, and telling them they voted for a genocide is false: it asserts criminal guilt, which none of them bears, and intent, which none of them had.

That is the only thing that is false about the charge. They do bear guilt. They bear political guilt, in Jaspers' sense — borne by citizens for the deeds of the state whose power governs them, graduated by degree of participation, and requiring neither intent nor knowledge nor approval. What they did was accept a known risk: Janša's alignment with Israel was among the most legible things about him. The transfer of a vote is a transfer of discretion, and discretion gets spent on things the voter did not itemise. A voter who did not intend this outcome, and could have foreseen the disposition that produced it, is not innocent of it. He is guilty of it in the way a citizen is guilty of what is done in his name and with his money, which is a real way and not a rhetorical one.

Three consequences follow and each narrows the claim in a direction its holder should want.

  • It is graduated, and the gradient is steep — across mandates as well as within them. A vote for a party whose ministers fought this from inside the cabinet and lost is not a vote for what the cabinet decided; Jaspers' graduation by degree of participation does that work, and it is the reason the 12.40 per cent sits differently from the 77.98. Within any mandate the gradient runs again: a party official who defended the policy, a voter who has since endorsed it, and a voter who has not thought about it since March do not carry the same weight.
  • The two large mandates are not equivalent, and neither is lighter in every respect. The current government's tier-one responsibility is heavier because it decided knowing the findings. The previous government's electorate conferred a mandate on the administration that built the material relationship, wrote the exemption that spared it, and declined the one act with legal teeth — and did so across two full terms, with more time to notice. Whoever wants a version of this in which their own vote is the clean one will not find it here.
  • It does not stop at any of these numbers. Political guilt attaches to citizens of the state, not to supporters of a government. On this account every Slovenian citizen bears some of it, including those who voted against, including those who protested on Dimičeva, and including the author. What separates them is not whether they bear political guilt but how much, and what moral guilt attaches to them individually, which is the category that actually tracks knowledge and available action, and the category in which the four blocs' voters and everyone else genuinely differ.
  • Guilt does not exhaust what is owed. Political guilt is backward-looking and cannot be discharged by acting; what can be discharged is the forward-looking part. Iris Marion Young's social connection model names it: responsibility arising from participation in structural processes, discharged by acting on those structures rather than by confessing. The interpellation, the constitutional charge, their own MPs, the next election. A voter who now knows and does nothing acquires moral guilt on top of the political guilt he already had, and that acquisition is his own.

Sixth: everyone, including me

Slovenian defence money flowed toward Israeli systems for seven years, by routes nobody had to explain, and it was never an election issue, never a referendum question, never a resignation, never a demonstration on Dimičeva until this year. It passed through parliament as a line in a procurement programme. It was reported. Nobody stopped it, and that includes the people who write.

This tier carries the residue of the political guilt described above — the share borne by citizens who did not vote for this government — together with Jaspers' metaphysical category, which arises from solidarity among human beings rather than from citizenship. He warned that the metaphysical category is the one most easily abused: turned into a cheap universal guilt that dissolves the specific responsibility of the people who actually decided. That is Arendt's objection arriving from inside Jaspers' own framework, and it is why this tier is placed last, named as the mildest, and never used to level the first tier down to it. It is real. It is also the smallest quantity in the document.

I am not exempting myself by naming the tier. I published a casualty analysis in April 2026 that stopped carefully at the border of attribution, and I did not write this document until a foreign minister landed in Ljubljana. That is late. The tier is real and I am in it.

11. The strongest objections

“Slovenia is small; its conduct makes no difference to Gaza”

True, and it is the best objection available. Slovenia is a country of two million people and the act at issue blocked a press statement. If responsibility required difference-making, Slovenia would have none.

It does not. Christopher Kutz's account of complicity exists for exactly this structure: in collective harms, individual causal contributions are frequently negligible, and if accountability tracked marginal causal difference nobody would be accountable for anything done by a group. What grounds accountability is participatory intention — what one intentionally takes part in, not the counterfactual difference one's participation made. A state that joins a cooperation programme, offers market access, and removes an obstacle to another state's conduct is participating, whether or not the removal changed an outcome.

Route one in section 9 also survives the objection independently, because the Convention does not condition the duty to prevent on decisive influence. It scales the duty according to influence, which is the next objection.

“The duty to prevent scales to capacity, and Slovenia's capacity is nil”

This is the reply the government has not made and should. In Bosnia v. Serbia the Court held the duty to be an obligation of conduct rather than result, whose scope depends on the state's “capacity to influence effectively the action of persons likely to commit, or already committing, genocide” — a capacity depending in turn on geographical distance and, in the Court's words, “the strength of the political links” between the state and the actors involved. Serbia's duty was extensive because Serbia's influence was.

Three answers, in ascending order of force.

First, the scope of a duty is calibrated to capacity, and Slovenia's capacity with respect to its own conduct is total. Whatever Slovenia cannot do about Israel, it can decline to revoke an embargo it had imposed, decline to withhold consent from a statement it had been prepared to sign, and decline to sign a defence and artificial-intelligence programme. It performed each of these acts, which establishes that it had the capacity to perform their opposites.

Second, the Court's standard is that a state possessing means likely to have a deterrent effect is under a duty to use them as circumstances permit. Slovenia possessed such means, demonstrably, because it had already used them: the embargo, the entry bans, the settlement-goods ban. A state that has exercised a lever cannot claim it has none.

Third, and most damaging to the government's own position: capacity to influence scales with the strength of political links. Janša's government has spent a hundred days strengthening Slovenia's political links with Israel — an embassy, a ministerial visit, a cooperation programme to 2030, a business forum, a declared intention to move an embassy to Jerusalem. On the Court's own test, it has enlarged Slovenia's duty while acting against it. The friendlier the relationship it advertises, the less available the excuse that Slovenia has no influence to exert.

“The previous government was worse, or the same, so this is partisan”

Section 10 puts the previous government in the third tier and states its charge in terms its supporters will not enjoy. If this document were partisan it would have stopped at section 8. The reason it does not is that a piece sending the procurement bill to one party's voters would be weakest exactly where it swings hardest, since the strongest “your money” evidence dates from the other party's term.

The tiers are ordered by contribution and stance, not by party. Janša's government is first because it decided, knew, and had alternatives. That is a conclusion, not a premise, and it would survive being applied to anyone.

“The previous policy was performative anyway, so normalising is the honest course”

This is the best argument the government has and the document hands it the premise, since section 10's third tier says the previous policy was declaratory where it was cheap and absent where it was expensive. A defender can fairly say: you have conceded that the embargo coexisted with record trade and budgeted missiles, so why is ending the performance worse than continuing it?

Because normalising is not the honest alternative to performative opposition. Ending the performance while keeping the substance is. There were two components: a declaratory one, which was cheap, and a material one, which was real. The honest correction was to keep the material measures, publish the procurement record, and drop the rhetoric.

The government did the opposite on every count. It abolished the arms-trade prohibition, which was material, not declaratory — the one measure with teeth. It has not published the procurement record. It added new material commitments in the form of a cooperation programme covering defence and artificial intelligence. And it kept a declaratory posture of its own, merely reversed in sign, since blocking a European statement is itself a speech act. What it removed was the substance; what it retained and inverted was the performance. “Your predecessors were performative” is an argument for doing more than they did, and it is being used to do less.

“Slovenia did more than almost anyone, so this is a strange target”

This is the objection with the best facts behind it, and it is here because a reader raised it rather than because the method found it. Slovenia was the first European Union member state to impose a full arms embargo on Israel, and for more than a month the only one; Spain followed with a total embargo in September 2025. Slovenia recognised Palestine and declared three Israeli ministers persona non grata. Against that, the states that actually arm Israel did almost nothing: SIPRI records the United States as the source of 66 per cent of Israel's major arms imports in 2020–2024 and Germany as the source of 33 per cent — ninety-nine per cent between them — and Germany signed a roughly €2 billion Spike procurement two months after suspending arms exports to Israel. Measured against the suppliers, Slovenia is not the story. Documented.

All of that is true and none of it is disputed here. It is stated because omitting it would repeat the exact fault this document has twice had to correct: a consideration admitted in one direction only. The comparative record was already in the piece — but only where it damaged Slovenia, in the observation that a state which thirteen months earlier had held the Union's only arms embargo was absent from the twelve-state coalition on settlement sanctions. Used against, not for. That was an asymmetry and it is now repaired.

It does not answer the charge, for three reasons of unequal weight.

  1. The duty is owed severally. Article I binds each party on its own terms and is not graded on a curve against other parties' compliance. That worse violators exist is not a defence available to any of them; if it were, it would be available to all of them, and the duty would bind nobody. This is the least interesting reason and the hardest to get around.
  2. It is not the charge. Nothing in section 10's third tier says Slovenia did too little relative to others. It says the measure Slovenia took exempted the category Slovenia actually used, and that seven months later the unexempted dependency was given as the reason for not going to court. That charge is untouched by what Washington or Berlin did or failed to do. It would read identically if Slovenia had been the only state on earth to act.
  3. The comparison indicts the present government, not the past one. Every item that makes Slovenia look good in it — the embargo, the entry bans, the settlement-goods ban — is the list Janša's cabinet revoked on 11 June 2026. A reader who finds the comparison persuasive has thereby measured what was destroyed. The objection rescues the third tier somewhat and makes the first tier worse.

One correction the objection does force, against this document rather than for it. Section 10 called the previous government's posture “worse than useless.” That is too strong applied to the acts, and it is now scoped. A measure is not worth less because it cost little; cheapness is a fact about what the state spent, not about whether the act was right. The embargo, the recognition and the expulsions were right, and Slovenia was almost alone in taking them. What was worse than useless was not the acts but the settlement they produced — a country persuaded that the question had been answered, which is why the exemption inside the measure went unexamined for a year and never reached a ballot.

“Calling this complicity cheapens the word”

Careless use cheapens it. So does politically selective non-use. The remedy is an indexed argument: define the term before applying it, name the duty and its trigger, name the acts, state the counterevidence, mark what is not established, and give the conditions under which the claim fails. That is what sections 1, 9, 12 and 15 attempt. Refusing the word without doing the same work is not caution. It is a conclusion hiding inside a tone.

“This is not neutral”

Correct, and the objection assumes something about journalism worth naming. As Kovach and Rosenstiel argue, the discipline that makes journalism trustworthy is verification, and objectivity as originally conceived was a property of the method, not a claim that the practitioner has no views; the transposition of the word onto the person is a later corruption. Jay Rosen's name for the result is the view from nowhere: a bid for trust made by advertising one's viewlessness, which functions mainly as a defence against accusations of bias and costs the practice its capacity to say what is true.

Daniel Hallin's spheres explain the specific failure risked here. A claim's treatment depends on whether the press files it under consensus, legitimate controversy, or deviance — and that assignment is made by convention rather than by evidence. “Israel is committing genocide” sits in different spheres in different countries with the same evidence in each. Deferring to the local assignment is not neutrality. It is a substantive position adopted without argument.

What this document owes instead is verification and disclosure, and it offers both: every claim sourced and marked, the standings defined, the index named, the open problem left open, and one quotation cut at drafting because it could not be verified beyond a headline.

12. What this does not establish

Stated plainly, because a document listing only what favours its conclusion is advocacy wearing evidence as a costume.

  • Not that a court has found genocide. None has, and none will before 2029 at the earliest. The finding relied on is the UN Commission of Inquiry's, authoritative in its field and binding on nobody.
  • Not that Slovenian weapons were used against Palestinians. Slovenia issued no new arms export permits to Israel after October 2023, and what it did ship under existing licences — €98,905 of rough-worked forgings and castings — is a quantity and a category from which nothing about use can be inferred.
  • Not that Slovenia paid Israeli arms manufacturers directly. The defence ministry states that Spike acquisitions were routed through NATO's procurement agency and a German-majority joint venture, with no payments to Israeli manufacturers. That statement is specific and I have found nothing contradicting it. What the piece claims is indirect funding through equity and licence, which is a lesser claim and a different one.
  • Not the criminal offence of complicity in genocide. Article III(e) requires knowledge of the principal's specific intent and the provision of aid or assistance to it. Not established, not claimed.
  • Not that Slovenia's conduct is causally significant to the outcome in Gaza. It is not. The argument concerns the character of Slovenia's own acts under its own obligations.
  • Not that Slovenia owes the Palestinians a direct duty as third parties. That requires closing the transitive step, which runs through κ and is unresolved. It is the claim most people arguing this case reach for first, and it is the one thing here I cannot underwrite.
  • Not that Black Cube worked for SDS, or that any meeting with Janša occurred. SOVA confirmed an arrival and named names; it explicitly did not confirm a meeting; SDS denies knowledge.
  • Not that the 2021 memorandum caused the dependency. The Check Point deployment predates it by more than a decade. The memorandum is context, not a causal finding.
  • Not that the Golob government was pro-Israel. It was the Union's most critical government and took real measures. Its charge is inconsistency at the point of cost, which is different and lesser.
  • Not collective criminal guilt, and not moral guilt asserted collectively. Section 10 does hold that Slovenian citizens bear political guilt in Jaspers' sense, graduated by participation, and argues for it. What it does not do is assert that any particular person is morally guilty; moral guilt is individual, tracks what each person knew and could have done, and cannot be read off a vote. Anyone who rejects Jaspers' second category outright, with Arendt, rejects the fifth and sixth tiers and keeps the first four.

13. What discharge would look like

A document that grades responsibility and stops has done half a job, and the half it skipped is the one that could matter. What follows is derived from the two routes in section 9 rather than assembled as a wish list, and each item is tied to the route that generates it. Nothing here requires Slovenia to have influence over Israel, because neither route depends on that.

From route one: the duty to prevent

The Court's standard is that a state possessing means likely to have a deterrent effect must use them as circumstances permit. Slovenia has demonstrated which means it possesses by having used them.

  • Reinstate the prohibition on military trade with Israel, or state on the record why the duty to prevent no longer requires it. The measure is material rather than declaratory and Slovenia has enacted it once already, so neither capacity nor precedent is in question.
  • Suspend procurement from Israeli defence manufacturers while the risk finding stands, or publish the reasoning under which the duty permits it to continue.
  • Stop withholding consent from European statements that restate settled law. Whatever the merits of quiet diplomacy, obstructing others' speech is not an instance of it.
  • Either join the proceedings at the International Court of Justice or publish the reasoning for not joining. The obligation is to use available means; a refusal that is never explained cannot be assessed as a use of judgement.

From route two: standing

Standing is lost by unexplained inconsistency, which means it is recoverable by explanation in a way that most political damage is not. This is the cheaper of the two lists and the more urgent.

  • Publish the list of companies that attended the business forum of 9 September. A state-organised event, on state premises, with a state secretary speaking, is not a private meeting, and the Chamber of Commerce's refusal converts a public act into an anonymous one. Section 10's fourth tier cannot be populated without it, which is presumably the point.
  • Publish the procurement record the defence ministry has withheld. Whichever way it reads, the withholding is currently doing more damage to Slovenia's position than the contents could.
  • Declassify the reasoning of the cabinet session of 12 March 2026. Not the individual votes, if a convention protects them — the reasoning. If Slovenia's legal capacity was genuinely constrained by its infrastructure, that is a fact the public is entitled to and a warning other small states need. If it was not, the country has been told something false about itself by its own government.
  • Answer the question the committees could not resolve on 4 September: who authorised the E1 decision. A foreign policy nobody will claim is not a policy; it is an evasion with a flag on it.
  • Do not move the embassy to Jerusalem and do not pursue the “freezing” of Palestine's recognition — which, per Petrič and Brglez, is not an available act and would in substance be a severance of diplomatic relations, while the embassy move would be de facto recognition of Israeli sovereignty over Jerusalem. Both are pure standing costs. Neither buys anything the government has been able to name, and the closing section records that nobody in the government has tried.

What citizens can actually do with the fifth tier

Section 10 says the political guilt is backward-looking and cannot be discharged by acting, while the forward-looking part can. The available instruments are specific and currently open: the interpellation of the foreign minister, the constitutional charge and the 46 votes it needs, and the two publication demands above, which are the ones an ordinary citizen can press on an ordinary MP without needing a position on anything contested. A demand to publish a procurement record is not a demand to agree about Gaza.

One consequence of the document's own structure should be stated rather than left implicit: most of this list is owed by whichever government holds office, not by this one uniquely. The procurement record predates Janša. The classified session was Golob's. A reader who wants this list applied only to the other side has not understood the ledger.

15. Load-bearing assumptions

Four. The argument fails cleanly if any is false, rather than degrading into something vaguer.

  1. The duty to prevent is triggered by serious risk rather than by judicial confirmation. Taken from the ICJ's construction of Article I in Bosnia v. Serbia. If the duty instead requires a completed merits finding, the government's position is defensible and this document reduces to a policy disagreement. This is route one and it stands or falls alone.
  2. An ought is agent-relative — indexed to a system rather than free-standing. Assumed, not argued; it is argued in the corpus and inherited here. Everything in route two hangs from it. A reader holding that oughts are categorical will find the indexing needless rather than wrong and will reach the same verdicts by a route I have not defended. A reader holding that there are no oughts at all still faces route one, which is a treaty and not a metaethics.
  3. A purchasing relationship transmits some responsibility to the purchaser. If a customer is morally inert with respect to what a seller does, the third and fourth tiers collapse and only the acts since June 2026 remain in evidence.
  4. The transfer of a vote transfers some discretion over its use. The fifth tier depends entirely on this. Someone holding that voters answer only for what appeared in a manifesto rejects that tier, and should. The rest does not depend on it.

One thing deliberately not assumed: that Slovenia owes the Palestinians a direct duty as third parties. That is route three, it runs through κ, and the document is built so that its conclusions do not require it.

16. Falsification and kill conditions

In descending order of how much each would remove.

  • The UN Commission of Inquiry's findings retracted or substantially discredited on methodological grounds. This removes the factual predicate of section 3 and most of what follows.
  • A demonstration that the general norm named in section 9 is a proxy rather than a persistence condition — that what actually sustains Slovenia is alliance membership and the absence of a motivated neighbour, and that the norm's standing is downstream decoration. Route one would stand, but section 10 would lose its index and reduce to a legal argument and a set of dates. This is the kill condition worth attempting, and it is the one I am least able to test from inside. Note that the neighbouring attack has already succeeded: route two's erosion form did not survive its own smallness objection and has been withdrawn in section 9, leaving only the standing form.
  • Evidence that the reported reason for the 12 March decision is wrong — that the intervention was declined for reasons other than dependence on Israeli systems and services. This would remove section 6, which is where the document's most distinctive claim lives.
  • Procurement records showing that the 2019–2023 total consisted wholly of purchases routed through European intermediaries, with no direct acquisition from Israeli manufacturers at any point. This would not clear the funding relationship, since licence revenue still reaches Rafael, but it would defeat any remaining implication of direct payment and would further narrow section 4. The reverse finding, documented direct purchases from Israeli manufacturers, would restore the stronger version the audit removed.
  • A record showing the E1 statement failed for reasons other than Slovenian opposition. Evidence that another member state also withheld consent would not clear Slovenia, since under unanimity a blocker is a blocker, and the document does not rest on Slovenia having been alone.
  • Publication of the cooperation programme showing its defence and artificial-intelligence provisions to be dormant framework language with no operative content. This weakens section 8 without touching sections 4 to 7.
  • Declassification of the 12 March 2026 session showing that the dependency was concretely assessed, quantified, and found binding — rather than asserted. This would defeat section 6's second charge (that Slovenia forfeited its standing on an untested estimate) while leaving the first intact, and I would want it recorded that the government's own disclosure was what defeated it.
  • SOVA's confirmation to KNOVS being withdrawn or shown to have been misreported. This removes the Black Cube passage, which is already the most heavily qualified part of the document and carries no weight elsewhere.

A future ICJ judgment against the genocide claim would be major contrary evidence requiring close engagement with its record and reasoning. It would not retroactively make the present inference irrational, and it would not touch route two, which does not depend on the genocide finding being correct — only on the risk having been serious enough to trigger a duty Slovenia then acted against.

Standing of this document

This is an investigative position note. It is not a legal opinion, a criminal accusation, or a claim that Slovenia caused what happened in Gaza. Its strongest components are the procurement record, the trade figures, the electoral arithmetic and the sequence of acts from June to September 2026. Its most consequential and most revisable component is the account, in section 6, of why Slovenia declined to go to court.

Where the author stands. This is an internal critique and that is not incidental to it. I was born in Slovenia and live here, and the tier this document assigns me is the sixth, alongside every other citizen who did not stop any of it. The standpoint is not a disclaimer hung on the argument; it is the argument’s standing. Route two in section 9 is a claim about what Slovenia’s own persistence requires, and that is not a claim a stranger could make on Slovenia’s behalf — it is the kind of claim a member of a thing makes about the thing he is a member of, which is why it is indexed to Slovenia and not to anyone’s general sympathies.

I hold, and state as a personal position rather than as anything this document establishes or needs, that Slovenia is in many respects among the better places on earth to be a person. It is an estimate and not a finding, it rests on no index, and it is marked here so it cannot be mistaken for either. Nothing in it softens a line above it, and the appearance of tension between the two is what this paragraph exists to refuse. A country is not served by the form of loyalty that requires silence when it acts against what it says it is. Slovenia’s argument for its own existence — that a small nation’s rights do not depend on a larger power finding them convenient — is an argument about principles holding when they are inconvenient, which is the only condition under which principles do any work. A citizen who watched that principle be set aside and said nothing would be keeping faith with the flag and losing the case the flag was raised for. Calling a state to its own stated terms is not hostility to it. On the account in section 9 it is the more demanding form of loyalty.

What is asserted here, and against whom. Every factual claim carries a standing mark and is traced in the audit below. Claims marked Argued are evaluative conclusions drawn from a stated factual basis on a named index; they are offered as the author’s judgment and not as assertions of fact, and the basis is given so that the judgment can be rejected by attacking either. Every person named is named for conduct in public office or public life, on the public record or performed in public. No criminal offence is alleged against any person named in this document. Sections 1 and 12 state that the criminal offence of complicity in genocide under Article III(e) of the Convention is neither asserted nor established, and the same holds for every other offence: where a criminal complaint brought by a third party is reported, it is reported as a complaint and not as a finding, and marked as such. No private individual is named. No company is accused of unlawful conduct; section 10 says so in terms. Where this document concludes that two accounts cannot both be true, it names both and leaves the reader to draw the inference the evidence supports.

Slovenia's founding claim about itself is that a small nation's right to exist does not depend on whether larger powers find it convenient, and that international law rather than sentiment or strength is what makes this true. That claim is not decorative. It is the argument the country made for itself in 1991 and the reason the argument worked.

The current government has been explicit that it is trading it for something. Janša: “Vlada ima jasno usmeritev glede prioritet svojega delovanja, ki so osredotočene na povečanje blaginje slovenskega človeka, zato bo vodila pragmatično politiko” — the government's priorities are focused on increasing the welfare of the Slovenian people, and it will therefore conduct a pragmatic policy. Kajzer, on the protesters outside the embassy: “Skušam razumeti ljudi, ki na primer nasprotujejo temu, smo demokratična družba.”

That is a coherent position and should be argued against on the merits rather than treated as unspeakable. Here is the merit.

The pragmatic case assumes Slovenia is buying something, and one member of the government has named what: Kajzer said economic relations with Israel had been neglected and predicted that trade would substantially increase. That is an asset, stated. It is also the weakest available one, because bilateral trade was already at a record, €244 million in 2025, under the government whose policy this reverses, and reached it during an arms embargo and a genocide finding. Whatever obstacle the new policy removes, the evidence does not show trade was being obstructed.

On 10 September, answering the constitutional charge and the announced interpellation, Kajzer named three more. He rejected the accusation outright — “Odločno zavračam očitke, da zunanje ministrstvo oziroma vlada ne vodi suverene eksterne politike”, and said the government conducts “zunanjo politiko, ki krepi varnost, mednarodni položaj in gospodarske interese naše države”: a foreign policy strengthening the country's security, its international standing and its economic interests. He added that “Dialog ni znak podrejanja, ampak osnovno orodje diplomacije” — dialogue is not a sign of subordination but the basic instrument of diplomacy. Documented.

The last of those is true and is not in dispute here; nothing in this document argues that a state should refuse to talk to another. The first two are claims with evidence against them. On international standing: two presidents of the republic in public opposition, a constitutional charge, an interpellation, absence from the twelve-state coalition on settlement sanctions, and a former head of state saying the world now reads Slovenian foreign policy as another state's instrument. On security: the only security argument the government's predecessors ever made in public about Israel was that Slovenia depends on Israeli systems, which is a description of exposure rather than of strength.

What has been produced besides is a cooperation programme, a business forum closed to the press, and an entry point to the single market offered to Israeli firms — a benefit conferred, not received. Four assets have now been named: trade, security, international standing, economic interests. None has been shown. And in the same statement, asked who ordered the veto that began all of this, the foreign minister did not say.

How to correct this document

Sections 12, 15 and 16 set out what this document does not establish, what it assumes, and what would break it. None of that is worth much without somewhere to send the answer, so here is the mechanism and the commitment attached to it.

What is most useful

The claim register in the source audit numbers every factual claim in the piece. A correction that cites a number — 6.3 is wrong, and here is the record — can be acted on in an afternoon. A correction that says the piece is biased cannot, because there is nothing to check. The most valuable submissions, in order:

  1. A document. Anything from the blocked list in the audit: the reasoning of the cabinet session of 12 March 2026, the defence ministry's procurement record, the text of the cooperation programme, the participant list from the business forum of 9 September, or the 31 July 2025 measure as published in the gazette. Any one of these would move claims this document has had to leave at Reported.
  2. An attack on route two. Section 9 rests on the claim that the general norm of self-determination is among the Slovenian state's persistence conditions rather than a proxy for alliance membership. I believe it and cannot demonstrate it. Three readers have now declined to attack it and it remains the document's live vulnerability.
  3. A structural asymmetry. The audit's own method note concedes that source-tracing cannot detect a category applied to one group and withheld from a comparable one. Two such faults were found before publication, one by a reader and one by a symmetry test run across the register, and neither by any source trace. There are probably more.
  4. A factual error, with the source that shows it.

What happens to it

Corrections are published in the audit above the drafting line, dated, naming the claim and what changed. If a correction moves anything load-bearing, the Conclusion is rewritten and its stamp records which revision and against which audit version, so that a reader holding an older copy can tell. Nothing is amended silently and nothing is amended by deletion.

The commitment has a failure condition, which is the only thing that makes it a commitment. If a correction arrives, is accepted, and the conclusion does not move, this document has failed on its own terms and the reader who sent it should say so in public. The ordering it claims — evidence, then audit, then conclusion — is either real or it is decoration, and the way to find out is to send something.

Leave corrections in the comments on this post. They are read, and a correction that names a claim number and cites a source will be acted on. A comment that is right will change the document; a comment that is wrong will be answered; a comment that is unanswerable will be recorded in the audit as an open gap under the name of whoever raised it.

If you are named here

Any person named in this document may have a reply published with it. The offer is unconditional as to content: the reply runs unedited and in full, at the same prominence as the passage it answers, with the date it was received. A reply that shows a fact wrong is a correction and is handled as above, dated in the audit, with the claim number named. A reply that disputes a judgment rather than a fact runs as a reply and is answered on the merits or not at all, as it deserves. Nothing in the offer is conditional on agreeing with anything here.

The same applies to the companies in section 10’s fourth tier, none of which is accused of anything unlawful and none of which can currently be named, and to any organisation whose conduct is described. A firm that wishes to state on the record why it attended the forum of 9 September, or why it continues or has ended a commercial relationship, will have that statement published here in full.

This is not a courtesy. A framework that survives only because nobody tested it has not survived anything, and the decay of correction mechanisms is a subject treated elsewhere in this corpus. A document that asks a country to answer for what was done in its name is in a poor position to be precious about being answered itself.

Conclusion

Live section. This is the one part of the document that is expected to move. It states what the evidence currently supports, and it is rewritten whenever the source audit below changes what that is. Revision state is tied to the audit's version, not the piece's: a reader comparing two copies should check the stamp at the end of this section first. The plain-language summary at the top of the document states the same conclusions without the apparatus and moves with this section, so the two never disagree. Current as of Audit v11, 17 September 2026.

Slovenia is complicit in the sense defined in section 1 — a state under a triggered duty to prevent that has moved consistently in the other direction, and since June 2026 has done so as declared policy. But the complicity is older and more bipartisan than the argument now running in Ljubljana allows, and its sharpest evidence is not any act of Janša's. It is that the European Union's only arms embargo on Israel, the measure that made Slovenia a moral exemplar, exempted in its own published text the precise category of Israeli supply Slovenia actually depended on: information and cyber-defence systems, named by the defence ministry the day after adoption. On the arms component it prohibited what Slovenia did not need and permitted what it did — which is not to say the measure was empty: Slovenia drew a real line on weapons, first in the Union and without being asked, and section 5 says so. Seven months later that same untouched dependency was the reason a classified cabinet declined to join the genocide case at the International Court of Justice — a constraint nobody has tested, since the research literature finds supplier leverage weaker than recipients assume, which means the capacity may never have been lost but only believed lost, and the record that would settle it was sealed. Around that sit the smaller confirmations: purchases routed through a German joint venture an Israeli state firm part-owns, by the route Spain and Germany use on the same justification; a transit ban announced by a ministry that had just said it keeps no record of transit; exports continuing under old licences. Janša's government built none of this. It inherited a state already unable to act and made the inability into a policy.

Responsibility for that is graded and none of it is nowhere. Heaviest on those who decided, and Janša is first among them — not for supporting Israel, which is a position, but for spending a veto on a settled question of law in the vocabulary of annexation. Real for the coalition groups who keep that government standing and can stop. Distinct and unflattering for the government that wrote the exemption and took credit for the remainder. And real, in Jaspers' sense and graduated by participation, for something much larger than the electorate of the current government: 919,964 people, 78 per cent of the votes cast in March and 54 per cent of the entire electorate, gave a governing mandate to one or other of the two administrations that between them built this and now live off it. Twelve per cent more voted for the two parties that were in the room and lost the argument, which is a different position and is recorded as one. Between those tiers sit the firms that actually conduct the relationship — lawfully, at low centrality, with no shared purpose, and with full knowledge since September 2025 — who cannot be named because the Chamber of Commerce declined to publish who attended the state's own business forum. The 54 per cent is an artefact of turnout: 504,317 people did not vote, a bloc half again the size of the largest party, and at an unchanged distribution full turnout would put the figure at 78 per cent of the country. There is no version of this arithmetic in which any large bloc's vote is the clean one, and the residue reaches every citizen of the state — those who marched on Dimičeva, and the author of this document. What follows from it is in section 13, and most of that is owed by whichever government holds office.

The ledger being kept is not only Slovenia's own. Anyone can read what a state did in the years a genocide was being determined by the institution competent to determine it. That record is being written now and it will not be amended later. Slovenia's entry currently reads: wrote the exemption, kept the purchases, declined the court, blocked the statement, opened the embassy.
