Source Audit

Every claim in the preceding document, traced to where its evidence actually terminates

Andraž Đurič

Audit v11 · 17 September 2026 · attached to Slovenia Is Complicit in a Genocide, Version 1 (published 17 September 2026)

What this is, and why it is separate

The confidence ledger in section 14 above records what standing each claim was given. It does not record why, and it does not show where the evidence stops. This document does both. It exists because a piece that accuses a sitting government should be checkable by a hostile reader without that reader having to take a single sentence on trust, and because the discipline of tracing every claim to its root is the only thing that reliably catches the claims that cannot be traced at all.

It is kept as a companion rather than folded into the piece for two reasons. The traces are long and would destroy the argument's readability. And an audit that lives separately can be revised when a chain closes or breaks without reopening the document it audits, which is what makes it a living record rather than a snapshot.

It is not a list of supporting sources. Where a published rebuttal to a claim exists, it is named, summarised at its strongest, and assessed. Where two of my own sources disagree, the disagreement is recorded rather than resolved by picking the convenient one.

Method

The chain trace

For each claim: the sentence as it appears above, the source cited for it, that source's own source, and the point at which the chain terminates. A claim is only as good as its terminal node, and the terminal node is frequently several steps behind the outlet that appears in the footnote.

Terminal node types

TypeMeaningWeight
Primary recordAn official register, court order, treaty text, statute, statistical series, or official gazette. The thing itself.Highest. Disputable only by claiming the record is wrong.
Institutional findingA body with a mandate, a stated evidentiary standard, and a published method. Not a court.High, and bounded by the body's own standard of proof.
Interested primaryA statement by a party with a stake, about itself. A ministry describing its own conduct; a company describing its own appointment.Reliable for what was said, unreliable for whether it is true.
Documentary journalismReporting that names the documents it worked from and can in principle be re-derived from them.Good. Inherits the strength of the documents named.
Single briefingSeveral outlets, one unattributed source. The plural appearance is not plural evidence.Weak, and the weakness is invisible without a trace.
UntracedChain could not be followed to any of the above within this pass.Marked and not relied upon.

Where digging pays, and where it does not

Drafting this document produced a usable rule, and it is narrower than “verify everything.” Tracing to bedrock is expensive and its yield is uneven. Every claim that took the form X said Y, with Y quoted from an article body, held through every pass. The claims that failed were a different kind entirely, and there were five of them.

The ministry declined to produce the records. The ministry's denial was an evasion. The embargo was a real material measure. The announcement amounts to freezing recognition. No export permits were issued, therefore nothing was sent. Each is a description of a document's content, scope or legal consequence, written from secondary accounts of that document rather than from the document. None was a quotation, and none survived retrieval.

The tell is grammatical. When you find yourself describing rather than quoting, you are standing on a document you have not read. That is where retrieval pays, and it is the only place it reliably pays.

The rule has a hard limit and it should be stated beside it. Source-tracing tests whether claims match their sources. It cannot test whether an argument's structure is symmetrical, whether a category has been applied to one group and not to a comparable one, or whether a number has been drawn from a denominator that flatters the conclusion. Those faults are invisible to every method in this audit, and the drafting of section 10 contained one of each. Two were caught by a reader and one by a symmetry test run across the register; none by any trace in this audit. An audit of sources is not an audit of reasoning, and no apparatus in this document should be taken to substitute for the second.

The checks that were pure hygiene are worth naming too, so the rule is not overstated. Pulling the election commission's register corrected the electorate by some fifteen thousand and shifted a percentage by three tenths. Pulling the Commission of Inquiry's report fixed a date. Both were right to do and neither changed an argument. A rule that sent an auditor after every number would have bought those two corrections at the cost of the five that mattered.

The independence test

The commonest failure in a small media market is counting one source several times. Slovenian outlets frequently carry the same agency copy, and a claim appearing in four places may have entered the world once. Wherever the piece above rests on several Slovenian reports, this audit asks whether they are independently derived or a single origin redistributed. Where the answer is the latter, the standing stays at Reported no matter how many outlets carried it.

The conclusion is downstream of this audit

The piece carries a live Conclusion section, and it is the only part of the document expected to move between versions. It states what the evidence currently supports rather than what the argument set out to show, which means it is revised whenever a chain in this audit closes, breaks or changes standing. Its stamp cites an audit version rather than a date, so that a reader can tell at a glance whether a copy predates a correction.

This is the ordering the document commits to: evidence, then audit, then conclusion. If a future pass breaks something load-bearing and the conclusion does not change, one of the two is wrong and the fault is the author's.

Verdicts

Confirmed: the trace reaches a terminal node consistent with the standing assigned. Upgraded: the trace reached a stronger node than the standing assumed, and the piece has been amended. Downgraded: the trace stopped short and the standing was reduced. Open: not yet traced to a terminal node; the closing action is stated.

This establishes that the carve-out was reported internationally at the time, not only domestically.

A convention, stated once. Everything below happened before first publication. It is drafting, not correction, and it is recorded here for one reason only: several of these changes are the evidence for the method described above, and a rule presented without its evidence is an assertion. The corrections log proper begins now. The document was published on 17 September 2026, and from this point this section records changes to claims a reader may already have read and believed, which is the only kind of change a reader is owed. Entries below the line are drafting; entries above it, when they appear, are corrections. Nothing here is a confession and none of it should be read as one. Drafts are wrong until they are finished; that is what drafting is.

  1. The arms figures and the ministry's denial — the substantial correction of this pass. The piece stated that Slovenia bought €57.5 million of Israeli weapons and treated the defence ministry's denial as evasive. The Commission's own verified count through 31 March 2026 is at least 20,179 killed and 44,143 injured. The two are now both present, and the apparent discrepancy is explained below rather than resolved by preferring one.

Chains worth reading in full

Most traces are unremarkable and appear only in the register. Six are not.

1. The genocide finding, and the published rebuttal to it

The piece's central factual predicate traces cleanly: press coverage → OHCHR press release of 23 June 2026 → A/HRC/62/CRP.2, dated 18 June 2026, covering 7 October 2023 to 31 March 2026 → the Commission's own investigation on a reasonable-grounds standard. Terminal node: institutional finding, correctly bounded in the piece as authoritative in its field and binding on nobody.

An audit that stopped there would be doing advocacy. A detailed rebuttal exists: UN Watch, a Geneva-based organisation whose declared purpose includes monitoring the UN's treatment of Israel, published a point-by-point response on 23 June 2026. It is an interested party. That does not dispose of its arguments, so they are assessed here.

Points that do not survive. Its central objection is that the Commission cannot show a single verified instance in which a soldier identified an individual as a child and selected that child for death. This misstates how special intent is established in genocide law, where inference from a pattern of conduct is the ordinary route and a confession is not required; it is the same objection the ICJ has repeatedly declined to treat as dispositive. Its claim that the report erases Hamas as a combatant force is an argument about emphasis rather than about the findings' truth, and would if accepted prove that no report focusing on victims can be accurate. Its complaint that the Commission converts uncertainty into definitive findings is answered by the Commission's stated standard, which is reasonable grounds, not certainty.

Points that have force. Three do. First, the forensic attribution objection is specific and checkable: the rebuttal argues that a bullet described as 3 cm cannot be the .338 Lapua Magnum the report identifies, since intact projectiles of that type measure roughly 3.8 cm or more. That is either right or wrong on the physical facts and I have not been able to resolve it. Second, the objection that medical witnesses are treated as competent on weapons systems, ballistics and targeting intent is methodologically real, whatever one concludes about the findings overall. Third, and strongest, it argues that if children were targeted as such, the sex distribution of minors killed should approximate the child population, whereas 97 per cent of minors killed in the West Bank were male.

Assessment. The third point is the most substantive and also the most misapplied: it is a West Bank statistic deployed against a Gaza finding, and the report treats those territories under different headings and different legal characterisations. It bears on the West Bank portion, where the Commission found war crimes rather than genocide, and it does not touch the Gaza finding it is offered against. The first two are real methodological criticisms that would matter to a court applying a higher standard and do not defeat a reasonable-grounds finding. Net effect on the piece: none of the load-bearing claims move. But the residual confidence in the Commission's forensic particulars should be lower than the confidence in its overall conclusion, and the piece relies only on the latter.

2. The two children figures, which disagree in the wrong direction

The piece carries approximately 21,300 children killed, sourced through my April 2026 casualty analysis to a UNICEF situation update of February 2026. The Commission's June report gives at least 20,179 killed through 31 March 2026 — a lower figure covering a later period. On its face that is impossible.

It is not a contradiction, and the explanation matters more than the numbers. The two bodies are counting different things by different rules: UNICEF reports figures attributed to the Gaza health ministry, while the Commission counts only what its own investigation verified to its own standard. A verification-limited count will always sit below a reported count and will lag it. The correct reading is that 20,179 is a floor established by independent verification and approximately 21,300 is a reported total, and that the true figure is at or above the higher one, since both bodies describe their counts as incomplete.

The piece now carries both with their provenance. A reader who sees only one and assumes the other is wrong has been failed by the presentation, not by the sources. Note for anyone re-running this: the Washington Institute has published its own analysis disputing aspects of UN Gaza fatality data; it is an interested party, it is not relied on here, and anyone auditing the casualty figures further should read it rather than take this paragraph's word for the shape of the dispute.

3. The 12 March cabinet decision: four outlets, plausibly one origin

This is the piece's most distinctive claim and the one whose chain is weakest, which is an uncomfortable combination and the reason it is set out at length.

Four outlets carry it: N1 and 24ur on 12 March 2026, Žurnal24 the same day, Euronews on 20 March. The decision is not in doubt — it was announced, the foreign minister commented publicly, and the coalition split over it. That part terminates in on-record statements and is Documented.

The reasons are a different matter. The session was classified. No minister has stated on the record that Slovenia declined because of dependence on Israeli systems. The reporting describes the security grounds consistently, which looks like corroboration and may not be: four outlets in a small market reporting the same closed session in the same week are as likely to be redistributing one briefing as to have four sources. I could not establish which. Terminal node: single briefing, presumed. The standing stays at Reported and the piece names it as the most fragile load-bearing fact it has.

What would close it: declassification of the session's reasoning, which section 13 of the piece asks for on independent grounds; or any minister stating the reasons on the record; or an outlet naming its source. Until then the piece's second charge in section 6 — that Slovenia may have forfeited its standing on an untested estimate — rests on an account of the reasoning that is itself untested. That symmetry is uncomfortable and is stated rather than hidden.

4. The arms figures: the chain that broke, and the correction it forced

This is the trace that most changed the piece, and it went against its first framing.

The chain looks, from the press coverage, like: reporting → Delo → budget documents and parliamentary answers obtained by Levica → the National Assembly's records, terminating in a primary record at one remove. On that reading the figures would be Documented and the defence ministry's denial would be an interested party's assertion offered without the dispositive documents.

Retrieving the ministry's actual words changed that reading.

The denial is not evasive. It states that since the beginning of the Gaza war Slovenia has purchased no weapons, ammunition or other military equipment in Israel, and has issued no export permits to Israel. On the Spike systems it states that the 2022–2023 acquisitions ran through NATO's procurement agency and through EuroSpike, majority-owned by Rheinmetall and Diehl, that no payments were made to Israeli weapons manufacturers, and that all components were produced in Europe. That is a specific, falsifiable account of the routing, not a refusal to engage. Nothing I traced contradicts it.

Levica's counter is equally specific: EuroSpike is co-owned by Rafael Advanced Defense Systems, which developed Spike, holds the intellectual property and receives licence revenue. Nothing contradicts that either.

Both are true. That is the finding, and it is better than the claim it replaced. Slovenian money went to a German-registered joint venture for European-made components under a NATO framework, and Israeli revenue flowed from it by equity and licence. Each party's formulation is engineered to make the other's inaudible: the ministry says “no payments to Israeli manufacturers” because payments went to the joint venture, and Levica says “Israeli weapons” because Rafael profits. Neither is lying and neither is complete.

Three things changed in the piece as a result. The figures were downgraded from Documented to Reported, since the composition of the 2019–2023 total is not established by anything traced. The ministry's denial was upgraded and its verdict reversed; the criticism now made of it is materially incomplete rather than evasive, which is a different and smaller charge. And section 4 gained the structural point that is larger than Slovenia: an embargo on purchasing military equipment in Israel does not touch acquisitions of Israeli-designed systems from European joint ventures, so such an embargo can be genuine, announced truthfully, and substantially hollow at the same time — which is how the Golob government could hold both positions without anyone in it lying.

The remaining open action stands and is now more valuable, not less: retrieving the parliamentary answers and budget lines directly would establish the composition of the 2019–2023 total, which is currently the largest unresolved factual question in the document.

4a. What the second pass found next: the carve-out, and the European route

Having broken the arms chain, the same pass followed two questions out of it. Both closed, and one of them produced the most consequential finding in either document.

The route generalises, and is used deliberately. EuroSpike GmbH is 40 per cent Rheinmetall, 40 per cent Diehl Defence, 20 per cent Rafael. Spain suspended a €285 million Rafael contract in June 2025 under its own embargo and in February 2026 acquired the identical missile through EuroSpike as MELLS, on the stated ground that the components are made in Europe — the same sentence Slovenia's defence ministry used. Germany, having suspended arms exports to Israel in August 2025, signed a roughly €2 billion Spike procurement through EuroSpike in October 2025 under a NATO framework, with industry sources telling the trade press that the joint venture's European ownership was what made it possible. Terminal nodes: documentary journalism on contracts and corporate structure, consistent across outlets and across three countries. The finding in section 4 is therefore not an inference about Slovenia; it is a described practice.

And then the decree itself. Chasing the scope of the Slovenian ban produced the thing neither the piece nor this audit had looked for. The decree of 31 July 2025 carried, from adoption, a written exception for equipment needed by Slovenia for security and resilience, and the government named the category as information systems and cyber-defence equipment. Two Slovenian outlets carry it independently and a state secretary is on the record. Terminal node: the government's own published position on its own measure.

Set that beside section 6. The dependency Slovenia cited in March 2026 as its reason for not going to the International Court of Justice was Israeli cyber and information systems in its critical infrastructure. The embargo of July 2025 exempted Israeli cyber and information systems by name. The Union's only arms embargo on Israel excluded, in its own text, the only Israeli supply relationship that was doing any work.

This was not reached by reasoning about the argument. It was reached by asking what a decree said and reading the answer. The piece carries both readings of the carve-out — prudence or design — because the record supports neither over the other, and records that nobody has been asked which it was.

5. The technology dependency: one outlet, public records underneath

Every concrete detail in section 6 — Check Point in HKOM, the €2.5 million renewal to 2028, the Krško and Ljubljana Pharmacy contracts, the Cellebrite purchases, the 23 August 2021 memorandum and its signatories — comes from a single Mladina investigation. There is no second outlet.

The mitigation is that Mladina names its sources as public procurement records, which are a primary record and are retrievable. So the claim is single-sourced in its reporting but not single-sourced in its evidence, and the distinction matters: a fabrication would be detectable by anyone who looks. The appropriate standing is Reported until someone looks.

Separately verified independently of Mladina: that Nadav Zafrir became chief executive of Check Point Software Technologies in December 2024, and his background founding IDF Cyber Command and commanding Unit 8200. Terminal node: the company's own announcement and contemporaneous business press, i.e. interested primary corroborated by documentary journalism. The piece states this and explicitly declines to draw an inference from it.

6. Black Cube: what SOVA confirmed, and the gap it left

Two chains, deliberately kept apart in the piece and kept apart here.

The allegation: Inštitut 8. marec, 16 March 2026, citing flight records and anonymous identification of passengers. Terminal node: an interested primary — an advocacy organisation making a claim in an election week — resting on records it did not publish in full.

The confirmation: SOVA to KNOVS, reported by 24ur, Siol and Delo. Terminal node: a state intelligence service's report to a parliamentary oversight commission, which is close to a primary record but reaches the public through unattributed accounts of a closed session. It confirms arrival on 22 December and further visits; it explicitly does not confirm a meeting.

The piece asserts only the second chain and reports the first as an allegation. That is the correct division and it is why the passage is legally and epistemically the most careful thing in the document, despite being the part that sounds most explosive. The gap between “operatives arrived” and “operatives met the party leader” is where the entire dispute lives, and nobody has closed it.
