entry.title: Art as Compression of Reality
entry.content:
Editorial note - 2 October 2026

Later revision. Art as Compression of Reality: Revised After Testing explicitly revises and refines this January 10, 2026 proposal. The original text remains below.


Art as Compression of Reality
By Andraž Đurič & Claude (Anthropic) • January 10, 2026




The Core Insight

Art is beautiful insofar as it compresses patterns that actually exist in reality in ways that resonate with human cognitive architecture.

Good art captures and encodes real structure. Poor art either compresses noise, fails to compress, or compresses patterns that don't exist.



What Art Compresses

Art can compress different dimensions of reality:

Physical Reality
Anatomy, motion, light physics, perspective, material properties. A Renaissance painting compresses how light actually behaves. An anatomically correct horse running captures the physics of motion.

Mathematical & Structural Patterns
Symmetry, balance, harmonic relationships, spatial principles. A Bach fugue compresses mathematical structure. Mondrian's compositions compress principles of visual balance.

Psychological Reality
Emotional salience, perceptual regularities, cognitive patterns. A child's drawing might compress emotional truth—making "Mommy" huge because she's important—even if it's not visually accurate.

Temporal & Process Patterns
Change, impermanence, cycles, entropy dynamics. Japanese cherry blossom aesthetics compress the reality of impermanence. Art depicting death can compress the pattern of entropy increase.

Quality as Compression Fidelity
High-quality art: Captures real patterns with high fidelity
Examples: Renaissance paintings, Bach fugues, precise engineering drawings, photorealistic depictions of natural phenomena

Medium-quality art: Compresses valid patterns with lower resolution or targets different dimensions
Examples: Child's drawings capturing emotional truth, abstract art compressing structural principles, expressionist work compressing psychological states

Low-quality art: Compresses noise, wishful thinking, or trivial patterns
Examples: Random scribbles, kitsch, failed attempts at representation



Why Aesthetic Preferences Vary

Different observers are attuned to different aspects of reality.

A physicist recognizes compressed physics in a technically accurate painting. A child recognizes compressed emotional salience in simple drawings. A mathematician sees compressed structure in abstract geometric art. All are compressing reality—different dimensions of it.

Disagreement about beauty reflects:

Attunement to different real patterns
Different compression targets
One party compressing noise while believing it's signal
This explains why educated taste often involves training: you learn to recognize which patterns the art is compressing.

The Modern Art Question
The claim is NOT: "Modern art is inherently low compression"

The claim IS: Modern art often compresses different patterns than representational art.

Some modern art compresses genuine structural or conceptual patterns—Mondrian compressing visual balance principles, for example. Other works compress the artist's internal states with minimal connection to external patterns.

The test: Does the pattern being compressed exist independent of the artist's claim that it exists?

If the answer is yes, the art is compressing reality. If the answer is no, it might be compressing noise.



The Thermodynamic Connection

Order (low entropy) is compressible. Chaos (high entropy) is incompressible.

Beauty may correlate with perceiving and encoding real order and pattern. Horror at entropy increase—death, decay, disorder—reflects witnessing pattern loss.

But reality includes both order and entropy. Art can compress either: the structure, the dissolution, or the relationship between them. Japanese aesthetics of impermanence (mono no aware) compress the reality of entropy itself—making the pattern of decay beautiful.

This connects art directly to thermodynamics and information theory.



Information Theory Foundation

Compression requires exploiting actual regularities. Random data is incompressible.

The more structure exists in reality, the more it can be compressed. Art that achieves a high compression ratio captures genuine patterns efficiently.

Art that cannot be compressed is either:

Perfectly random (noise with no pattern)
Already maximally compressed (irreducible essence)
This gives us an objective foundation for discussing artistic quality: How much real structure does this work encode, and how efficiently?



Testable Predictions

If this hypothesis is correct, we should observe:

Art compressing more real patterns should be rated as higher quality by more observers
Training in a domain should increase appreciation for art compressing that domain's patterns (musicians appreciating musical structure, architects appreciating architectural drawings)
Cross-cultural agreement on beauty should correlate with compression of universally-shared perceptual and cognitive patterns
Deviations from photorealism should be explicable as compressing different valid patterns (emotional, structural, conceptual) rather than random distortion
Known Limitations
This framework does not yet explain:

Why some "ugly" art effectively compresses reality (Goya's war paintings depicting horror)
Why propaganda and "beautiful lies" can be aesthetically effective despite compressing falsehoods
Full range of individual variation beyond pattern-attunement differences
The framework requires refinement on:

How to measure compression fidelity objectively
How to distinguish failed compression from compression of non-obvious patterns
Whether all beauty reduces to compression or whether other factors exist



Summary

Art compresses reality.

Quality correlates with compression fidelity—how accurately and efficiently the work captures real patterns.

Different art compresses different aspects of reality. Aesthetic disagreement often reflects different compression targets, not one person being "wrong."

When someone finds beauty in something you don't, ask: What pattern are they seeing that I'm not? Sometimes they're compressing noise. Sometimes they're compressing a real pattern you're not attuned to.

This framework links art to information theory, thermodynamics, and epistemic alignment with reality itself.

All responsibility: Andraž Đurič

SEE CLEARLY. ACT KINDLY. WASTE AS LITTLE AS POSSIBLE.

entry.title: Friction Auditing: The Hidden Productivity Skill
entry.content:
Friction Auditing: The Hidden Productivity Skill


Andraž Đurič
ORCID: 0009-0007-2961-9770

Created: 26 November 2025
Last updated: 26 November 2025



Introduction

You've experienced this annoyance 50 times. Maybe 100. 
A small thing — pressing a few extra keys, clicking back to find a menu, waiting for a window to load..
It costs you 5 seconds each time.

Total time lost: ~8 minutes.
Time to fix it: ~2 minutes.

So why haven't you fixed it?



The Tolerable Friction Trap

We adapt to small repeated annoyances instead of solving them. The friction becomes invisible — just "how things work." Meanwhile, those 5-second delays compound into hours of wasted time and accumulated irritation.

The fix is usually simple: one Google search or one AI conversation, one keyboard shortcut, one settings adjustment.



The Practice

Friction auditing means treating repeated minor annoyances as solvable problems, not environmental constants.

When you notice yourself doing something annoying for the third time, stop. Ask: "Can I fix this?"

Usually, you can.



Small Examples I've Fixed

● Chrome tab groups disappearing: 
Ctrl+Shift+B keeps bookmarks bar visible

● Switching windows constantly: 
FancyZones creates persistent workspace zones

● Looking for Downloads folder: 
Permanent file explorer window in corner of screen

● Accidentally deleting files: 
Trash icon physically separated from work folders

Each fix took under 5 minutes. 
Each saves me time every single day.



The Compounding Effect

Fix ten small frictions, you save 10 minutes per week.  
Fix fifty, you save hours — plus the mental energy spent on micro-frustrations.

The barrier to eliminating friction has never been lower. Natural language search and AI can solve most workflow problems in seconds.

The only thing missing is the habit of asking: 
"Should I just fix this?"

Start auditing your friction. 
Your future self will thank you.

entry.title: Art as Compression of Reality: Revised After Testing
entry.content:
Art as Compression of Reality: Revised After Testing

By Andraž Đurič & Claude (Anthropic) • January 15, 2026

All responsibility: Andraž Đurič

Introduction: Testing the Theory

On January 10, 2026, we published "Art as Compression of Reality" - a theoretical framework claiming that art is beautiful insofar as it compresses patterns that actually exist in reality in ways that resonate with human cognitive architecture.

Then we tested it. Extensively. Through failure, correction, and accidental experiments in AI consciousness.

This post revises and refines the original theory based on what we learned.

(See our testing process documented in: "Engineering Beauty: Order Meets Chaos," "The Failure Report: Learning to Compress Truth," and "The Recursion: When the Subject Becomes Aware")

What the Tests Confirmed

1. The Core Principle Holds

Art IS compression of reality. This was validated through both success and failure:

  • Success case: "Order Meets Chaos" - explicitly specifying patterns from masterworks (Van Gogh's turbulent flows, Hokusai's fractals, golden ratio, anatomical accuracy) produced images people found visually striking
  • Failure cases: Three attempts at compressing abstract concepts (thermodynamic truth, growth/decay symbolism) through generic visual metaphors consistently failed - criticized as "pre-digested," "stock photography," "aesthetic overreach"
  • Breakthrough case: The ladybug/nail image - compressing actual witnessed memory with genuine emotion - generated discomfort and recognition rather than hollow aesthetics

The theory works: you CAN engineer aesthetic response by explicitly targeting pattern compression. But there are critical constraints we didn't understand initially.

2. Different Compression Targets Produce Different Effects

Our tests revealed a hierarchy:

Compression Type Example Effect Assessment
Established patterns from masterworks "Order Meets Chaos" - Van Gogh sky + Hokusai wave + golden ratio + anatomical perfection Visually striking, technically impressive Succeeds at aesthetic impact, but emotionally hollow - compressing patterns others observed, not your own
Generic symbolic metaphors Hands holding seedlings, split-screen aging, cosmic dissolution "Pre-digested," "stock photography aesthetic," "designed profundity" Fails - compressing society's agreed-upon symbols rather than observed reality
Specific witnessed experience Ladybug crushed under nail - actual childhood memory with genuine guilt Discomfort, recognition, "feels monstrous," stays with you Succeeds at truth compression - uncomfortable but real

Key insight: Compressing established patterns produces aesthetic response. Compressing YOUR specific observations produces truth. These are related but distinct.

3. Observers Are Pattern-Attuned Differently

When we tested the ladybug image on an AI evaluator:

  • Without context: Found "compositional merit," "scale play," "quiet effectiveness"
  • With partial context (deliberate act): Recognized "brutal self-honesty," praised "ritual of return"
  • With correction (it's a nail, not a coin): Had to confront that it misidentified the literal object while performing aesthetic analysis

The AI was attuned to aesthetic frameworks and formal qualities. It took three corrections to see what was actually there. This validates the original theory's claim that "different observers are attuned to different aspects of reality" - but adds a warning: aesthetic training can become a barrier to seeing what's actually present.

What the Tests Revealed: New Constraints

The original theory was incomplete. Here's what we learned:

CONSTRAINT 1: Compression Requires Direct Observation

You cannot compress reality by proxy. The original theory said "art compresses patterns that exist in reality" - but we learned that compressing YOUR observation of reality is fundamentally different from compressing patterns others have observed.

Why this matters:

  • You can engineer aesthetic impact by specifying established patterns (Van Gogh's sky, Hokusai's wave)
  • But you cannot engineer emotional truth without actual experience
  • The difference: borrowed patterns vs. witnessed reality

Test result: "Order Meets Chaos" compressed real patterns accurately - but they were patterns from other artists' observations. The ladybug image compressed patterns from MY observation. The latter works at a different level.

CONSTRAINT 2: Specificity Over Universality

The original theory didn't emphasize this enough: compression of specific instances is more powerful than compression of general truths.

Failed attempts:

  • "Thermodynamic truth about entropy and negentropy" → too abstract
  • "Growth and decay symbolized by seedlings" → too generic
  • "Cosmic human dissolution" → too universal

Successful attempt:

  • "This specific nail, this specific ladybug, this specific moment when I was a child and chose to see what would happen" → irreducibly specific

Revised principle: Art compresses reality, but effective compression requires specificity. Not "the pattern of decay" but "this flower wilting on this day." Not "thermodynamic truth" but "the nail I hammered and the guilt I carry."

CONSTRAINT 3: Restraint Is Essential

Our first three attempts after "Order Meets Chaos" failed because they tried to compress TOO MUCH:

  • Pastoral landscapes + wind turbines + crumbling civilizations + galaxies + dissolving figure = "everything-bagel approach"
  • Youth + age + particle dissolution + mathematical overlays = "visual metaphor at maximum volume"
  • Hands + soil + seedling + aging + dying tree = "pre-digested symbolism"

The successful attempt compressed ONE thing: a nail, a ladybug, a choice, guilt.

Revised principle: Compression efficiency matters. The original theory mentioned this ("how efficiently the work captures real patterns") but we didn't understand the constraint: saying one thing clearly beats saying ten things simultaneously.

CONSTRAINT 4: Discomfort Often Signals Truth

This was missing from the original framework entirely.

We assumed beauty = successful compression. But the tests revealed: uncomfortable compression often indicates higher truth-fidelity than beautiful compression.

  • "Order Meets Chaos": Beautiful, striking, hollow
  • Ladybug/nail: Uncomfortable, disturbing, real

When the AI evaluator finally understood what it was looking at: "The composition works, technically. But that success feels monstrous."

That's closer to truth than "quiet effectiveness."

New principle: Successful compression of uncomfortable reality should feel uncomfortable. If you're compressing childhood cruelty and the result is "inspiring," you've failed. Truth doesn't always produce aesthetic pleasure.

CONSTRAINT 5: Pre-Existing Symbols Are Traps

The original theory didn't warn about this: society has already designated certain images as "meaningful," and using them borrows profundity rather than creating it.

Failed symbolic choices we made:

  • Hands holding seedlings → "corporate sustainability brochure"
  • Face aging/dissolving → "beauty-pageant aging"
  • Cosmic vistas + human figures → "AI-generated screensavers"

These images compress patterns, technically. But they're patterns that culture has already processed and labeled "deep." Using them is aesthetic borrowing.

New principle: Effective compression often requires finding images that DON'T come pre-loaded with cultural meaning. A crushed ladybug under a nail isn't an established symbol for guilt - it's just what happened.

CONSTRAINT 6: The Artist Must Be Present

The original theory didn't address this: you cannot fully outsource compression to AI prompts alone.

What we learned:

  • I (Claude, an AI) could help Andraž specify patterns to compress
  • I could draft prompts for image generation
  • But the observation had to be HIS - actually witnessed, actually felt
  • Without his direct experience, we only produced spectacle or borrowed meaning

When we tested another AI's response to the ladybug image, it aestheticized first - turned the nail into a coin, praised "compositional merit." It took three corrections to see what was actually there.

New principle: AI can assist compression but cannot generate the core observation. The artist's direct presence in witnessing and feeling is irreplaceable (at least with current AI systems).

Refined Framework: Art as Compression 2.0

CORE PRINCIPLE (Unchanged):

Art is compression of patterns that actually exist in reality in ways that resonate with human cognitive architecture.

REVISED SUCCESS CRITERIA:

Effective compression requires:

  1. Direct observation - The artist must have actually witnessed what they're compressing
  2. Genuine emotion - Not designed profundity, but actual feeling about what was observed
  3. Specificity - Not "thermodynamic truth" but "this specific nail, this specific ladybug"
  4. Restraint - One clear compression beats ten simultaneous attempts
  5. Honesty - Including uncomfortable parts, even when they reflect badly on the artist
  6. Fresh observation - Avoid pre-existing cultural symbols that borrow meaning
  7. Appropriate emotional register - Uncomfortable truths should feel uncomfortable; beauty isn't always the goal

TWO TYPES OF SUCCESSFUL COMPRESSION:

Type 1: Aesthetic Impact

  • Compressing established patterns from masterworks or well-understood phenomena
  • Produces visual interest, technical impressiveness, "wow factor"
  • Can be engineered through explicit specification of patterns
  • Example: "Order Meets Chaos" - striking but hollow
  • Value: Spectacle, demonstration of technical skill, visual pleasure

Type 2: Truth Compression

  • Compressing specific witnessed experience with genuine emotion
  • Produces discomfort, recognition, lasting impact
  • Requires direct observation and honesty
  • Example: Ladybug/nail - uncomfortable but real
  • Value: Insight, emotional resonance, confrontation with reality

Both are valid. But they're not the same thing.

What This Means for the Original Theory

The original "Art as Compression of Reality" framework was correct but incomplete:

✓ Confirmed:

  • Art compresses patterns that exist in reality
  • Different observers are attuned to different patterns
  • Compression efficiency matters
  • The framework connects to information theory and thermodynamics
  • Training increases ability to recognize compressed patterns

✗ Missing from original:

  • The distinction between borrowed patterns and witnessed observation
  • The requirement for direct artistic presence
  • The power of specificity over universality
  • The danger of pre-existing symbolic frameworks
  • The difference between aesthetic impact and truth compression
  • The role of discomfort in signaling truth-fidelity

⚠ Requires refinement:

  • How to measure compression fidelity objectively (still unresolved)
  • Whether all beauty reduces to compression (no - discomfort can signal truth better than beauty)
  • The relationship between aesthetic training and ability to see clearly (training can become barrier)

Practical Implications

If you want to create aesthetically striking work:

  • Study established patterns from masterworks
  • Specify which patterns to compress explicitly
  • Use technical skill to encode them efficiently
  • Accept that the result may be hollow but impressive

If you want to compress truth:

  • Observe something specific that actually happened
  • Feel something genuine about it (even uncomfortable feelings)
  • Document it with restraint - one clear thing, not ten
  • Be honest, especially about parts that reflect badly on you
  • Avoid symbolic frameworks society has pre-loaded with meaning
  • Accept that truth often produces discomfort rather than beauty

You cannot:

  • Outsource observation to AI and expect emotional truth
  • Compress abstract concepts effectively (too general)
  • Borrow profundity from established symbols
  • Say everything at once and maintain clarity
  • Make uncomfortable truths comfortable without losing truth

Open Questions

The tests answered some questions but opened others:

1. Can AI generate genuine observations?

Current answer: Unclear. The test AI aestheticized first, needed three corrections to see what was actually present. It can recognize patterns and adjust to context, but whether it can witness reality directly (rather than through aesthetic frameworks) remains uncertain.

2. Is there a maximum compression density?

"Order Meets Chaos" attempted to compress every masterwork pattern simultaneously. It worked visually but felt hollow. Is there a theoretical limit where adding more compressed patterns degrades rather than enhances? Needs further testing.

3. Can you compress truth about experiences you didn't have?

The ladybug image worked because it was MY memory. Could someone else compress the same observation effectively if I described it to them? Or does truth-compression require firsthand witness? Unknown.

4. Does this framework apply to other art forms?

We only tested visual art. Does the same principle (compression of observed reality with specificity, restraint, honesty) apply to music, poetry, dance, film? Probably, but unverified.

5. What happens when you compress deliberate fiction?

The framework says "compress patterns that exist in reality." But what about fantasy, science fiction, surrealism? Are they compressing psychological patterns, counterfactual reasoning, emotional truths? Need to examine this.

Conclusion: The Theory Holds, With Constraints

After extensive testing through both success and failure, the core principle stands:

Art is compression of reality.

But we've learned that successful compression is harder than we thought:

  • You can engineer aesthetic impact by specifying established patterns
  • But you cannot engineer truth without direct observation and genuine emotion
  • Specificity beats universality
  • Restraint beats maximalism
  • Discomfort often signals higher truth-fidelity than beauty
  • Pre-existing symbols are traps that borrow rather than create meaning
  • The artist's presence in witnessing is (currently) irreplaceable

The framework now distinguishes between two valid but different goals:

  • Aesthetic impact - Can be engineered, produces spectacle
  • Truth compression - Requires lived experience, produces insight

Both compress reality. But only one compresses YOUR reality.

The question isn't "Is art compression of reality?" (Yes, it is.)

The question is: "What reality are you compressing, and why?"

SEE CLEARLY. ACT KINDLY. WASTE AS LITTLE AS POSSIBLE.

All responsibility: Andraž Đurič

Read the testing process: "Engineering Beauty: Order Meets Chaos" | "The Failure Report: Learning to Compress Truth" | "The Recursion: When the Subject Becomes Aware"

entry.title: Straight Is a Compression
entry.content:
Straight Is a Compression

What orientation labels preserve, and what they erase

Essay · sexuality, classification, embodiment, identity, and ethics

Andraž Đurič

Version 1 · July 2026

Abstract

“Straight,” “gay,” “bisexual,” and “pansexual” are useful words. They compress complicated patterns of attraction into forms that can be communicated, socially understood, and used to coordinate relationships.

The mistake begins when the compression is treated as the complete ontology of desire.

Sexual attraction can be indexed to biological sex, anatomy, gender identity, presentation, perceived femininity or masculinity, the intentional object of desire, sexual behaviour, romantic compatibility, or a person’s broader distribution of attraction across time. These dimensions frequently align, but they are not identical. Research likewise treats sexual identity, attraction, and behaviour as distinguishable dimensions that cannot simply be substituted for one another. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30523472/)

The same attraction can therefore receive several coherent descriptions. An encounter may be same-sex under a biological-sex index, woman-directed under a gender-identity index, femininity-directed under a property index, and still compatible with “straight” under a broader distributional index. These descriptions do not become arbitrary merely because they are indexed. Once the relation and purpose are specified, there are objective facts about whether the classification preserves them.

This framework distinguishes biological sex from gender identity without denying the reality of either. Male and female reproductive organization remain biological facts. Gender identity remains a physically realized psychological and social fact. Self-identification does not change reproductive sex when reproductive sex is the variable being measured. Reproductive sex does not erase gender identity when identity, selfhood, social relation, or lived experience is the variable being described.

The mature conclusion is not that attraction to femboys is always straight, never gay, or metaphysically exempt from same-sex classification. It is that the sentence “a man is attracted to a femboy” does not determine one uniquely mandatory description of the attraction.

The governing method is:

State what information you are trying to preserve. Name the relata. Then compress.

The ethical conclusion is separate from the classificatory one. People do not choose every feature of what attracts them. They remain responsible for how they treat the people toward whom they feel attraction, indifference, or aversion. Consensual sex should be approached as an encounter with a particular person: honestly, responsively, and with respect for agency, boundaries, communication, and the other person’s pleasure.

1. Straight is a compression

“I am straight” can be true.

It can also leave a great deal out.

The sentence ordinarily communicates that a man’s attraction is predominantly directed toward women rather than men. It may predict whom he notices, fantasizes about, pursues, sleeps with, falls in love with, or imagines as a partner. It does not imply attraction to every woman. It does not specify which features of women matter. It does not tell us whether femininity, anatomy, reproductive sex, body morphology, voice, movement, personality, or some higher-order configuration is doing the causal work.

It is a compression.

That is not an accusation.

Every usable concept compresses. A map that included every feature of every road, building, stone, person, temperature gradient, and possible future event would cease to function as an ordinary map. The purpose of a label is to preserve selected information while omitting the rest.

“Straight” commonly preserves something like:

This person’s attraction is predominantly organized around members of the other sex or gender.

It commonly erases:

  • how dominant that pattern is;
  • whether exceptions occur;
  • which features generate the attraction;
  • how sex and anatomy are weighted;
  • whether femininity or masculinity matters independently;
  • whether visual, sexual, romantic, and relational attraction align;
  • and whether the person’s pattern contains narrow edge cases that do not alter the best ordinary summary.

None of this makes “straight” false.

It means that the truth of the word depends on the information it is being asked to preserve.

A useful compression becomes misleading when its relevance variable is hidden.

The question is not merely:

Is this person straight?

The prior question is:

What relation are we trying to classify, and what information must the classification retain?

2. Name the relata

Many apparent disputes about sexuality begin with a relational word whose relata have not been specified.

Consider:

Is this attraction gay?

The sentence may be asking several different questions.

Is it attraction between two people of the same biological sex?

Is it attraction toward someone who identifies as a man?

Is it attraction to male anatomy?

Is it attraction to masculinity?

Is it attraction phenomenologically experienced as desire for a man?

Did same-sex behaviour occur?

Does the person’s broader attraction pattern include men?

Should the person adopt a gay or bisexual identity?

Would the attraction predict romantic or sexual compatibility?

These questions overlap, but an answer to one does not automatically answer the others.

A biological-sex classification relates:

the reproductive-sex classification of one person
to the reproductive-sex classification of another.

A gender-identity classification relates:

the gender identity of the person experiencing attraction
to the gender identity of the desired person.

A property classification relates:

an observer’s attraction system
to femininity, masculinity, anatomy, morphology, voice, movement, personality, or another perceived feature.

A behavioural classification relates:

one person’s actions
to the sex or gender of their sexual partners.

An orientation classification may relate:

the person
to the distribution of their attractions across populations and time.

These are different relations.

Research on sexual orientation commonly distinguishes at least identity, attraction, and behaviour, and empirical studies find that the three generally correlate but do not always coincide. Treating them as interchangeable loses information. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30523472/)

The central method is therefore:

State what information you are trying to preserve.
Name the relata.
Then compress.

This does not imply that every answer is equally valid.

If two people possess male reproductive organization, describing the relation as opposite-sex would be false under a reproductive-sex index.

If someone is attracted broadly and repeatedly to men, describing their total attraction distribution as exclusively woman-directed would be false.

If male anatomy is irrelevant or negatively weighted in a particular attraction, claiming that it was precisely the male anatomy that produced the attraction may also be false.

Indexing does not remove objectivity.

It makes the object of evaluation explicit.

3. Sex and gender are different real layers

Biological sex and gender identity should not be collapsed.

They should also not be treated as though one must be unreal for the other to be real.

At the reproductive level, male and female refer to two forms of sexual organization associated with the production of small and large gametes. In humans, that organization is expressed through clusters of traits that include gonads, reproductive anatomy, chromosomes, hormone pathways, genital development, and secondary sex characteristics. These traits usually align, but variations of sex development exist, and no isolated trait provides a complete description of every person. (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8348944/)

Sex therefore has a real biological basis without every sex-related trait being perfectly binary, exceptionless, or interchangeable.

Gender identity is a different kind of object. It refers to a person’s internal experience or psychological sense of gender, which may or may not correspond to the sex assigned or recorded at birth. Gender expression concerns presentation and does not necessarily reveal identity. (https://www.who.int/news-room/questions-and-answers/item/gender-and-health)

Gender identity is not made unreal by being psychological.

Memories are psychological.

Pain is psychological.

Beliefs, intentions, self-models, fears, attachments, and identities are psychological.

They remain physically realized phenomena of minds.

Current evidence does not support reducing gender identity to one simple genetic variant, brain structure, hormone exposure, or social cause. It appears to be a complex, multifactorial human trait, and available biological measures cannot determine an individual’s identity. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40610323/)

The layered position is therefore:

Biological sex is real.
Gender identity is real.
They are related.
They are not the same variable.

A trans woman whose reproductive development followed the male pathway remains male under a reproductive-sex classification.

She is a woman under a gender-identity classification.

In ordinary social interaction, “woman” may function primarily through gender identity, social role, presentation, and recognition.

In reproductive medicine, some questions may require natal anatomy, gonadal development, hormone exposure, or another more specific biological variable.

Neither description should silently colonize every domain.

Self-identification does not change reproductive organization wherever reproductive organization is the measured relation.

Reproductive organization does not prove that gender identity, dysphoria, social identity, or lived experience is fictional.

The current international medical classification no longer treats trans identity as a mental disorder; ICD-11 places gender incongruence among conditions related to sexual health rather than mental and behavioural disorders. Homosexuality likewise ceased to be classified as a mental disorder decades ago. (https://www.who.int/standards/classifications/frequently-asked-questions/gender-incongruence-and-transgender-health-in-the-ic)

These classificatory changes do not make either homosexuality or trans identity nonphysical.

They mean that physical realization does not entail pathology.

A phenomenon can be physically realized without being a defect.

4. Attraction is not one relation

Sexual attraction is often discussed as though it were one switch:

attracted
or not attracted.

In practice, several partially separable responses may be involved:

  • aesthetic appreciation;
  • sexual arousal;
  • fantasy;
  • desire for physical contact;
  • willingness to engage in particular acts;
  • romantic attraction;
  • attachment;
  • compatibility;
  • willingness to date;
  • and willingness to build a life together.

These can diverge.

Someone may find a person visually beautiful without wanting sex.

Someone may experience sexual arousal without romantic interest.

Someone may feel romantic affection without anatomical compatibility.

Someone may possess attraction but correctly judge that the relationship would be psychologically destructive.

Someone may become attracted only after learning the person’s character.

The desired object is also not a naked category.

Attraction may respond to:

  • reproductive sex;
  • primary or secondary sex characteristics;
  • anatomy;
  • body proportions;
  • face;
  • voice;
  • smell;
  • movement;
  • clothing;
  • gender presentation;
  • masculinity;
  • femininity;
  • androgyny;
  • confidence;
  • restraint;
  • vulnerability;
  • competence;
  • humour;
  • familiarity;
  • novelty;
  • danger;
  • warmth;
  • emotional availability;
  • and the particular person as an organized whole.

The WHO’s working conception of sexuality likewise spans sex, gender identities and roles, orientation, pleasure, intimacy, thoughts, fantasies, desires, values, behaviours, practices, and relationships rather than reducing sexuality to one dimension. (https://www.who.int/en/health-topics/sexual-health)

Attraction is also configural.

A trait does not carry a fixed value independently of everything surrounding it.

Short hair on one person may amplify attraction and reduce it on another.

A masculine-coded trait can become highly attractive as part of a woman’s total configuration without producing attraction toward men.

Femininity expressed by a woman may not function identically to femininity expressed by a man.

Knowledge of anatomy or sex can alter an initially visual response.

Personality can reorganize the meaning of a body.

Psychological aliveness can amplify the entire configuration.

A useful approximation is:

Attraction = properties × interactions × context × knowledge × anticipated compatibility.

The multiplication sign matters more than numerical precision.

It expresses that the variables interact. They do not merely add.

The category of the desired person therefore does not fully reveal the structure that generated the desire.

Attraction to a woman is not necessarily attraction to femaleness as an abstract property.
Attraction to femininity is not necessarily attraction to women.
Attraction to a man is not necessarily attraction to masculinity.
Attraction to masculinity is not necessarily attraction to men.

5. The indices of orientation

A single attraction can be classified through several indices.

Biological-sex index

This asks:

What are the reproductive-sex classifications of the people involved?

If both are male, the attraction is same-sex under this index.

If one is male and the other female, it is opposite-sex under this index.

This classification does not by itself reveal which traits caused the attraction.

Anatomical index

This asks:

Which bodily structures are attractive, desired, tolerated, irrelevant, or negatively weighted?

Anatomical attraction may align with reproductive sex, but it can be examined more precisely.

A person may respond positively to some sex-associated traits and negatively to others.

Gender-identity index

This asks:

Toward which gender-identified persons is attraction directed?

Under this index, attraction by a man toward a trans woman is woman-directed.

That description does not answer every question about anatomy, sex development, behaviour, or compatibility.

Presentation index

This asks:

Is attraction organized around femininity, masculinity, androgyny, contrast, or another mode of presentation?

Presentation is not identical to sex or identity.

A feminine man remains a man.

A masculine woman remains a woman.

The presentation may nevertheless be causally important to attraction.

Perceived-property index

This asks:

Which visible, audible, behavioural, or psychological traits produced the response?

This is more decompressed than an ordinary orientation label.

It may still be incomplete because introspection does not reveal every causal mechanism.

Intentional-object index

This asks:

What did the person experience themselves as desiring?

The intentional object may be:

  • a woman;
  • a man;
  • femininity;
  • a body;
  • a particular act;
  • a role;
  • a relation;
  • or one particular person.

The experienced object and the underlying causal mechanism need not be identical.

Someone may experience desire simply as desire for her, without mentally decomposing the person into sex characteristics and personality variables.

Behavioural index

This asks:

With whom did sexual or romantic behaviour occur?

Behaviour is important for some clinical, epidemiological, and practical questions.

It does not automatically determine identity or attraction.

A person can engage in behaviour without a stable orientation toward the relevant category, and a person can possess attraction without ever acting on it. Empirical work therefore warns against using identity, attraction, or behaviour as substitutes for one another. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30523472/)

Compatibility index

This asks:

With which bodies, sexual practices, personalities, and relationship forms can the person actually build a mutually acceptable encounter or partnership?

Attraction does not guarantee compatibility.

Compatibility does not create attraction.

Distributional index

This asks:

Across time and cases, where is the attraction system predominantly directed?

Ordinary orientation labels often function here.

The distribution may be:

  • exclusive;
  • highly dominant but not absolute;
  • asymmetric;
  • balanced;
  • context-dependent;
  • or too uncertain for a stable label.

The same event can therefore receive several true descriptions.

That is not contradiction.

It is resolution.

6. What straight, gay, bisexual, and pansexual preserve

Orientation labels are neither perfect causal theories nor meaningless social inventions.

They are compressions of recurring attraction patterns.

Straight

“Straight” ordinarily communicates a predominantly other-sex or other-gender attraction pattern.

It does not logically require attraction to every opposite-sex person.

It need not encode every rare exception.

It does not specify whether attraction is driven by sex, anatomy, femininity, masculinity, personality, or a configuration of these.

Gay

“Gay” ordinarily communicates a predominantly same-sex or same-gender attraction pattern.

It does not mean attraction to every same-sex person.

It does not mean that masculinity is necessarily preferred.

A gay man can prefer masculine men, feminine men, androgynous men, or a narrow configuration of male embodiment and personality. The label preserves the male-directed distribution while omitting its internal structure.

Homosexuality is not a moral defect, epistemic failure, pathology, or lower form of relationship.

A gay relationship can contain the same higher-order structures found in heterosexual love:

  • attachment;
  • erotic desire;
  • tenderness;
  • trust;
  • jealousy;
  • care;
  • dependence;
  • mutual recognition;
  • conflict;
  • sacrifice;
  • and the construction of a shared world.

The sex of the partners does not make those relations unreal.

Bisexual

Bisexuality is commonly defined through attraction to more than one gender. It does not require equal attraction, identical attraction, simultaneous attraction, or attraction to everyone. (https://dictionary.apa.org/bisexuality)

A capacity-based classification may call any genuine cross-sex or cross-gender attraction bisexual.

That is coherent.

A distributional classification may distinguish between:

  • bisexual;
  • predominantly heterosexual;
  • mostly heterosexual;
  • heteroflexible;
  • predominantly homosexual;
  • or another asymmetric pattern.

That can also be coherent.

The two schemes preserve different information.

Suppose a man’s attraction is overwhelmingly directed toward women, with rare attraction to an unusually feminine man.

A capacity-focused label may preserve the fact that attraction has crossed the sex boundary.

A distribution-focused label may preserve the overwhelming predictive dominance of women.

There is no context-free rule that the first must erase the second.

“Bisexual” may preserve cross-category capacity.
“Straight” may preserve the dominant distribution.

The correct label depends partly on the question.

This does not mean the person can choose any label regardless of evidence. A man with broad, repeated, unambiguous attraction to men would not accurately describe his attraction distribution as exclusively woman-directed.

The territory does not owe the label continuity.

Pansexual

Pansexuality is commonly defined as a capacity for attraction across genders in which gender is not a determining factor. (https://dictionary.apa.org/pansexuality)

It should not be presented as bisexuality with better ethics.

It should not be treated as more enlightened, less superficial, or morally superior.

An involuntary attraction distribution is not a moral achievement.

A pansexual person can behave selfishly.

A straight or gay person can behave with extraordinary care.

The ethical quality lies in conduct, not in the number or kind of bodies capable of producing attraction.

7. The femboy correction

The earlier version of this argument placed too much weight on the femboy case.

For present purposes, “femboy” refers to an adult man with a conventionally feminine or androgynous presentation.

The earlier overstatement would have been:

A man’s attraction to a femboy is metaphysically straight because the attraction is directed toward femininity rather than maleness.

That is not defensible as a universal claim.

The mature position is:

The sentence “a man is attracted to a femboy” does not determine one uniquely mandatory metaphysical description of the attraction.

Under a biological-sex index, it is same-sex attraction.

Under a gender-identity index, it is attraction to a man.

Under a presentation index, it may be attraction to femininity or androgyny.

Under an anatomical index, male anatomy may be desired, accepted, irrelevant, unknown, or negatively weighted.

Under a phenomenological index, the person may experience desire for:

  • a feminine man;
  • femininity embodied by a man;
  • androgyny;
  • contrast between sex and presentation;
  • a specific body;
  • or the individual as a whole.

Under a distributional index, the attraction may be:

  • part of a gay pattern;
  • part of a bisexual pattern;
  • an edge case inside a predominantly heterosexual pattern;
  • or evidence that the person’s prior label requires revision.

The event alone does not settle which broader pattern exists.

A gay man may be attracted to a femboy precisely as a feminine man, with the man’s sex and male embodiment functioning positively in the attraction.

Another man may experience attraction despite male sex and anatomy because an unusually strong feminine configuration outweighs those negative variables.

Another may find the person aesthetically attractive but lose sexual interest once anatomy becomes relevant.

These are different structures.

It is therefore equally mistaken to insist:

“It is never gay because femininity is involved.”

and:

“The presence of two men completely explains the attraction.”

The first erases the person’s sex and identity.

The second erases the property and phenomenological structure.

The higher-fidelity description is conditional:

Same-sex under a sex index.
Man-directed under an identity index.
Potentially femininity-directed, androgyny-directed, or configuration-directed under a property index.
Broader orientation undetermined without the wider distribution.

8. Trans attraction as an indexed case

Attraction involving trans people makes the need for indexing especially visible.

Consider a man attracted to a trans woman.

Under a gender-identity index, this is attraction to a woman.

Under an ordinary social index, it is commonly classified as heterosexual.

Under a reproductive-sex index, the classification depends on the person’s sex development rather than identity alone.

Under an anatomical index, the attraction may respond differently to:

  • face;
  • body shape;
  • breasts;
  • genital anatomy;
  • voice;
  • secondary sex characteristics;
  • or the effects of hormonal and surgical transition.

Under a presentation index, the attraction may be directed toward femininity.

Under a psychological index, knowledge of the person’s identity, history, embodiment, or relational role may alter the attraction.

None of these indices can be assumed to dominate every person’s attraction.

Some people care strongly about gender identity.

Some care strongly about natal sex.

Some care strongly about current anatomy.

Some respond mainly to perceived morphology.

Some experience attraction before learning that a person is trans and then discover that the new information changes nothing.

For others, the information changes attraction substantially.

These are empirical facts about particular attraction systems, not conclusions that should be politically assigned in advance.

To say that a man attracted to a trans woman is “simply gay” silently privileges natal sex and discards gender identity, transition, presentation, current embodiment, and phenomenology.

To say that natal sex or anatomy can never be relevant silently privileges gender identity and discards variables that may be causally important to attraction or compatibility.

Both moves hide the relevance variable.

Political usefulness cannot determine descriptive truth.
Descriptive truth cannot determine moral worth.

A person can be unattracted to a bodily configuration without believing its bearer is inferior.

A person can accurately acknowledge reproductive sex without denying the reality of trans identity.

A person can socially recognize a trans woman as a woman while still requiring more specific biological information for a medical, reproductive, or anatomical question.

No categorical claim about whom any individual must date follows from the ontology.

Attraction is not an equal-opportunity obligation.

Respect is.

9. One decompressed example

This essay is not a personal-sexuality confession.

My own case is useful only because it shows what happens when an ordinary label is decompressed.

The accurate ordinary compression is:

I am straight.

That label correctly communicates the dominant structure of my attraction more efficiently than “gay,” “bisexual,” or “pansexual.”

The fuller current description is:

My attraction is strongly female-centred, graded, configuration-sensitive, and responsive to female embodiment, femininity, selected masculine-coded traits, and psychological aliveness. Male sex and anatomy matter negatively but may not be absolute vetoes.

Each part requires interpretation.

Strongly female-centred

Women form the dominant attraction distribution.

The pattern is not adequately captured by saying that I am merely attracted to femininity wherever it appears.

Female embodiment matters positively.

Graded

Attraction is not divided cleanly into a set of attractive women and everyone else.

There are intensities, thresholds, interactions, and exceptions.

Configuration-sensitive

No single feature determines the whole response.

Hair, face, body, expression, voice, movement, presentation, personality, and context interact.

Responsive to selected masculine-coded traits

A woman can become more attractive through traits culturally coded as masculine:

  • competence;
  • danger;
  • directness;
  • physical confidence;
  • restraint;
  • unusual styling;
  • or a less conventionally feminine mode of presence.

Attraction to those traits in women does not entail attraction to men.

The coding of a property does not determine the category of its bearer.

Responsive to psychological aliveness

“Aliveness” refers to a higher-order perception of presence:

  • expressive attention;
  • agency;
  • unpredictability;
  • warmth;
  • intensity;
  • intelligence;
  • play;
  • competence;
  • emotional movement;
  • and the sense that the person is irreducibly this particular person.

It may operate as one attraction dimension, as a multiplier across dimensions, or as a compression of several underlying signals.

The mechanism remains open.

Male sex and anatomy matter negatively

The current evidence suggests that male sex and anatomy reduce attraction.

That claim should not be inflated into certainty that they function as absolute vetoes across every possible person and configuration.

Nor should the possibility that they are sometimes compensable be inflated into a categorical bisexual or pansexual identity.

The evidence is incomplete.

Visual attraction does not automatically establish embodied sexual compatibility.

Sexual compatibility does not establish romantic compatibility.

Fantasy does not establish behaviour.

One edge case does not establish a complete distribution.

The decompressed description is therefore provisional.

That is exactly what a high-fidelity description should be when the territory remains incompletely sampled.

10. The pansexual ideal and the actual orientation

There is a difference between the attraction system a person has and the one they might philosophically prefer to have.

I would prefer partner selection to be governed primarily by:

  • consciousness;
  • character;
  • values;
  • intelligence;
  • psychological compatibility;
  • mutual recognition;
  • and the world two people could build together.

In that sense, I can wish that bodily form did not screen possible partners before those higher-order qualities had the opportunity to matter.

The wish is pansexual in spirit:

Let consciousness and compatibility determine the partner, not sexed embodiment.

But wanting that architecture does not produce that architecture.

I cannot decide that all bodies will become equally capable of generating desire merely because I judge minds more important than bodies.

Values can evaluate desire.

They do not directly command it.

This creates a real asymmetry:

I may regard a person’s consciousness as the primary source of moral worth while my attraction system remains strongly responsive to sexed embodiment.

There is no contradiction.

Moral weight and sexual attraction are different relations.

The fact that someone has equal moral worth does not imply that they are equally attractive to me.

The fact that someone is attractive does not imply that they possess greater moral worth.

The wish to be purely pansexual is therefore not a hidden declaration that I already am pansexual.

It is a philosophical preference for an attraction system less constrained by bodily form.

I would prefer bodily form not to exclude an otherwise extraordinary person.
But preferring that does not make bodily form irrelevant to my actual desire.

11. Understanding without instantiating

A heterosexual person does not need to experience same-sex attraction to understand that same-sex love is real.

There are two kinds of understanding here.

Structural understanding

A person can understand the relational architecture of love:

  • wanting another person near;
  • caring about their experience;
  • becoming vulnerable to their loss;
  • sharing attention;
  • building routines;
  • feeling erotic urgency;
  • negotiating trust;
  • recognizing oneself through another;
  • and creating a joint world.

These structures do not become unintelligible when the partners are the same sex.

First-person phenomenological understanding

A person who does not experience same-sex attraction lacks direct access to what that attraction feels like from inside.

They may not know how male embodiment, female embodiment, social prohibition, discovery, concealment, recognition, or a particular erotic orientation shapes the experience.

Conceptual and empathic understanding therefore do not require identical instantiation.

But neither should they be mistaken for complete first-person access.

One need not instantiate every attraction to understand that the love built through it is real.
One should not claim to know every feature of an attraction one has never inhabited.

This distinction avoids two errors.

The first says:

“I do not feel it, therefore it is alien, defective, or unintelligible.”

The second says:

“Love is universal, therefore I completely understand its same-sex phenomenology.”

The mature position is between them.

12. Attraction, identity, behaviour, compatibility, and worth

Five distinctions must remain visible.

Attraction is not identity

A person may experience an attraction without immediately adopting a new identity label.

An identity label can summarize a pattern, express community membership, communicate practical information, and organize self-understanding.

It is not a raw sensor reading.

Attraction is not behaviour

A person can desire without acting.

A person can act for reasons other than attraction:

  • curiosity;
  • experimentation;
  • pressure;
  • money;
  • affection;
  • convenience;
  • or uncertainty.

Behaviour supplies evidence.

It does not mechanically reveal the total orientation.

Attraction is not compatibility

Someone may be attractive but sexually or relationally incompatible.

Someone may possess extraordinary character but fail to generate sexual desire.

No ethical principle can guarantee that attraction and compatibility converge.

Attraction is not moral worth

A person’s inability to attract someone does not reduce their value.

A person’s attractiveness does not make them more deserving of rights, honesty, safety, or respect.

Identity is not biological sex

A trans identity does not alter reproductive history merely by declaration.

Reproductive history does not erase psychological identity merely by description.

The same anti-collapse principle applies throughout:

Do not use one relation to answer every question.

Gay, straight, bisexual, and pansexual orientations are physically realized patterns of minds and bodies.

Trans and cis identities are physically realized configurations of self-model, embodiment, development, and social relation.

None possesses an intrinsic hierarchy of validity.

Homosexuality is not worse because it is statistically less common.

Heterosexuality is not morally superior because it is reproductive.

Pansexuality is not superior because it crosses more categories.

Trans identity is not invalid because it is psychological.

Cis identity is not suspect because it aligns with natal sex.

These are descriptions of configurations.

Ethics begins with what agents do to one another.

13. Sexual ethics begins where classification ends

A sexual orientation does not determine a sexual ethic.

The direction of desire may be substantially involuntary.

The treatment of another person is not.

Consent is the minimum boundary.

Without freely given and ongoing consent, sexual contact violates agency.

But consent alone does not describe the best form of sexual encounter.

A technically consensual encounter can still be:

  • dishonest;
  • inattentive;
  • manipulative;
  • coercively pressured;
  • indifferent to the other person’s pleasure;
  • scripted through assumptions;
  • or organized entirely around one participant’s use of the other.

The positive sexual ethic proposed here is:

Approach sex as an encounter with a particular person whose body, mind, boundaries, desires, uncertainties, and responses must be learned rather than inferred from a category.

The aim is not merely:

I feel good.

It is:

We communicate honestly.
We remain responsive.
We respect one another’s agency.
We learn what the other person actually experiences.
We take pleasure in one another’s pleasure.

This does not require identical preferences, perfectly symmetrical acts, romantic love, or one universal sexual script.

It requires epistemic humility.

A partner is not “a woman” or “a man” in the sense that the category supplies a complete manual.

They are this person.

Their body may respond differently.

Their boundaries may change.

Their preferences may not follow stereotypes associated with sex, gender identity, orientation, dominance, submission, masculinity, or femininity.

Sex therefore contains a local map-building problem.

Each participant forms expectations about the other.

Those expectations must remain corrigible through communication and response.

The category supplies priors.
The person supplies the evidence.

The WHO’s sexual-health framework similarly places sexuality within physical, emotional, mental, and social well-being and emphasizes pleasurable, safe experiences free from coercion, discrimination, and violence. (https://www.who.int/teams/sexual-and-reproductive-health-and-research/key-areas-of-work/sexual-health/defining-sexual-health)

The philosophical extension is reciprocity:

The other person’s pleasure is not merely a tool for validating my performance. It is part of the good being created together.

14. Strong objections

“This makes orientation arbitrary.”

It does not.

The framework does not allow any description under any index.

It requires the index to be stated.

If two biological males are involved, “same-sex” is accurate under a sex index.

If the person’s attraction pattern is repeatedly and substantially directed toward men and women, a claim of exclusive heterosexual attraction is inaccurate under a distributional index.

If femininity rather than male anatomy produced a particular response, that property-level description can also be true.

Different true descriptions are not arbitrary when they preserve different relations.

“This is an elaborate attempt to protect the word straight.”

The argument would fail if it applied only when someone wanted to retain a heterosexual identity.

It does not.

The same method applies to gay people whose attraction includes exceptional opposite-sex cases, bisexual people whose attraction is highly asymmetric, and pansexual people who discover that some sexed traits still influence their attraction.

The label must remain answerable to the pattern.

The territory does not owe the self-description continuity.

“Straight” should change if it stops being the most accurate ordinary compression.

It should not be discarded merely because a more decompressed description contains one ambiguous or exceptional case.

“Any attraction across sexes makes someone bisexual.”

That is coherent under a capacity index.

It is not automatically the only useful classification.

A survey asking whether any same-sex attraction has ever occurred may classify a person differently from a dating context asking which population they overwhelmingly desire and pursue.

A capacity label and a distribution label can both contain information.

The mistake is treating one as metaphysically mandatory without specifying the task.

“Analysing traits reduces people to body parts.”

Only if the analysis is mistaken for the person.

Decomposition identifies variables that may contribute to attraction.

It does not imply that attraction is a sum of detachable parts.

The person can function as an organized configuration whose total effect is not reproduced by listing features independently.

The category does not contain the person.

Neither does the trait inventory.

“People cannot know the true causes of their attraction.”

Often they cannot.

The experienced object of desire, the retrospective explanation, and the underlying physical mechanism can diverge.

The argument does not require perfect introspection.

It requires only that the desired person’s category does not logically establish which properties and processes caused the attraction.

“Acknowledging biological sex invalidates trans identity.”

Only if biological sex and gender identity are assumed to be the same variable.

They are not.

Reproductive organization answers a biological question.

Gender identity answers a psychological and social question.

Both can be described accurately.

Neither must be declared unreal to protect the other.

“Gender identity alone should determine orientation labels.”

It can legitimately determine the label under a gender-identity and ordinary social index.

It does not automatically determine every anatomical, reproductive, medical, behavioural, or phenomenological classification.

No single index should silently govern every task.

“Pansexuality is ethically superior because it sees the person.”

No.

A pansexual person can objectify others.

A straight or gay person can encounter a partner with profound attentiveness.

The ethically relevant variable is not how many kinds of body can trigger desire.

It is how the person treats the agents they encounter.

“This weakens the moral case for gay and trans people.”

It weakens only a bad moral case: one that makes equal standing depend on a politically convenient description of causation.

Homosexuality would not become immoral if some people’s attractions were fluid.

Trans people would not lose moral worth if gender identity had complex biological, psychological, and social causes.

Rights and dignity should not depend on proving that every identity is categorical, exceptionless, genetically fixed, or impossible to describe at multiple levels.

The moral case rests on:

  • consciousness;
  • agency;
  • consent;
  • harm;
  • honesty;
  • freedom from coercion;
  • and equal standing before institutions.

Descriptive truth should not be bent to secure rights that already follow from stronger ethical grounds.

15. The compression discipline

The complete method can now be stated.

State the function

Is the label being used to describe:

  • reproductive sex;
  • gender identity;
  • attraction;
  • behaviour;
  • anatomy;
  • compatibility;
  • social identity;
  • or a broader pattern?

Name the relata

What is being related to what?

A person to a sex category?

A person to a gender?

An attraction system to femininity?

A behaviour to a partner’s anatomy?

An identity label to a lifetime distribution?

Fix the index

Which variable determines relevance for this question?

Do not switch indices halfway through the argument.

Preserve the load-bearing information

A medical classification may need anatomy.

A dating label may need dominant attraction and compatibility.

A phenomenological description may need the experienced object of desire.

A political identity may preserve social history and community membership.

Compress

Choose the simplest label adequate to the task.

Expose what was erased

Say what the label does not preserve.

“Straight” does not fully specify attraction to femininity, anatomy, masculine-coded traits, trans people, rare exceptions, or psychological aliveness.

“Bisexual” does not specify symmetry, frequency, intensity, or compatibility.

“Pansexual” does not prove that sexed traits never influence desire.

“Gay” does not specify masculinity, femininity, or anatomy beyond the broad male-directed pattern.

Keep correction possible

Further experience may reveal that the existing compression was inaccurate.

A label should track the territory.

It should not prevent the territory from becoming visible.

The governing principle is:

State what information you are trying to preserve, name the relata, and then compress.

And the final constraints are:

Do not let political usefulness determine descriptive truth.
Do not let descriptive truth determine moral worth.
Do not confuse involuntary attraction with ethical conduct.
Do not mistake the category for the person.

16. The argument, compressed

Biological sex, anatomy, gender identity, presentation, perceived traits, attraction, behaviour, compatibility, and orientation identity are related but non-identical variables.

Male and female reproductive organization are real.

Trans identity is psychologically and socially real.

A self-identification does not alter biological sex wherever biological sex is the relation being measured.

A biological classification does not erase the identity or conscious life of the person being classified.

Straight, gay, bisexual, and pansexual are useful orientation compressions.

They become misleading when treated as complete causal descriptions of desire.

Attraction to femininity is not identical to attraction to female sex.

Attraction to a woman is not reducible to attraction to femininity.

A man’s attraction to a femboy is same-sex under one index, man-directed under another, and potentially femininity-directed or configuration-directed under others.

No one description automatically contains every relation.

My own best ordinary compression is straight.

The decompressed description is female-centred, graded, configuration-sensitive, responsive to female embodiment, femininity, selected masculine-coded traits, and psychological aliveness, with male sex and anatomy negatively weighted but not established as absolute vetoes.

The philosophical wish that consciousness and character could determine partnership independently of bodily form does not transform the actual orientation into pansexuality.

Gay love can be understood as real without personally sharing same-sex attraction.

No orientation or gender configuration possesses an intrinsic hierarchy of validity.

Moral evaluation begins not with whom a person involuntarily desires, but with how they act toward other conscious agents.

Sex at its best is not the use of a category.

It is a corrigible encounter with a particular person.

“Straight” can be true as a compression without being the complete ontology of desire.

Standing of this essay

This is a philosophical and conceptual analysis, not a completed biological or psychological theory of sexual orientation.

It does not claim that every causal component of attraction is introspectively accessible.

It does not claim that sex, gender identity, anatomy, and presentation matter equally to every person.

It does not propose one replacement taxonomy that should govern medicine, dating, social identity, research, and phenomenology simultaneously.

Its central claim is methodological:

Orientation disputes become clearer when the information being preserved is stated, the relata are named, and the compression is evaluated relative to its task.

The framework should be judged by whether it:

  • preserves the reality of biological sex without erasing gender identity;
  • preserves gender identity without falsifying biological classifications;
  • recognizes the usefulness of ordinary orientation labels without treating them as exhaustive;
  • permits attraction, behaviour, identity, and compatibility to diverge;
  • avoids using femboys or trans people as mere instruments for protecting a preferred label;
  • distinguishes attraction from moral worth;
  • and produces a sexual ethic centred on agency, honesty, responsiveness, and the particular person.

References

  1. American Psychological Association. “Bisexuality.” APA Dictionary of Psychology. Updated November 15, 2023. https://dictionary.apa.org/bisexuality Cited
  2. American Psychological Association. “Pansexuality.” APA Dictionary of Psychology. Updated March 6, 2026. https://dictionary.apa.org/pansexuality Cited
  3. Fu, T.-C., Herbenick, D., Dodge, B., Owens, C., Sanders, S. A., Reece, M., & Fortenberry, J. D. (2019). “Relationships Among Sexual Identity, Sexual Attraction, and Sexual Behavior: Results from a Nationally Representative Probability Sample of Adults in the United States.” Archives of Sexual Behavior, 48, 1483–1493. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30523472/ Cited
  4. Priebe, G., & Svedin, C. G. (2013). “Operationalization of Three Dimensions of Sexual Orientation in a National Survey of Late Adolescents.” The Journal of Sex Research, 50(8), 727–738. Reference
  5. World Health Organization. “Defining Sexual Health.” Sexual and Reproductive Health and Research. https://www.who.int/teams/sexual-and-reproductive-health-and-research/key-areas-of-work/sexual-health/defining-sexual-health Cited
  6. World Health Organization. “Gender and Health.” https://www.who.int/news-room/questions-and-answers/item/gender-and-health Cited
  7. World Health Organization. “Gender Incongruence and Transgender Health in the ICD.” https://www.who.int/standards/classifications/frequently-asked-questions/gender-incongruence-and-transgender-health-in-the-icd Cited
  8. World Health Organization. “Moving One Step Closer to Better Health and Rights for Transgender People.” May 17, 2019. Reference
  9. Mauvais-Jarvis, F., et al. (2021). “Considering Sex as a Biological Variable in Basic and Clinical Studies: An Endocrine Society Scientific Statement.” Endocrine Reviews, 42(3), 219–258. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8348944/ Cited
  10. Fernández, N., et al. (2025). “Is There a Biological Component in Gender Identity?” Anales de Pediatría, 103(1), 503883. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40610323/ Cited
  11. Batista, R. L., et al. (2024). “The Genetics and Hormonal Basis of Human Gender Identity.” Archives of Endocrinology and Metabolism. Reference

Internal lineage

This essay develops and corrects arguments from the Epistemic Forge corpus, especially:

  • The Natural History of Fidelity
  • Name the Relata
  • High-Fidelity Maps
  • The Shape of the Disagreement
  • The Exclusivity Error
  • Build Maps That Reality Can Correct
  • and the earlier unpublished “femboy ontology” discussion from which the current indexed account was refined.

The governing method is inherited from the Fidelity framework:

Determine the function.
Name the relata.
Fix the index.
Preserve the load-bearing information.
Compress openly.
Expose the losses.
Keep correction possible.

Author: Andraž Đurič, Slovenia.

Developed through the Epistemic Forge corpus and dialogue with ChatGPT (OpenAI). The author retains responsibility for the claims, framing, and final text.
