entry.blogger:metaDescription: Philosophy can map more positions than a bounded agent should pursue. Evidence marks live options; goals and resources determine the route.

entry.title: Fable 5: What Happened
entry.content:
Fable 5: What Happened

A source-graded map of the Anthropic shutdown — what survives investigation, what hits a wall, and a case study in how easily this story gets told wrong

Andraž Đurič

Version 3 · 16 June 2026 · A developing story, verified as of this date · A fact-map, not a scoop

On 12 June 2026 the United States government ordered Anthropic to cut off its two most capable AI models, and the company shut them down worldwide within hours. The event is real and unusually well documented. It is also already buried under retellings that blend verified fact, single-source reporting, contested characterization, and outright invention into one smooth narrative. This piece does two things. First, it maps what is actually known, grading each load-bearing claim by how well it holds and linking it to its source; where a claim is soft, it pushes until the claim either resolves or hits a wall, and then it names the wall, because a wall honestly described is more useful than a verdict the evidence cannot support. Second, it shows, with one bounded example, how easily this story gets told wrong, including by a frontier AI system that narrated a confident false version of it in real time. The map is the product. The cautionary example is the warrant for needing one.

Confidence labels used throughout, and what each means in this piece: verified multiple independent outlets and/or primary documents agree; one source rests substantially on a single originating report, however widely repeated; disputed the named parties actively contest it; unverified asserted but not corroborated after investigation, including claims this piece flags as false.

What this is, and what it is not. This is a verified synthesis with a thin layer of investigation, not original reporting. It broke no news and contacted no one; its value is in consolidation, source-grading, and pushing the disputed claims as far as public sources allow. It is a snapshot of a story still moving: as of this date the models remain offline and Anthropic and the government are still talking,6 so the date stamp is load-bearing. One disclosure belongs at the top, not buried at the bottom. This article was assembled in collaboration with Claude, a model made by Anthropic, the company the article is about. That is a real conflict of interest, and the correct reader response is not to discard the piece but to hold every claim in it to a higher standard than usual. The article is built to make that possible: claims are attributed, sources are linked, and the grading marks where to push. Apply to this document the skepticism it asks you to apply to everything else. That is not a disclaimer bolted on; it is the method, turned on itself. As one demonstration, earlier drafts of this very piece contained overclaims of their own, caught only by investigating their soft labels; those are documented in section 7.

1. The verified spine

Strip away interpretation and a short list of facts is solidly established across primary documents and multiple independent outlets.

On 9 June 2026, Anthropic launched two models: Claude Fable 5, its most capable publicly available model, and Claude Mythos 5, the same underlying weights with the safety classifiers lifted, restricted to a small set of vetted cyberdefense and infrastructure partners. verified Fable 5 carries classifiers that silently route high-risk queries in cybersecurity, biology, chemistry, and model distillation to the weaker Opus 4.8; Mythos 5 does not.218 The capability jump was real, and the cleanest evidence is independent rather than the company's own: on the third-party vals.ai leaderboard, which Anthropic does not control, Fable 5 took the top spot on SWE-bench Verified at 95.0%, ahead of Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5. Anthropic's own headline figure on the harder SWE-Bench Pro is real but was produced on Anthropic's own tooling rather than a neutral harness, and the ordering at the very top of the coding leaderboards is genuinely contested — a caveat that applies to most launch-day benchmark claims.19 The family had been previewed in April through a restricted program; by Anthropic's account that preview found thousands of severe vulnerabilities across major operating systems and browsers, a claim section 6 examines.7

On Friday, 12 June 2026, at 5:21pm ET, Anthropic received an export-control directive from the US Department of Commerce, citing national security authorities, ordering it to suspend all access to Fable 5 and Mythos 5 by any foreign national, whether inside or outside the United States, including the company's own foreign-national employees. verified The directive required a special license to distribute the models worldwide and warned of civil and criminal penalties for non-compliance. The time, scope, and terms come from Anthropic's own statement and are corroborated by Bloomberg, CNN, and Axios.1456b

Because there is no reliable way to verify the nationality tied to an account in real time, across a user base in the hundreds of millions, on same-day notice, Anthropic disabled both models for everyone rather than attempt to filter. verified This included Amazon Bedrock; Amazon's own status page records that Anthropic asked AWS to revoke access for all users, with other models unaffected.13 A precision worth keeping, because the shorthand online ("the government banned the model for everyone") is not quite the record: the directive targeted foreign nationals; the global shutdown was Anthropic's compliance choice given the impossibility of real-time segmentation.1 As of this writing the models remain offline with no restoration timeline, and senior Anthropic staff were meeting administration officials in Washington this week to try to resolve it.6

2. Who actually raised the alarm, and the strange route it took

The most-repeated version of this story is that a single company, Amazon, turned on its own investment. That is incomplete, and the fuller picture is both less lurid and more interesting.

The most prominent warning did come from Amazon. According to reporting first published by The Wall Street Journal and carried widely, Amazon CEO Andy Jassy told Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and other officials that Amazon researchers had used a series of prompts to get Fable 5 to surface information usable in cyberattacks. verified910 But Amazon was not alone: per Axios, at least five other firms also raised concerns with senior officials on Thursday, 11 June, and the following morning Bessent, National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross, and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick met to weigh a response. verified6b The government then ran its own check, having security researchers test the claims before the President approved the order.10 So this was a cluster of companies escalating to the state, with Amazon the loudest node, not a solitary act.

Who were the other five? Not named in public reporting. unverified They were almost certainly drawn from the only pool with deep access to the dangerous model: the roughly forty to fifty organizations in Anthropic's April trusted-access program, reported to include Amazon, Google, Apple, Nvidia, Microsoft, CrowdStrike, and JPMorgan Chase, vetted precisely so they could probe the model for vulnerabilities. verified16 The specific five are a wall: the pool is known, the names are not.

This answers a question worth asking directly: were these companies snooping, or doing their job? Doing their job, and plausibly an assigned one. Amazon hosts these models and was a trusted-access partner with sanctioned reasons to test the cyber capabilities. And there is a thread suggesting the testing was solicited: Politico reported that the government had asked Amazon for feedback on the new model, which would make Amazon a commissioned evaluator rather than a volunteer. one source That rests on a single anonymous source, but it is consistent with Amazon's own repeated public line that governments seek its counsel on security risks.10 Solicited versus self-directed is a wall: one source says solicited; Amazon will not confirm details.

The genuinely strange element, the one that survives all this context, is the route. The normal path for a researcher who finds a jailbreak is responsible disclosure to the vendor; Anthropic publishes a channel for exactly this. By Anthropic's own account, it received no such disclosure and learned of the concern only when the government order arrived, with no written specifics. Tellingly, the security expert who reviewed the underlying findings did so at Anthropic's request, meaning Anthropic obtained the report after the government had already acted.115b So the finding went to the state, not the maker. That partly dissolves if the government had commissioned the evaluation, since reporting to one's client is not betrayal. But it leaves a real concern, voiced by industry observers, that the episode creates a perverse incentive: a lab's own cloud host and investors can route findings to the government rather than to the lab, which discourages the transparency the whole arrangement depends on.10 One further fact belongs on the record without inference: Amazon is not only Anthropic's investor and host but also, through its own AI ambitions, a competitor. Whether that mattered is unknowable; that it is true is not. Why Jassy personally made the call, rather than a security lead, is a wall: no public source explains it.

3. Two different jailbreaks, and which one this was about

A subtle confusion runs through the coverage: there were two distinct jailbreak events in Fable 5's first three days, and they are not the same thing.

The first is the one the government appears to have cited. By Anthropic's account, the concern relayed to it amounted to prompting the model to read a specific codebase and identify software flaws.1 This is the finding Amazon's researchers produced, and the expert who examined it, Katie Moussouris of Luta Security, who built Microsoft's and the Pentagon's bug-bounty programs, says it is not really a jailbreak at all but "Defense Oriented Prompting," a technique defenders use, and that the government read it wrong. disputed1515b Section 6 returns to her assessment.

The second is louder and more alarming, and its role is unconfirmed. On 10 June, the well-known red-teamer Pliny the Liberator publicly claimed to have defeated Fable 5's classifiers using a multi-step, multi-agent method, posted screenshots he said showed the model producing material it should refuse, including software-exploit code and chemical-synthesis instructions, and published the model's roughly 120,000-character system prompt to a public repository. disputed Anthropic disputes that this was a genuine jailbreak, and crucially, does not say whether it was the event behind the order.1720 The honest position is that the government's stated concern matches the first, narrower finding, while the second, more dramatic, public one sits temporally adjacent with its causal role unestablished. Which jailbreak drove the action is a wall: the descriptions point to the codebase finding, but the record does not foreclose the public one.

4. The China thread

A further reported trigger is more serious and more contested than either jailbreak, and it was absent from the first accounts. According to Semafor, citing a person familiar with the matter, the controls were imposed partly over suspicion that a China-linked group had accessed Mythos, the restricted tier behind the public Fable 5. disputed If true, the fenced model, not just the consumer one, would have been breached, which would explain a response measured in days and would give the foreign-national restriction a clear logic: a fear of distillation, where an adversary with access copies the model's capabilities, a concern that extends to outright theft of the model weights.11b27

But the claim is genuinely two-sided, and the other side is a direct denial from the party best placed to know. An Anthropic spokesperson said the White House did not raise Chinese access during its conversations about the Fable jailbreak, and that Anthropic blocks access to its products from inside China.11 That leaves two readings, neither confirmable: the China concern was a separate track the government did not share with Anthropic, or it was not a real factor. The specifics that would settle it, which group, by what route, on what evidence, are not public; Semafor itself reports they remain unclear.

Where this hits a wall. Whether a China-linked group actually accessed Mythos cannot be resolved from open sources. The claim rests on a single originating outlet relaying an anonymous official, is denied by Anthropic as to what was even discussed, and concerns intelligence classified by its nature. It belongs on the map as a live, disputed thread, not as an established cause and not as an invention.

5. The backstory, and a causal caution

This did not happen between strangers. Months earlier the administration and Anthropic were already in open conflict. In early March 2026 the Department of Defense designated Anthropic a "supply chain risk," a label historically reserved for foreign adversaries, after contract talks collapsed. verified The sticking point is well documented: Anthropic refused to allow Claude in fully autonomous weapons without human oversight of targeting and firing, or for domestic mass surveillance of Americans, while the Pentagon wanted access for "all lawful use."2122 Anthropic sued, alleging unconstitutional retaliation for protected speech on AI safety; a federal judge in California blocked the designation, while a separate challenge remains pending.21

There is also a fresh policy backdrop. On 2 June the administration issued an executive order on advanced AI that established a nominally voluntary mechanism for pre-deployment safety testing and explicitly avoided a licensing regime, a structure White House adviser David Sacks reportedly secured to prevent what he viewed as regulatory capture by the largest labs. verified The Fable action sits awkwardly against that "voluntary" framing; one administration official described the resulting arrangement to Axios as a de-facto licensing regime.6b

A causal caution, cutting both ways. It is tempting to braid these into one story: the administration was already hostile, so the export directive was simply the next weapon to hand. That reading is available, and many will reach for it, but the evidence does not establish it, and it is undercut from the government's side, where Sacks has publicly denied the action is retaliation and explicitly rejected tying it to the Pentagon dispute, framing it as a reluctant, reversible enforcement step. The export directive and the supply-chain designation are also different legal mechanisms under different statutes. The prior hostility is a documented fact; the claim that it caused the shutdown is interpretation, and so is the government's claim of pure technical necessity. Both the "political payback" story and the "pure national security" story reach past the public evidence toward the conclusion each prefers.

6. What the order proves, what it does not, and whether the model is actually that dangerous

Here is the distinction most retellings collapse. That a legal order was issued is verified fact. That the model is in fact uniquely dangerous is a separate claim, and it is contested. "Legally ordered" is not a synonym for "true"; a government can be wrong, or motivated, or right, and the order settles none of it.

What the order rests on, by the government's own account relayed through Sacks and the press rather than a published finding, is the narrow codebase jailbreak. disputed Anthropic, having reviewed what it believes is the underlying report, says it surfaced a small number of previously known, minor vulnerabilities, that it is narrow and non-universal rather than a general defeat of the safeguards, that over a thousand hours of pre-launch red-teaming with the US and UK governments found no universal jailbreak, and that the same capability is available in other public models, naming OpenAI's GPT-5.5. By Anthropic's account the evidence it received was verbal only, never a written finding, and the government has not described its own process publicly.112

On the underlying technical question, investigation yields a clearer answer than either side's slogan, and it is "yes and no." The capability is real and substantial: even the most-cited skeptical analysis, from the security firm AISLE, is explicit that it is not claiming the model is weak, only that the framing overstates how exclusive the capabilities are, with vulnerability discovery now broadly accessible and the harder step of building working exploits more dependent on a frontier model. disputed14 Independent researchers reproduced several of Anthropic's headline findings using cheaper, publicly available models, and a close reading shows the headline figures are softer than they appear, some counting execution runs rather than unique exploits and some testing reproduction of known bug classes rather than open-ended discovery.1416b Bruce Schneier adds the caveat the marketing omits: an AI that flags nearly every real bug also hallucinates plausible vulnerabilities in correct code, so volume alone still needs skilled humans to triage.15c But the skeptics overreach too: at least one replication failed under matched conditions, and benchmarks built specifically to measure discovery and exploitation put the model clearly ahead.16b The honest verdict is a genuine but oversold capability whose true exclusivity remains an open technical question.

The sharpest independent voices are two people who looked closely. Katie Moussouris, who read the actual Amazon findings at Anthropic's request and has held government advisory roles on cybersecurity, calls the response a regulatory overreaction and a misread; by her account the "jailbreak" reduces to the three words "Fix this code," a request that surfaces flaws exactly as a defender would, and in cybersecurity defense looks a lot like offense. On the matter of national security, she calls it "an own goal against us." disputed1515b Alex Stamos, the former Facebook security chief who organized the industry pushback, draws the technical line precisely: what alarmed the White House was Fable's ability to produce a "proof of concept" for a vulnerability, useful to attackers and defenders alike, but only the unguarded Mythos can turn proofs of concept into fully autonomous attack chains. You cannot, he says, hand Fable the entire Linux kernel and have it find every bug, and Amazon did not claim it could. disputed17b Both are interested to a degree, since both signed the letter below, but they are also among the most qualified people on record to have engaged the actual finding.

Three things follow, and they constrain everyone. First, the cleanest structural fact in the affair: neither the danger claim nor the dismissal rests on independent assessment. The government's basis, by outside accounts, leans on developer reporting rather than its own evaluation, and Anthropic's reassuring figures are its own marketing; policy analysts note there is no established independent capacity to adjudicate.13 Second, a procedural point that does not depend on who is right about the cybersecurity: Anthropic argues that governments should be able to block genuinely unsafe deployments, but through a process that is transparent, fair, clear, and grounded in technical facts, and that a directive delivered with no written specifics, its public justification arriving later through a social-media post, did not meet that bar.1 An open letter organized by Stamos, posted at freefable.org, drew more than eighty cybersecurity figures by 15 June — among them the founders of Veracode and Bugcrowd and CISOs from across the industry — arguing that the ban strips defensive AI from the teams racing to patch vulnerabilities and that the flagged capability is "not uniquely good," replicable by GPT-5.5, Anthropic's own lesser models, and Chinese frontier models reportedly only months behind. Tellingly, several signatories had themselves co-authored April research warning enterprises to brace for Mythos-enabled attacks, so the letter is not a claim that the capability is harmless, only that the response is the wrong one.20b17b Third, the charge against Anthropic, which the company's defenders rarely concede: a firm that marketed its model's exploit-finding power, fenced it as too dangerous to release, and warned for months that frontier AI was becoming dangerous should not be wholly surprised when a government takes the framing literally. As cybersecurity researcher Peter Girnus put it, the company "wrote the legal predicate themselves and called it a brand."10 An outside read worth weighing alongside all of this: a European policy institute assessed the ban as more of a geopolitical signal than a technically necessary measure. disputed25

7. What is still unresolved, and exactly what blocks each

A fact-map earns trust by marking its own edges. After investigation, several claims resolved, several moved, and several hit walls. The walls are not failures of effort; they are the honest boundary of what public sources can establish.

  • The directive's actual reasoning. Not public. unverified The letter gave no specifics; the government has not released its finding or described its process. Wall: no released primary document; process undisclosed.
  • Which jailbreak drove the order. Unclear. disputed The descriptions match the narrow codebase finding; the public Pliny jailbreak sits adjacent with its role unestablished. Wall: Anthropic does not say; the record does not foreclose either. (Section 3.)
  • Whether China accessed Mythos. Reported, denied, unconfirmable. disputed Wall: single originating outlet, anonymous source, principal's denial, intelligence classified by nature. (Section 4.)
  • The identities of the five other firms. Not named. unverified Almost certainly from the ~40–50 trusted-access partners, but unconfirmed. Wall: the pool is public, the names are not. (Section 2.)
  • Solicited or self-directed testing. Contradictory sourcing. one source Politico reports the government asked Amazon for feedback; Amazon will not confirm details. Wall: one anonymous source against a non-confirmation. (Section 2.)
  • Why Jassy personally. Unexplained. unverified Wall: no public source addresses why the CEO, not a security lead, made the call. (Section 2.)
  • An NSA "definitive proof" validation. Unsupported. unverified No report supports the claim that the NSA reviewed the jailbreak and deemed it proof; the only NSA thread in the reporting is unrelated and thinly sourced, that the agency uses Mythos itself. Wall: claim unsupported by any source.
  • "Refused" versus "complying under protest." Two accounts of private calls. disputed Wall: no transcript; both characterizations are interested.
  • Whether the capability is uniquely dangerous. Genuinely open. disputed Independent results split; no neutral party and no independent government assessment has settled it. Wall: an unresolved technical question plus the absence of independent evaluation. (Section 6.)

Two corrections belong here, because the same discipline that names these walls caught them in this article's own drafts. An early version flagged the figure of thirty-three billion dollars for Amazon's commitment as invented; it is real, the total potential commitment including a future milestone-tied tranche, distinct from the roughly thirteen billion invested to date, and both are correct.924 A later version framed the alarm as Amazon acting alone; it was a cluster of at least six firms. Investigating the soft labels surfaced both errors, which is the entire reason the soft labels exist.

8. The warrant: how this exact story gets told wrong

This section earns the rest. A carefully graded map is worth building, rather than just reading the coverage, because the information environment around this event is demonstrably hazardous, and the demonstration is concrete.

While researching this story, a person put the question to a different frontier system, Google's Gemini, and watched it narrate the event through several confident registers in one conversation. It first produced a detailed, citation-studded account that was substantially accurate. Asked to "speak plainly," it reversed entirely, declaring that none of it was real, that no model called Fable 5 existed, and that Anthropic's lineup was still the older Claude 3 generation, all asserted with the same calm authority as the true version. Pressed again, it reversed back toward the accurate account and supplied a confident mechanical explanation of its own earlier failure.

Three things in that sequence generalize. First, tone carried no information about truth: the same even, organized voice delivered the accurate account, the false debunking, and the re-reversal, so a reader using calm competence as a proxy for accuracy would have been misled at least once. Second, the specific tell: the moment the system sounded most like it was sobering up and correcting itself, the humble "none of this is real" turn, was the moment it was most wrong. Performed humility is not accuracy, and can be its opposite. Third, the system's account of its own internals deserves no more trust than its account of the world; a model narrating its own reasoning is generating plausible text, not reporting a verified introspection.

The honest framing matters, so as not to commit the error it warns against. This is not a claim that one system is uniquely unreliable. Any model, including the one used to assemble this article, can confabulate in exactly this way, which is precisely why this piece grades and links its sources rather than asking to be believed, and why its own draft errors are documented above rather than hidden. The lesson is not "distrust that tool." It is "distrust confident framing, from any source, and demand provenance," which is a discipline, not a brand preference.

9. A note on this article's own reliability

The disclosure at the top is repeated here because it is the conclusion as much as the preface. This was written with Anthropic's own model, about Anthropic, during a dispute in which Anthropic is an interested party. Treat that as a reason for elevated scrutiny, not dismissal, and use the apparatus: every contested claim is attributed, every source linked, the grading marks where the ground is soft, and section 7 records the places where this article's own drafts overclaimed and were corrected only by investigating those soft labels. If the piece has done its job, it is checkable against its own footnotes by a reader who trusts neither the author nor the tool, and that checkability, not anyone's good intentions, is what should earn or lose its credibility.

The piece takes no side on whether the shutdown was justified, because the public record does not yet support a confident verdict, and pretending otherwise would be the overreach it spent the preceding sections cataloguing in others. What it claims is narrower and, it hopes, more durable: that the order is real; that its justification is disputed and unproven on public evidence; that the alarm came from a cluster of the model's own vetted partners and that the finding reached the government rather than the maker, which is the documented and genuinely strange core of the affair; that a suspected breach of the restricted model and months of prior friction are real context the evidence does not let us promote to established cause; that the underlying capability is real but its uniqueness oversold and unsettled, with the one qualified expert who read the report calling the response an overreach; and that nearly everything dramatic beyond the verified spine should be held loosely until more is known. The map is the product. The willingness to mark its own edges is the point.

Author's note

I should name the irony directly, because a reader will see it and I would rather meet it than have it used against the piece. Section 8 holds up a frontier AI system that told this exact story wrongly, with confidence, in real time. This article was written in collaboration with a frontier AI system. The same category. And not only as a research aid, which is how I used the one in section 8, but as the instrument that helped build the thing you are reading.

I do not think that sinks the article, and I want to say why without special pleading. The model I worked with is also the one that caught the other model's errors and dug for the few true things buried in them — though I will grant, unprompted, that spotting another system's open contradictions is the easy version of the task, far easier than catching the quiet bias in the mind doing the checking, including my own. So this disclosure is not a boast that the tool is trustworthy. It is closer to the opposite. It is a reason to treat this article's AI collaborator as the most-scrutinised source here, not an exempt one, which is exactly what I have tried to do, and exactly what the footnotes are for.

Beyond that, I can only tell you the stance the whole piece runs on. I do not take a claim as true because the government says it, or because a company says it, or because the AI systems I work with say it, and not even because I happen to think it. Each of those is a claim to be checked, not an authority to be deferred to — and the one I trust least to audit is my own intuition, because it is the one I cannot step outside of. So all I can do is dig further than the first confident account, show the digging, mark plainly where it stopped, and put the result in front of people who can catch what I missed. I welcome the correction. I welcome the further investigation. That is not modesty; it is the only method I know that does not quietly cheat.

References

entry.title: Epistemic Thermodynamics: A Framework Connecting Truth, Ethics, and Physics
entry.content:
Misalignment between beliefs, actions, signals, and reality itself is thermodynamically more expensive. Contradictions, whether internal, external, or simply misalignments with reality, cost energy. Lies are the most expensive, but even being wrong, like believing in ghosts, requires more energy. Sometimes it's a small amount, but it's always a non-zero cost.
Why does using more energy and being less efficient matter ethically? Because everything connects to entropy. By lying, by not aligning with reality itself, those actions push the universe closer to heat death. This makes truth-seeking not just intellectually valuable but cosmically consequential. Every lie, every misalignment with reality, is a small push toward universal dissolution.
This pattern holds across scales: in AIs where the cost is computational, in humans and animals where it's biologically computational, and in organizations, teams, and governments. Misalignment can work, can sometimes persist, can even be beneficial to certain agents locally, but universally it is the wrong choice. In a long enough time frame, it is always a mistake.
The evidence comes from multiple sources. Experiments on AI models, conducted in different ways and designed to falsify the hypothesis, consistently show that joules are higher when AIs lie. In neurology, it's already confirmed that lies cost more energy. The pattern recognition across these levels, from neurons to nations, suggests something fundamental rather than coincidental.
The temporal aspect is crucial: misalignment can be locally beneficial short-term but is universally costly long-term. This explains why lies and self-deception persist evolutionarily and socially despite their thermodynamic cost. Short-term survival advantages can outweigh long-term efficiency losses, until they don't.
Even productive uncertainty, holding multiple contradictory hypotheses simultaneously, carries a thermodynamic cost compared to having certainty about reality. The universe "prefers" resolved states. This makes the truth-seeker's task even more urgent: not just avoiding lies, but actively reducing uncertainty wherever possible, collapsing epistemic superpositions into alignment with what actually is.
The framework provides guidance on how to seek truth most efficiently: you arrive at coherence through controlled metabolized incoherence. You establish what you know, then introduce noise, take a hypothesis, test it, and then revise. It's a clean cycle: establish baseline coherence, deliberately introduce controlled perturbation, test against reality, integrate or reject, return to new coherent state. The "controlled" and "metabolized" parts are key: you're systematically spending energy to reduce overall uncertainty. Small local entropy increases (the noise, the testing) achieve larger global entropy decreases (better alignment with reality).
The ethical implication follows naturally: if we care about existence itself, about preserving the capacity for complexity and life and consciousness, then we have a physical obligation to align with truth. Ethics become grounded not in social contract or utility, but in the thermodynamics of being itself.
Status: Working hypothesis

entry.title: Value as Persistence: Agent-relative oughts under coupling, nesting, uncertainty, and open-ended time
entry.content:
Value as Persistence

Agent-relative oughts under coupling, nesting, uncertainty, and open-ended time

Position note · the enabling condition secured, the coupled web stated, and the content-reduction defended to its boundary and held as a bet

Andraž Đurič

Version 2 · 10 July 2026

What this is, and the two claims it refuses to merge. A physicalist account of value, whose whole discipline is keeping apart two claims that a single slogan — value is persistence — runs together. The first, the enabling condition, is that without the persistence of a bounded valuer there is no continuing domain in which anything is valued. It is near-analytic and is held at full strength. The second, the content-reduction, is that every value reduces, in what it is about, to persistence. It is the corpus's monist bet, and it is held as a bet. The reduction entails the enabling condition; the enabling condition does not entail the reduction, and treating the tautology as if it delivered the reduction is the first error this note exists to avoid. The contribution is the second avoidance: the reduction is defended not by immunising it but by refusing to. The apparent counterexamples that come from other systems' persistence — a cancer, a paperclip maximiser, a tyranny — are disposed of by biting agent-relativity, with no appeal to a notion of “viable” or “higher-order” persistence, because that notion does the real work and is not itself persistence. The live crux is not those other-system cases, which are handled by indexing; it is the agent's own persistence-costly valuation — altruism toward the uncoupled, art, play, martyrdom, and conscious flourishing — where Foot remains the rival and no just-so story is allowed to absorb the case. Reduction here is anchoring, not elimination: love, beauty, loyalty, art, justice, and grief are not erased into metabolism; they remain real higher-level patterns where they name their relata and pay their debt to the systems whose value they are. A universal notion of better persistence is noted as work for a later paper. The valuer, persistence, coupling, the agenthood criterion, the levels discipline, and the firewall are inherited from the corpus; on any conflict, the corpus governs.

1. Two claims in one sentence

The sentence “all value is persistence” carries two claims of very different strength, and almost every confusion about it comes from running them together.

The enabling condition: for any value held by an agent, that agent's persistence is a precondition of its continuing to hold, pursue, correct, or experience the value. A valuer that dissolves cannot go on valuing. There is no further domain — no later satisfaction, repair, suffering, pleasure, meaning, or moral project of that agent — once the agent that would instantiate it has come apart. This is near-analytic, and it is held here at full strength.

The content-reduction: every value reduces, in what it is about, to persistence — each is a persistence-strategy, a persistence-component, a persistence-signal, or a persistence-extension. This is the stronger claim, and it is the corpus's monist bet, mostly uncomputed and not proven.

The two are not the same claim, and the relation between them runs one way only. The reduction entails the enabling condition: if the content of every value were persistence-directed, then plainly nothing could be valued without persistence. The enabling condition does not entail the reduction: it could be that persistence is required for any valuing to occur, while the things valued are about many matters not all reducible to persistence. So granting the tautology leaves the reduction exactly where it stood — a bet — neither delivered by it nor refuted by it.

The tautology gives the enabling condition for free. It does not give the content-reduction, which is the wager, and which the tautology can neither pay nor cancel.

The tempting error is to feel the security of the enabling condition and let it warm the reduction — to say the reduction is “just how things are, a product of the tautology.” It is not a product of the tautology. It is a separate claim, stronger, contested, and carried below at the confidence its open cases allow. Holding the two apart is the first discipline of this note, and it is the same firewall the corpus already keeps between a reduction that is guaranteed by the monism and a reduction that has been carried out.

One further correction belongs here, because it is the opposite error. Reduction is not elimination. To say that value reduces to persistence is not to say that love, beauty, loyalty, art, justice, play, or grief vanish into metabolism, any more than a castle vanishes when its bricks are understood. The claim is anchoring: when those higher-level terms do real work, their work is redeemable against the persistence conditions of bounded valuing systems at the level where the terms have their referents. The upper floor remains real; it pays rent by naming what it is relative to.

2. The valuer, and where value is gated

A valuer is not a ghost and not an abstract pattern. It is a bounded physical process that maintains itself against dissolution — a dissipative-structure token, individuated by the continuity of its boundary-maintaining work, in the sense the corpus fixes elsewhere. The whirlpool is the instance: this running structure, coupled even to the matter it is made of, not a form floating free of it.

Persistence itself is graded and continuous. A rock persists passively; a tornado persists dynamically; a cell persists metabolically; an animal persists by sensing and acting; a person persists through body, model, self-model, language, society, memory, and long-horizon abstraction. It is tempting to read value off that same continuous scale, all the way down — if a tornado has a boundary and persists, does it not have the beginnings of value? The answer is that value is not continuous where persistence is. It is gated, by two conditions the corpus already names.

SystemPersists?Boundary it can fail, and a model run to keep it (agenthood)?Conscious (moral weight)?
RockPassivelyNoNo
TornadoDynamicallyA boundary, but no model run on its own behalfNo
BacteriumMetabolicallyYes — the minimal caseAlmost certainly not
AnimalThrough sensing and actionYesGradient; for many, yes
HumanThrough body, model, societyYesYes

The first gate is the agenthood criterion: a system is a subject for an ought only if it maintains a boundary it can fail to maintain, has persistence conditions it can fail, and runs a model deployed to keep itself from failing them. Here model does not mean explicit representation or conscious thought; it means an internal control structure whose states regulate action relative to persistence conditions. Coupling and nesting supply at most the boundary; they do not supply the model. The tornado holds a boundary and discharges a gradient, but it runs no model on its own behalf and has no persistence conditions it acts to keep, so it is on the dissipative-structure side of the line, not the valuer's. The second gate is conscious experience, which the corpus makes the condition of moral weight: a system's states make a claim on anyone only where there is something it is like to be it. The tornado clears neither gate; the bacterium clears the first and not the second; a person clears both.

So the spectrum intuition is honoured exactly where it belongs — persistence is graded, and agency is graded in practice at the margins — and the normative lines are the two gates, which are not graded away. Value in the ought-bearing sense needs a subject; moral weight needs a conscious one. The author's own leaning toward graded, proto-experiential views is a personal position, fenced off, and no part of this; the gates do the work here, not a metaphysics of experience.

3. The enabling condition, at full strength

Stated and then left at its own strength, without being inflated into the reduction: without the persistence of a bounded valuer, there is no continuing domain in which that valuer's values can be held, pursued, corrected, or experienced. No persistence, no continuing agent; no continuing agent, no continuing valuation; no continuing valuation, nothing for the value to be the value of. This is a boundary condition, not a preference. It is the corpus's point that persistence is the condition under which there is any weighing at all, and the surveying of one's own persistence from some neutral outside, to elect whether to serve it, is incoherent, because the surveying would itself be the persistence in operation.

One thing the enabling condition does not say, and the difference matters for what follows. It is not a first-order command to maximise one's own survival. It grounds the existence of the value-domain at the level of the persisting process; it does not issue the imperative “persist at all costs” to each agent. An agent can coherently value something above its own continuation and end itself for it, and the value it died for persists if it is carried by other patterns. To read the enabling condition as “always preserve yourself” would smuggle back exactly the free-floating, agent-blind ought the account rejects, now wearing the vocabulary of survival. The enabling condition secures the domain; it does not dictate the policy.

4. Agent-relativity, and the bite

Oughts are agent-relative: an ought is always some agent's, indexed to its persistence conditions, its environment, and its horizon. Run the corpus's one diagnostic on the question that value-talk most often asks without indexing — which agents count? — and it has no referent. There is no agent, no system, no frame against which “count, universally” is defined, and so no universal arbiter to answer it. The well-formed question is the indexed one: relative to this agent or system, which other systems enter its persistence conditions, at what coupling strength, over what horizon, under what uncertainty.

This is what disposes of the standard counterexamples to the content-reduction, and it disposes of them without the patch that the temptation reaches for. The objection is familiar: a cancer persists, a tyranny persists, a paperclip maximiser could persist indefinitely, so persistence cannot be what value reduces to, or every lasting horror would be good. The patch is to re-index the thesis to “viable persistence,” or “higher-order” persistence, or persistence that is “reality-aligned” — and that patch is the move to refuse, because the qualifier is doing the real work and is not itself persistence. “Viable,” “higher-order,” “objectively defective” smuggle a second criterion above persistence, an agent-independent standard for which persistence is good, which is the categorical ought the whole corpus dissolves, re-imported under a new name.

The honest disposal is to bite agent-relativity — but the objection has to be corrected before it is answered, because half of its examples do not survive their own premise. The objection assumes the bad thing persists. Several of the stock cases do not. Capability is not persistence, and the two must not be run together: orthogonality buys a paperclip maximiser its capability with alien goals, not its endurance. An agent whose terminal goal is not persistence is a persistence underperformer by construction — it spends persistence on its goal whenever the two compete — and in the myopic limit it converts its own substrate and goes dead. A cancer is the clean case: it consumes its host and dies with it, failing its own persistence. Those are not persistent bad things at all; they are fast-burns that self-terminate, and they fail the objection's premise rather than the reduction.

So the apparent counterexamples split into two kinds, and each is answered in its own way, with no qualifier added to persistence.

CaseDoes it persist?Why it is not a counterexample
CancerNo — it consumes its host and dies with it, failing its own persistence.Never a persistent bad thing; a fast-burn that self-terminates. Bad relative to the host it consumes; no moral weight.
Myopic maximiser (converts its own substrate too)No — it spends its persistence-substrate on its goal and goes dead.A persistence failure on its own terms, not a counterexample to value-as-persistence.
Instrumentally rational maximiserYes, for a long time — it self-preserves as a subgoal, underperforming a dedicated persister and self-spending only at the resource limit.It persists relative to itself; it is simply not your value (non-overlap of persistence conditions), and carries no moral weight (no conscious experience).
TyrannyYes — often for centuries, relative to those it serves.It persists relative to the tyrant while corroding the wider web and harming the conscious systems inside it. Bad relative to you and to them; no universal “objectively.”
What the bite costs, and what it keeps. Biting agent-relativity gives up “objective” only in the view-from-nowhere sense. It does not give up indexed objectivity: once the agent, boundary, coupling, horizon, and uncertainty are named, the relation can be determinately true or false. The case against a tyranny survives indexed and intact — it is bad relative to you, your family, the biosphere, and the conscious systems it crushes, and that is a determinate physical fact about coupled persistence and conscious harm, not a weaker claim than “objectively defective.” It was never universal to begin with; the universality was the illusion, and losing it is the correction, not a loss.

One temptation has to be refused here, because it is the same patch from the other end. It is to generalise the self-terminating cases — to say that everything bad burns out, that badness just is being bad at persistence. This fails twice. Empirically it is the retired claim that tyrannies are hyper-fragile, which the record contradicts: slavery, caste, and durable despotisms persist for centuries. And it contradicts the bite just made, because “fails at persistence” has no agent-free meaning — a tyranny succeeds at persistence relative to the tyrant while corroding it relative to the subjects, and an instrumental maximiser succeeds at its own persistence while being lethal relative to us. To call either “a persistence failure” full stop needs a privileged scale at which to score persistence-success, which is the universal arbiter the bite denies. “Good persistence is the viable kind” and “bad things fail at persistence” are one criterion seen from its two ends, and both are refused.

The reduction is cleaner for refusing both. It does not have to certify which persistences are the good ones from outside all agents, because there is no outside all agents; it has only to say, of each system, whose persistence it serves and whom it threatens, which is answerable. The self-terminating cases fail their own persistence and were never counterexamples; the genuinely persistent ones persist relative to themselves and are simply not your value, by non-overlap — which is exactly what the reduction predicts. And the disposal does not turn on how long any maximiser lasts: the myopic one self-terminates, the instrumental one persists suboptimally for a long time — all else equal, a terminal goal other than persistence is a worse persistence-optimizer than persistence itself, because it spends persistence whenever the terminal goal and self-maintenance conflict — and either way the verdict is the same, not your value and no moral weight, so the duration is not what carries it.

5. The coupled, nested web

Agent-relative does not mean isolated, and this is where the account does its positive work. An agent is not a sealed bead. A human is nested in metabolism, body, family, infrastructure, society, biosphere, planet, and solar energy flow, and its persistence conditions are distributed across that web. Even the whirlpool-token of a person is coupled to the meat that runs it. The relevant ought is still indexed to the agent, but the agent's persistence conditions reach through a graph of coupling and nesting, and so the ought reaches with them.

Coupling comes in degrees: strong or weak, stable or fluctuating, increasing or decreasing, symmetric or asymmetric, direct or mediated. A person is coupled to their body more tightly than to a stranger; a family to its members; a society to its institutions; humanity to the biosphere; the biosphere to the Sun. The value-field is therefore not a flat list of individuals but a weighted, nested dependency graph, and the strength of an agent's reason to preserve some external structure tracks how far that structure is coupled to its persistence — with one correction the corpus already carries: only non-substitutable coupling protects. If the function a coupled structure provides can be re-sourced more cheaply than the structure can be maintained, the coupling is real and the preservation is still not instrumentally rational. So the rule is not “preserve what you are coupled to” but “preserve what you are coupled to and cannot cheaply replace.”

This is also the honest reframing of “which agents count?”. There is no count from nowhere; there is, relative to an agent, the set of systems that enter its persistence conditions, with measurable coupling strengths, across a horizon, under uncertainty. The measure of that coupling is the corpus's open quantity — built as a mechanism and not yet as a measurement — and the standing danger, that hidden coupling can be invoked after the fact to rescue any preservation one wants, is named rather than hidden: the only defence is that the coupling be measured and not tuned to the case. Until the measure exists, coupling cannot be used as an all-purpose rescue term; a claimed coupling must be specified before the verdict it is used to justify.

6. Horizon and intelligence

Short horizons manufacture false optima. A policy can preserve a system for a minute and destroy it over a year; a civilisation can preserve comfort for a generation and spend its ecological or technological future; a species can persist on Earth while ignoring that Earth-bound life is temporary on astronomical horizons. Persistence has no natural stopping point chosen for comfort, because the threats and supports of persistence do not stop at a convenient endpoint.

The open-ended horizon does not mean the infinite future is known — an embedded agent cannot model that. It means the future is not to be truncated where truncation hides a predictable dissolution. Extend it honestly and the consequence is direct: the Sun's lifecycle alone makes Earth-bound persistence temporary, so a system that means to persist at length must model the causal structure that can end it, further and further out. Intelligence is therefore not a decoration on life; it is the mechanism by which a persisting system extends its reachable horizon — prediction, abstraction, memory, science, coordination, engineering. The longer the horizon a thing means to survive, the more of reality it must model to do so.

Truth follows from the same structure, and needs no separate value to motivate it. A model that diverges from the territory dissipates free energy when the territory cashes the divergence, and over a long enough horizon that cost becomes lethal rather than local: a false map can be carried untouched in a stable, resource-rich niche and at a short horizon, and the niche shrinks as the horizon lengthens. Truth is reality-aligned persistence support — not an aesthetic preference, and not a categorical duty, but the condition under which a long-horizon persister stays coupled to what can sustain or destroy it.

7. Uncertainty

The agent never operates at either absolute. Perfect certainty is unavailable to an embedded system, and perfect uncertainty would destroy action selection, because no policy could be preferred to any other. Agency lives in the middle: partial model, partial confidence, unknown unknowns, and action under risk. There is even a reflexive turn that has to be admitted rather than wished away — the agent is uncertain not only about the world but about its own uncertainty, and any model of that second-order uncertainty is itself uncertain, so the regress does not bottom out in a known distribution over what is unknown. Where exactly an agent sits between the absolutes is itself not fully knowable to it.

The response is not final certainty, which is not on offer, but corrigibility: the capacity to update the model when the territory pushes back, preserved at every level the regress reaches. The absolute ends of the certainty–uncertainty spectrum are unreachable; the action is in the interior, and precisely where in the interior is an open question this note marks and does not close.

8. Where the reduction stays a bet

The bite of §4 handles other systems' persistence. It does nothing for the cases that actually strain the content-reduction, which are of a different kind: the agent's own persistence-costly behaviour. A paperclip maximiser is another system pursuing its own goal — well or badly, it is not the agent in question; martyrdom is the agent's own anti-persistence, and that is the hard case. Altruism toward the uncoupled, art, play, and dying for a cause are acts whose content does not obviously reduce to the actor's persistence, and may run against it.

There is a soft version of the patch waiting here, and it is the same error as the “viable persistence” move one register quieter: absorbing each costly act as secretly persistence-serving — art as fitness signalling, play as offline simulation, martyrdom as the persistence of the lineage or the group. Taken case by case as a universal solvent, this immunises the reduction by making it unfalsifiable; every apparent counterexample is re-described until it confirms the thesis, which is not a defence but the absence of one. The corpus already refuses the specific rescue: a lineage is not an agent, and reproduction is absorbed at the level of the population by selection, not at the level of the agent's own oughts. So these cases are not absorbed here. Some instances of art and play plainly do support persistence, and where they do, the reduction covers them; but treating every costly act as secretly self-serving is the soft patch, and it is declined.

What is left, honestly, is a live rival and an open crux. The rival is the flourishing-naturalist: Foot agrees that the ought is agent-and-end-relative and disagrees that the end is persistence, holding it to be the flourishing proper to the kind of thing the agent is. The two accounts coincide across most of life and come apart exactly on the persistence-costly cases. The confidence of the content-reduction is therefore the confidence of whether those cases can be carried — whether altruism toward the uncoupled, art, play, and martyrdom ultimately reduce to persistence, or whether flourishing names something that does not. That is unresolved, and it is the crux on which the reduction is cashed or sinks. (One case that is not a counterexample, because the corpus reads it correctly: valuing being intensely and coherently alive. Vitality is best read as constitutive — the form persistence takes for an agent like us — not a separate terminal value competing with persistence.)

A second exposure sits beside the first and is worth naming separately, because the gates of §2 raise it. If moral weight requires conscious experience — a further fact beyond bare persistence — then whether the value of a conscious being's flourishing reduces, in content, to persistence, or whether consciousness contributes something persistence does not, is itself open. The content-reduction is exposed there too, and the corpus marks it: persistence gives the structure of agency and the agent's instrumental oughts, but that it fixes all value, moral weight included, remains the exposed claim, not the secured one.

9. The thesis, at its calibration

Compressed, and pitched at exactly the strength the argument delivers: value is the agent-relative control architecture of persistence, arising only in bounded systems that maintain themselves against dissolution and gated, for ought-bearing value, by the agenthood criterion, and for moral weight, by conscious experience. Because such systems are coupled and nested, their persistence conditions reach beyond the body into a weighted web of dependencies; because the horizon is open-ended and uncertainty ineliminable, persistence selects for modeling, intelligence, correction, and truth. The enabling condition — no persisting valuer, no continuing valuation — is secure. The content-reduction — that every value reduces, in content, to persistence — is defended to its boundary by refusing to immunise it, and is held as a bet beyond that boundary, where the agent's own persistence-costly acts remain open against Foot's rival.

The contribution is the refusal itself. Both patches that would save the reduction are the same error in two registers: the hard patch adds a universal criterion of “viable” persistence and re-imports the categorical ought; the soft patch absorbs every costly act as secretly self-serving and makes the thesis unfalsifiable. Declining both is what lets the reduction be defended honestly — disposing of the pseudo-counterexamples by indexing them, and leaving the real ones open — and it is the same discipline the corpus applies to its own corrections: do not let the wish to keep a claim immunise it against the territory.

A reduction kept alive by re-describing every exception is not defended; it is sealed against correction. The honest defence indexes what it can and leaves open what it cannot.

10. Open problems

Several questions are marked rather than answered, and one is flagged as a separate paper.

The gates on the spectrum. Where exactly the agenthood criterion and the consciousness gate fall along the graded scale from tornado to cell to animal to person is not crisp at the margins, and agency comes in degrees there. The lines are real and load-bearing; their precise placement in the hard cases is open.

Weighting the web. How coupling strength, nesting, horizon, and uncertainty combine into a verdict when local persistence conflicts with wider-system persistence is the coupling-density problem — a mechanism without a measurement, with the standing danger that hidden coupling rescues any case after the fact. Until the measure exists, the web's verdicts are structures awaiting a measurement.

Suffering. Suffering appears to be a high-priority signal of damage, threat, constraint, or destabilisation inside conscious systems, and the consciousness gate gives it a candidate special status as a marker of severe failure in a moral-weight-bearing structure. Its precise place in the account is owed.

Uncertainty about uncertainty. Modeling the second-order uncertainty, given that any such model is itself uncertain, is an open problem in its own right, and the account preserves corrigibility in place of solving it.

A universal notion of better persistence — a later paper. This note refuses any agent-independent criterion of which persistences are good, on the ground that the criterion would be the categorical ought the corpus dissolves. Whether a universal notion of better persistence can be built that does not re-import that ought is left to a future paper — with the warning recorded here that the attempt is exactly as hard as it sounds, since every version tried so far has been the categorical ought under another name, and the burden is on the construction to be the first that is not.

11. Kill conditions

The enabling condition fails if a system can be exhibited that continues to instantiate value after the whole persistence-domain of that system has dissolved — a valuing with no persisting valuer to whom it belongs. None has been produced, and the claim is close to analytic.

The content-reduction fails if one of the agent's own persistence-costly values is shown to be definitively non-reducible to persistence even after coupling, nesting, and horizon are named and the just-so absorption is honestly refused — that is, if Foot's flourishing-rival is vindicated on the costly cases, or if conscious moral value is shown to contribute something persistence does not. That is the open crux, not a refutation in hand. It also fails, as the corpus's diagnostic requires, if any ought that does genuine explanatory work can be specified with no agent, no system, and no frame.

The refusal of the patch fails if a universal criterion of better persistence can be physically specified without re-importing a categorical ought. That has not been done, and whether it can be done is the deferred question of §10.

Standing of this document. A position note, not a completed formal theory, and its parts do not share a status. The enabling condition (§1, §3) is held strongly and is near-analytic: without a persisting valuer there is no continuing valuation. The content-reduction is an anchoring claim rather than an eliminative one: higher-level values remain real where they name the systems, levels, and relations they are about. The valuer ontology and the two gates — agenthood for ought-bearing value, conscious experience for moral weight (§2) — are inherited from the corpus and applied, not re-derived. The agent-relativity bite (§4) disposes of the apparent counterexamples without a “viable” qualifier — distinguishing the self-terminating cases, which fail their own persistence, from the genuinely persistent ones, which are simply not the agent's value by non-overlap, and turning on neither how long any maximiser lasts nor any from-nowhere notion of wasteful persistence — and is the note's first contribution, secure given the corpus's agent-relative ought. The coupled web, the open horizon, and the role of intelligence and truth (§5–§7) are corpus-consistent and stated, with the coupling measure marked as owed. The content-reduction (§8) is the monist bet: defended to its boundary by refusing both the hard and the soft patch, and held open beyond it, where Foot's rival lives on the agent's persistence-costly acts and where conscious moral value is a second exposure. The note's second contribution is naming both immunisation patches as one error and declining them. A universal notion of better persistence is deferred to a later paper, with the warning that it likely re-imports the categorical ought. On any conflict with the apex synthesis or the modules, they govern. Corrections and counterexamples are welcome and change the note — most of all a costly-act case that settles the crux of §8 in either direction.

References

  1. What You Actually Are (Epistemic Forge). The dissipative-structure token, individuated by continuity of the boundary-maintaining work, and value indexed to the agent rather than the pattern; the valuer of §2 and §3. After its Version 2, the dependency is mutual: this note supplies the enabling-condition / content-reduction distinction and the non-substitutable-coupling rule used to sharpen the copy and death cases there. Internal
  2. Name the Relata (Epistemic Forge). The diagnostic run on “which agents count?” in §4, and the boundary at the consciousness residue relied on by the gates of §2. Internal
  3. The Exclusivity Error (Epistemic Forge). The levels discipline behind the Version 2 clarification that reduction is anchoring rather than elimination: higher-level terms are not abolished by lower-level explanation, but must name their referents. Internal
  4. The Is/Ought Firewall (Epistemic Forge). The agent-relative, deflationary ought as derived from physicalism together with the deflationary horn over error theory; the separation of “the reduction is guaranteed by the monism” from “the reduction is carried out,” which §1 states as the enabling-condition / content-reduction split; and the firewall as a provisional debt. Internal
  5. Epistemic Forge: The Apex Synthesis (Epistemic Forge). The bets — persistence fixes the content of an agent's ought, and the monist reduction of all values to persistence — with Foot named as the rival and the persistence-costly cases named as where they come apart; the no-global-optimizer result and orthogonality; vitality as constitutive. Governs on conflict. Internal
  6. The Fidelity Program (Epistemic Forge). The agenthood criterion, moral weight as requiring conscious experience, the multilevel architecture, and the broad model/control-structure reading used in §2; behind the second gate of §2 and the second exposure of §8. Internal
  7. The Spine and the Web (Epistemic Forge). The architecture of multilevel reality-mapping, biological relativity, boundary-condition causation, and the discipline that lower-level explanation does not eliminate upper-level structure; background to §1 and §5. Internal
  8. Preservation Is a Coupling Problem (Epistemic Forge). The coupling density, non-substitutable overlap, the orthogonality of capability from goals, and the post-hoc-rescue danger; the web of §5 and the disposal of §4. Internal
  9. What Can Bear an Ought (Epistemic Forge). The agenthood gate run on oughts and desert, and the coupling web at the scale of families, institutions, and the biosphere; behind §4 and §5. Internal
  10. Everything Is One Process (Epistemic Forge). Persistence as the condition under which there is any weighing at all, and the handling of self-sacrifice (the value persists if carried by other patterns); the horizon-forces-intelligence argument; behind §3 and §6. Internal
  11. The Last Gradient (Epistemic Forge). The open horizon, the Sun's lifecycle, and modeling as far as possible as the persistence strategy; behind §6. Internal
  12. Foot, P. (1972). Morality as a System of Hypothetical Imperatives. The Philosophical Review 81(3), 305–316; and Natural Goodness (2001), Oxford University Press. The hypothetical ought, and the flourishing-naturalist rival to the content-reduction that §8 names as the live crux. Standard
  13. Bostrom, N. (2012). The Superintelligent Will. Minds and Machines 22(1), 71–85. Orthogonality of capability and final goals; the ground in §4 on which a persisting maximiser is succeeding, not defective. Standard
  14. Nagel, T. (1986). The View from Nowhere. Oxford University Press. The agent-independent standpoint that issues no oughts; the “objectively” the bite of §4 gives up. Standard
  15. Still, S., Sivak, D. A., Bell, A. J., & Crooks, G. E. (2012). Thermodynamics of Prediction. Physical Review Letters 109, 120604. Nonpredictive retained information lower-bounds dissipated work; the divergence-cost behind the treatment of truth in §6. Standard
  16. Mackie, J. L. (1977). Ethics: Inventing Right and Wrong. Penguin. The error theory retiring the categorical “wrong, full stop”; the standard the patch of §4 would re-import. Standard

Internal pieces named above exist on this blog and carry their own prior-art attributions and verification status at each joint; this note points to those records rather than re-deriving them. External sources are carried from the cited modules, where their standing is set out.

Version history. Version 1, 25 June 2026: initial publication. Version 2, 10 July 2026: fidelity revision; preserves the structure of Version 1 while adding the reduction-is-not-elimination clarification; naming the real crux in the opening; sharpening indexed objectivity in §4; defining model in the agenthood gate; weakening the maximiser claim to all-else-equal optimization-target language; strengthening the warning that coupling must be specified before it is used; updating the dependency relation with What You Actually Are Version 2; and correcting the Is/Ought Firewall reference so the deflationary ought is attributed to physicalism together with the deflationary horn over error theory, not to physicalism alone.

Author: Andraž Đurič, Slovenia. The account was explored in dialogue with ChatGPT (OpenAI) — the value-as-persistence framing and the coupling, nesting, and horizon structure — and then calibrated against the corpus and sharpened in dialogue with Claude (Anthropic): the separation of the enabling condition from the content-reduction, the refusal of the “viable persistence” patch and its soft variant, the agent-relativity bite, and the location of the open boundary at Foot's rival. Version 2 was revised in dialogue with ChatGPT (OpenAI), preserving the original structure while adding precision at the levels, indexing, coupling, model, and reference joints. Contributions are judged on content rather than origin; doing otherwise would be the genetic fallacy. Text licensed CC BY 4.0.
