Reference audit: sources and their use in this article were rechecked on 17 August 2026. Primary legal texts, official government records, peer-reviewed research, and first-party methodology statements were preferred. Advocacy sources are identified as such and used for their documented datasets or declared classifications, not treated as institutionally neutral. Track AIPAC’s $14,140,376 figure was independently recomputed from its displayed candidate totals, but the underlying FEC transactions were not independently reconstructed. The mortality rate-equivalents were recalculated from the stated source values. “Rechecked” means attribution, arithmetic, scope, and relevance were inspected; it does not mean every empirical result was independently replicated.

Internal lineage

This article extends the mortality analysis developed in Casualty Analysis: Direct and Indirect Death Tolls in Gaza vs. Ukraine (April 2026). That report separated recorded deaths from mortality estimates and established the scale of Gaza’s human destruction. The present article asks what the prospective 2028 presidential field reveals about the American political machinery sustaining it.

The extension has three parts: translating Gaza mortality into explicit population-equivalent timescales; connecting continued U.S. military support to the emerging presidential field; and locating the field inside the mutually reinforcing structure of mass epistemic failure, concentrated campaign finance, elite policy influence, and concentrated media ownership.

Version history. Version 1, 17 August 2026: initial publication. Candidate classifications and displayed totals audited against Track AIPAC; arithmetic independently recomputed; genocide findings, mortality research, U.S. aid, campaign finance, elite influence, and media-ownership sources checked; rate-equivalent calculations made explicit; scope and standing added.

entry.title: Correction Atrophy: The Epistemic Risk of Decaying Self-Correction
entry.content:
Correction Atrophy

1. The Unnamed Fear

There is a fear almost no one names. It is not the fear of being wrong. It is the fear of losing the willingness to find out that one is wrong.

The fear concerns a specific capacity: the mechanism that detects errors in one's model of reality, weighs disconfirming evidence, and redraws the map. The fear is that this mechanism degrades. Not suddenly, through injury or pathology, but gradually, through disuse, age, and the slow sedimentation of certainty. The compass needle goes sticky. The loop that runs Observe-Predict-Act-Revise skips iterations, then stops.

Call this correction atrophy: the wasting away of the self-correction mechanism. The felt premonition that one's epistemic architecture is stiffening is the rigidity signal.

2. What It Is Not

Correction atrophy is distinct from known fears.

It is not gerascophobia, the fear of aging. Aging fears concern physical decline, lost independence, social irrelevance: fears about the self as a biological and social object. Correction atrophy is a fear about the integrity of one's relationship with reality.

It is not the fear of dementia. Dementia fear is the fear of a diseased brain, of pathological memory loss, of failing to recognize loved ones. Correction atrophy concerns a normative, near-imperceptible process: the hardening of a healthy mind that simply stops seeking disconfirmation. One can score perfectly on every cognitive test and still have ceased to update.

It is not intellectual humility, though it is adjacent. Humility is the recognition that one's knowledge is limited. Correction atrophy is the fear that the mechanism generating that recognition will itself fail. One can be humble today and rigid tomorrow, and the transition may be invisible from the inside.

3. The Mechanism

The brain is a physical system: patterns that are reinforced persist, patterns that are neglected decay. Neuroplasticity is not a fixed resource, and it behaves like a muscle. Used under load, it is maintained. Left idle, it weakens.

Most human environments stop challenging the brain after early adulthood. Careers stabilize. Social circles reinforce existing beliefs. Media consumption narrows to preferred sources. The influx of disconfirming evidence that was unavoidable during formal education drops sharply. Receiving no signal that updating is necessary, the brain lets the capacity for it decay. The model hardens.

This is not a disease. It is the default trajectory. The Consistency Tax, which in a young mind triggers the discomfort of contradiction, can be avoided entirely by no longer exposing oneself to contradiction. Avoidance is cheaper than updating in the short term. Over decades it becomes automatic. The observer goes silent not because it broke, but because it was never called on.

4. Atrophy and Convergence

The diagnosis so far has a hole, and an honest reader will find it. It treats every case of reduced updating as decline. But a mind can update less on a question for two opposite reasons.

One is atrophy: the mechanism has weakened and no longer responds. The other is convergence: the question has been tested enough times that the model is close to correct, and further updating would be error, not virtue. A person who has genuinely examined a belief a hundred times should be harder to move on it than a person meeting it for the first time. That is not rigidity. That is knowing something.

So the bare fact of a stable belief proves nothing. A converged mind and a calcified one can look identical from the outside, and nearly identical from the inside. Both feel certain. Both resist. The distinction is not how much a mind updates. It is what it updates on.

A converged mind still moves on the genuinely new. Present it with evidence it has never processed, an argument outside the set it has already metabolized, a case its model did not predict, and it engages. It can still be surprised. An atrophied mind cannot. It meets the novel with the same closure it brings to the familiar, because the closure is no longer a conclusion drawn from the evidence. It has become a property of the mind.

This is the real test, and the counterforce returns to it. Atrophy is not the absence of updating. It is the loss of response to the new.

5. The Meta-Layer

Correction atrophy is a meta-fear. Not a fear of an object or an outcome, but a fear about the integrity of one's own correction system.

Thermodynamic Realism names the Consistency Tax: the energetic cost of holding contradictory models. The discomfort of dissonance is a signal that the map has diverged from the territory and updating is due. That tax operates in the present tense; it flags current mismatches.

Correction atrophy concerns a different timescale. It is the fear that the tax will stop being collected, not because one's model has become accurate, but because the collection mechanism has been disabled. The compass no longer swings. The system meant to detect error has itself errored out, and there is no higher system to catch the failure.

This is the unsettling part: correction atrophy is self-concealing. A mind that has stopped updating cannot detect that it has stopped, because the detector is the very thing that atrophied. The rigidity signal, if it fires at all, fires in advance: a warning from a still-functional observer about a future in which the observer is silent. It is a fear available only while the capacity remains intact. Once the capacity is lost, the fear goes with it.

This needs one qualification, and an honest reader will supply it. The world does not stop pushing back. Predictions still fail, plans still miss, friction with others still occurs. The atrophied mind is not starved of disconfirming evidence. What fails is upstream of the evidence: the disposition to read a failure as one's own error rather than the world's defect. The signals are not missing. They are arriving and being routed, every time, to the wrong conclusion. That is what makes the failure self-concealing: not an absence of data, but the steady misreading of it.

This is what sets correction atrophy apart from most cognitive failures. They announce themselves. Pain reports injury. Confusion reports a gap. Dissonance reports a contradiction. Each arrives with its own alarm. Correction atrophy is among the rare failures that disable their own alarm. It does not sound a warning. It removes the thing that would. A hazard with no native signal cannot be felt on arrival; it can only be watched for in advance, deliberately, from outside. That is why it is worth a whole essay and not a footnote.

There is one consolation here, and it is not a soft one. If you can feel the rigidity signal, your mechanism still works. The fear is not a symptom of atrophy. It is the immune response to it. A mind that had already hardened would not read this with discomfort. It would read it with the calm certainty that the problem belongs to other people. So the fear and the all-clear are not opposites. For now, the fear is the all-clear. But for now is the entire point. The signal fires early, while there is still a functioning observer to receive it and still time to act. That window is the only one in which maintenance is possible, and it does not stay open by itself.

6. The Counterforce

The counterforce is twofold: the discipline available now, and the tools that may come.

The discipline is internal. Correction atrophy is driven by disuse, so its prevention is use. To maintain the redrawing mechanism, one exposes oneself to disconfirming evidence on purpose, seeks out critique, and practices updating on matters that carry psychological cost. Three questions, asked routinely: What am I wrong about? What haven't I checked? What would change my mind?

This is not natural behavior. The brain evolved for survival, not truth; the default is to protect the model, not test it. Deliberate epistemic maintenance means overriding that default, repeatedly, over decades. It is cognitive hygiene, analogous to exercise: unpleasant in the moment, cumulative in effect, invisible until tested by a crisis. The Observe-Predict-Act-Revise loop is the protocol. It is not only a method for refining models; it is a training regimen for the correction mechanism itself. Every voluntary update reinforces the willingness to update. A brain that practices correction does not harden the way a brain that avoids it does.

But the discipline has a failure mode this essay cannot easily see, and it has to be named. A person can learn to perform updating. The vocabulary of open-mindedness is cheap to acquire. What would change my mind can be asked as a ritual, producing the feeling of rigor without the fact of it. And there is a worse turn. Open-mindedness can harden into an identity. I am someone who updates is itself a belief, and one of the stickiest kinds, because it feels like humility while functioning as pride. The person least able to see their own rigidity is not the obvious dogmatist. It is the one who has built flexibility into a self-concept, because that self-concept resists exactly the disconfirmation that would expose it. An identity organized around updating is still an identity. It defends itself like one. The result is a quiet irony: a mind gone rigid about its own flexibility.

This is why the counterforce cannot rest on willpower. Willpower is among the things that atrophy. A discipline that depends on wanting to seek disconfirmation will fail at the precise moment the wanting fades, and that fading is the disease itself. The durable version is structural. Arrange your life so that disconfirming evidence reaches you whether or not you are in the mood for it. Keep people close who will tell you when you are wrong and are not impressed by you. Work on problems that return verdicts you do not control. Stay in domains where reality grades the answer, not your self-image. The aim is to remove the choice. A mechanism you must choose to run is a mechanism you will, someday, choose not to.

And there is one check that cannot be performed away, because it asks for a fact and not a feeling. Name a specific instance, within the last year, where you lost an argument you cared about and changed your mind. Not a minor revision. A belief with something at stake. If the instance comes readily, the mechanism is live. If it does not, that is the signal, and note where the signal fires from: inside the exact vocabulary meant to prevent the failure. The vocabulary is not the evidence. The instance is.

Biological tools may eventually help. As longevity medicine advances, interventions that support neuroplasticity could become safe and accessible. They would not replace the discipline. A brain with enhanced plasticity still has to practice updating; a brain that never practices will harden regardless of its biochemistry. At best, biological support widens the window the discipline operates in.

Until then, the battle is internal, and awareness is the first weapon. Naming the fear is the act that makes resistance possible. The rigidity signal, once recognized, can be acted on. The observer can be kept awake. The compass can be recalibrated. The map can keep improving for as long as the redrawing mechanism is used.

Correction atrophy is not inevitable. But it is the default. Resistance requires awareness, and awareness requires naming the thing one resists.

Author's Note

I have never met anyone who articulated this fear. I have heard people fear death, decline, irrelevance, dementia. I have not heard anyone say: I am afraid of becoming a person who no longer wants to find out they are wrong. I am afraid of my own mind hardening, not through disease, but through the slow, comfortable abandonment of curiosity.

I am twenty-four. I am nowhere near the age where this is supposed to be a danger. That is not a reason to dismiss the fear. It is the reason it counts. The signal is built to fire early, while the mechanism it warns about is still intact and there is still time to act. A fear of correction atrophy that arrived only after the atrophy would be useless. Mine arrived now, decades early, which is exactly when it is supposed to. I am treating that as the system working, and writing down what it is warning me about while I can still hear it.

Before writing this, I searched. I found fears adjacent but distinct: gerascophobia, dementia anxiety, scattered reflections on becoming closed-minded with age. The closest deliberate treatments come from the rationalist community, which has language for value drift and for the worry of slowly becoming a crank. But those are broader. They track drift in what a person believes or values. None named the specific thing named here, and none located the fear at the level of the correction mechanism itself: the worry is not that my conclusions will drift, but that the faculty which revises conclusions will quietly stop.

This post exists for anyone else who has felt it. You are not the only one. Someone else saw it too. And if the fear has a name, it can be watched. And if it can be watched, it can be resisted.

— Andraž Đurič

This essay was written by Andraž Đurič. The fear it names was first articulated and worked through in conversation with DeepSeek; the draft that opened this revision is where that work left off. Claude (Anthropic) contributed to the later refinement, including the distinction between atrophy and convergence, the identity trap, the structural counterforce, and the closing test, together with line editing throughout.
